title: [parity][bug][regex] POSIX submatch offsets for empty/nullable quantified groups diverge from glibc (drop to [-1,-1] instead of participating empty span)
description:
Found by NEW regex_empty_iter_capture_differential_fuzz (live glibc oracle, ERE concat of {literal,.,group,*,+,?}, NO alternation — isolates submatch capture). The OVERALL match (group 0) agrees with glibc in every case; ONLY the submatch offsets of empty/nullable groups under a quantifier diverge: glibc records the PARTICIPATING empty span [p,p], frankenlibc drops them to [-1,-1].

Confirmed reproducers (ERE; cflags=REG_EXTENDED), glibc vs fl:
  pat=.()*a      sub=ba     glibc g1[1,1]            fl g1[-1,-1]
  pat=(a?)*      sub=.baaa  glibc g1[0,0]            fl g1[-1,-1]
  pat=(a*)*b?    sub=b      glibc g1[0,0]            fl g1[-1,-1]
  pat=((a?b?))*  sub=''     glibc g1[0,0] g2[0,0]    fl g1[-1,-1] g2[-1,-1]
  pat=a(a*)*     sub=.ab    glibc g1[2,2]            fl g1[-1,-1]
  pat=((a*)*a)   sub=abaaa  glibc g1[0,1] g2[0,0]    fl g1[0,1] g2[-1,-1]
  pat=|()        sub=''     glibc g1[0,0]            fl g1[-1,-1]   (alternation empty-capture tiebreak; same class)

ROOT CAUSE: fl's Pike VM (run_from) uses first-thread-priority epsilon-closure + longest-OVERALL-match selection. For an unbounded repeat compiled as 'Split(body,exit); body; Jump(entry)', the loop exit is reached by the ZERO-iteration closure BEFORE the body's Save survives (PC-dedup, first-wins), so an empty iteration's capture is never recorded. This is NOT a simple structural fix: a naive 'post-body split' restructure (entry Split + post-body Split, exit carries post-body slots) DOES record the first empty iteration BUT then a TRAILING empty iteration overwrites a non-empty capture — e.g. '..(b*)+' on 'aabba' regressed to g1[4,4] (glibc keeps g1[2,4]). Proven+reverted this session.

CORRECT POSIX rule (glibc-equivalent): a */+ may take AT MOST ONE empty iteration, and only as the FIRST iteration (no looping on zero progress); a non-empty iteration's capture must NOT be overwritten by a later empty one. Implementing this needs per-thread loop-progress tracking (record sp at loop-body entry; forbid empty re-entry) — a real VM change, not a one-liner. Full glibc parity here is the classic 'POSIX submatch in nested/empty quantified groups' problem.

ORACLE: crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/regex_empty_iter_capture_differential_fuzz.rs (committed #[ignore]d; un-ignore to drive 200k live-glibc cases). Subsumes bd-aedwrn item 4 (.()*a, |()) and generalizes it. Whole-match parity is intact; this is submatch-offset-only.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: PARTIAL FIX shipped (ChartreuseGrove): single-level empty/nullable-group submatch offsets now match glibc via a new RepeatExitGuard NFA instruction + 2 hidden per-loop progress slots (group-start sp, iter-start sp). Unbounded repeat now compiles as Save(Hg-before-min-copies); split; Save(Hi); body; Split(loop,guard); guard=RepeatExitGuard(Hg,Hi); the guard lets an iteration flow to the loop exit (recording its capture) only if it consumed input (sp>Hi) OR the whole repeat is still empty (sp==Hg) — so a genuinely-empty group records [p,p] (.()*a->g1[1,1], (a*)*b? on b->g1[0,0], ((a*)*a) on abaaa->g2[0,0]) while a TRAILING empty never overwrites a non-empty capture (..(b*)+ on aabba keeps g1[2,4] — the case the prior naive post-body-split regressed). Hidden slots bounded out of caller pmatch (regex_exec/regex_exec_bytes copy only (num_groups+1)*2). Committed core unit test empty_iter_submatch_offsets_match_glibc pins all 7 reproducers. NO REGRESSIONS: conformance_diff_regex(8), regex_newline/midpattern/bre_anchor fuzzers, regex_startend, core string(454) all green. STILL OPEN: deeply-NESTED loop-in-loop empty iterations (e.g. (.(b*)*)*, ((a*)+b?)* on bbbb) still diverge in the 200k oracle (re-#[ignore]d with updated note) — the multi-level POSIX disambiguation interaction needs more work. title: [blocker][build] frankenlibc-membrane tests cannot build from a cold cargo home: asupersync-conformance 0.3.4 on crates.io is missing its own include! files
description:
Blocks the membrane half of the bd-aykfv1 sweep. 'cargo test -p frankenlibc-membrane --lib' fails at COMPILE, not at test:

  error: couldn't read .../asupersync-conformance-0.3.4/src/../../artifacts/conformance_registry_contract_v1.json
    --> .../asupersync-conformance-0.3.4/src/reference_registry.rs:12  include_str!(...)
  error: couldn't read .../asupersync-conformance-0.3.4/src/../../src/raptorq/rfc6330_systematic_index_table.inc
    --> .../asupersync-conformance-0.3.4/src/rfc6330_fixtures.rs:189   include!(...)
  error: could not compile asupersync-conformance (lib) due to 2 previous errors

The published .crate does not contain the files its own include_str!/include! reference — they sit outside the packaged src/ tree (../../artifacts, ../../src/raptorq). That is an upstream packaging bug, not a frankenlibc one.

REPRODUCED ON TWO DIFFERENT WORKERS (vmi1227854 and ovh-a), each with a fresh rch cargo home. It is NOT worker-specific luck: any build starting from a cold registry hits it.

WHY IT HAS NOT BEEN NOTICED: abi and core builds have succeeded all session because their target dirs already contain a compiled asupersync-conformance from an older, good copy. Only a cold cargo home re-extracts the broken package. So membrane's unit tests are effectively DARK — the same class as bd-86hcwh, reached by a different route.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY DELETING THE DEPENDENCY. I checked: it is a DEV-dependency (crates/frankenlibc-membrane/Cargo.toml, [dev-dependencies]), membrane's src/ has zero references to it, but examples/killer_demo.rs uses it extensively (asupersync_conformance::{Checkpoint, SuiteResult, write_json_report, logging::...}). Removing it breaks that example, and AGENTS makes asupersync leverage mandatory.

LIKELY FIX, NOT ATTEMPTED HERE: point the workspace dependency at the local companion checkout (AGENTS documents it at /dp/asupersync) instead of the crates.io package, or pin a version whose package actually contains its includes. Both change a workspace-level dependency and affect every remote build, so this wants a deliberate decision rather than a drive-by edit.

DONE = 'cargo test -p frankenlibc-membrane --lib' compiles and runs from a cold cargo home, with its failures then triaged into bd-aykfv1 like the core and abi sweeps.

description:
Found by NEW getopt_long_differential_fuzz (live glibc oracle; reset optind=0 + fresh argv copy per engine — the conformance header's claim that live differential is 'not reliable' is wrong with proper resets). The long-option ABBREVIATION gap is now FIXED (exact-first + unambiguous-prefix with glibc has_arg/flag/val ambiguity rule; see getopt_long_abbreviation_matches_glibc). TWO classes remain (the random fuzz is committed #[ignore]d as the oracle):

1) BARE '-' OPERAND: in default/permute and POSIX modes a bare '-' argv element is a NON-OPTION operand (glibc permutes it / leaves it; never returns it). fl instead (a) returns it as '?' with optopt='-'(45), or (b) consumes it as the required argument of a preceding option. E.g. optstr='f:' argv=['-fval','-','-f']: glibc -> 'f'(val), then '?' optopt='f' (missing arg), operands tail optind=3; fl -> 'f'(val), then 'f' with optarg='-' (WRONG). Also optstr='ob' argv=['-',...] -> fl returns '?' optopt='-'.

2) PERMUTATION INTERMEDIATE optind: with a leading operand, glibc's optind during processing of the permuted options is +1 (points past the operand block) relative to fl, even though the FINAL optind agrees. E.g. optstr='o:o' argv=['operand','-ab']: glibc optind 2,3; fl 1,2 (final 2 for both). Pervasive across operand-before-option cases.

ORACLE: crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/getopt_long_differential_fuzz.rs (un-ignore + re-add the bare '-' token and 'operand' permutation to drive 60k cases). optopt-on-success and longindex-on-error are POSIX-unspecified and normalized out. Fix in parse_getopt_long / the permutation block of unistd_abi.rs.
close_reason: Reimplemented getopt as glibc's PERMUTE exchange model (first_nonopt/last_nonopt cross-call state) in a unified getopt_internal shared by getopt/getopt_long/getopt_long_only; fixes bare-'-' operand handling, required-arg-takes-operand, and intermediate optind. 60k-case getopt_long_differential_fuzz un-ignored (bare-'-' + operand permutation re-added) now 0 divergences vs live glibc.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: INVESTIGATED: the root cause of BOTH remaining symptoms (bare-`-`/operand consumed as required arg, AND intermediate optind off-by-one) is that fl's permutation uses an in-place ROTATION model (rotate next option-block to front of the operand run) whereas glibc uses an EXCHANGE/region model tracking [first_nonopt,last_nonopt). Consequences: (1) a required-arg option rotated in front of an operand wrongly takes that operand as its argument — glibc associates the arg by ORIGINAL position (the element immediately after the option), and reports missing when the option was the last token; (2) optind during permuted processing points PAST the operand region in glibc but at the rotated slot in fl. A pre-permute-before-dispatch patch was tried (fixes the long-option-short-parse optopt=45 case) but it ROTATES a required-arg LONG option in front of its operand and getopt_block_takes_next_arg doesn't understand long options, so blk=1 drops the real arg and the operand becomes the arg (`operand --file val` -> fl optarg=operand vs glibc val). REVERTED. PROPER FIX = reimplement parse_getopt_short permutation as glibc's exchange model (cross-call first_nonopt/last_nonopt state); ~multi-function change on the shared getopt path, needs its own session. Repro: zz_scratch_getopt or un-ignore getopt_long_differential_fuzz + re-add the bare-`-` token.

title: aarch64: raw syscall veneer
description:
aarch64 raw syscall veneer implementation.

Goal: Implement raw Linux syscall interface for aarch64.

Technical Details:
aarch64 syscall convention:
- Syscall number: x8
- Arguments: x0, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5
- Return value: x0
- Error: negative return value
- Clobbered: none (callee-save ABI)

Syscall Numbers:
aarch64 has different syscall numbers than x86_64.
Reference: /usr/include/asm-generic/unistd.h

Key Differences from x86_64:
- No 32-bit compat syscalls
- Different TLS mechanism (TPIDR_EL0)
- Different signal frame layout
- Different function calling convention

Implementation:
1. syscall_veneer.rs for aarch64 target
2. Conditional compilation with cfg(target_arch)
3. Same safe Rust interface as x86_64
4. Inline assembly for syscall instruction

Testing:
- Cross-compile to aarch64
- Test under QEMU user mode
- Compare syscall behavior with x86_64
- Verify error handling

Success Criteria:

title: aarch64: TLS implementation
description:
aarch64 TLS (Thread-Local Storage) implementation.

Goal: Implement TLS mechanism for aarch64.

Technical Details:
aarch64 TLS uses TPIDR_EL0 register:
- Read: mrs x0, tpidr_el0
- Write: msr tpidr_el0, x0

TLS Layout:
- Different from x86_64 (fs: segment)
- Thread pointer points to TCB (Thread Control Block)
- Static TLS follows TCB
- Dynamic TLS uses dtv (Dynamic Thread Vector)

Implementation:
1. Thread pointer read/write primitives
2. TLS initialization during thread creation
3. Static TLS allocation
4. __tls_get_addr for dynamic TLS

Interactions:
- pthread_create must set up TLS
- TLS variables (__thread) must work
- Membrane TLS cache must work

Testing:
- __thread variable access
- pthread_getspecific/setspecific
- TLS across thread boundaries

title: [perf][unresolved] strcasestr vs in-process glibc: two live runs disagree in SIGN on the absent case — no publishable ratio
description:
Requested as a strcasestr bench rebuild + live measure. NO REBUILD WAS NEEDED: crates/frankenlibc-bench/benches/string_inprocess_survey_bench.rs already exists, builds, and is the right shape — core-only (no abi-bench feature, so no fl no_mangle shadowing), with REAL ifunc-resolved in-process glibc arms in the SAME invocation. It surveys strcasestr in two groups.

MEASURED, twice, on rch workers, release profile, 100 samples, 5s measurement time:

  survey_strcasestr            run1 fl 149.52 ns [144.78,153.52]  glibc 71.585 ns [66.221,77.717]  -> fl 2.09x SLOWER
                               run2 fl 143.91 ns [132.99,154.88]  glibc 98.901 ns [92.637,104.80]  -> fl 1.46x SLOWER
  survey_strcasestr_absent60   run1 fl 71.996 ns [71.398,72.742]  glibc 40.079 ns [37.005,43.335]  -> fl 1.80x SLOWER
                               run2 fl 54.375 ns [51.699,56.894]  glibc 63.754 ns [60.093,67.177]  -> fl 1.17x FASTER

NO RATIO IS PUBLISHABLE FROM THIS. The absent60 case FLIPS SIGN between runs. The glibc arm — the harness's own control for machine speed — moved +38% (71.6 -> 98.9) and +59% (40.1 -> 63.8) between runs while fl's arms moved less. A machine that shifts the control that far in minutes cannot resolve a 1.2-2x effect, and quoting either run's number would be manufacturing a result.

WHAT THE TWO RUNS DO AGREE ON: direction for the FOUND case (survey_strcasestr) — fl slower in both, with non-overlapping CIs within each run. Magnitude spread 1.46x-2.09x, so the direction is suggestive and the magnitude is not established.

WHAT IS NEEDED FOR A REAL NUMBER, and none of it was done here:
  1. A pinned quiet cpuset (the fleet quiet-gate keys on the caller's cpuset; unpinned on a shared worker is unwinnable).
  2. An A/A null arm — a byte-identical copy of the fl closure registered between the two real arms. This harness has none. bd-5ibpa3's closure added one to a different harness and found a ~5.6% systematic arm-position effect there, which bounds what any ratio from an unnulled harness can resolve.
  3. Runs interleaved in time rather than back to back, so ambient load cannot alias into the comparison.

CONTEXT WORTH CHECKING WHEN SOMEONE TAKES THIS: several strcasestr optimisation beads are closed as wins — bd-2g7oyh.127 (absent dual-anchor folded first+last byte prefilter) and bd-2g7oyh.6 (absent scan first-byte SIMD candidate probe) both target the absent case that flipped sign here. If a real measurement confirms a loss on that case, those closures need revisiting; if it confirms a win, this bead is just noise. Establish the number first.

DONE = a pinned, A/A-nulled, time-interleaved measurement of both groups with a stated ratio and CI, recorded in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md if it is a loss. Do NOT close this by re-running the same unpinned harness and quoting whichever run looks better.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Epic Notes: Harness Integration (asupersync + frankentui)

### Why This Exists
Runtime math and membrane healing are only valuable if we can:
- reproduce decisions deterministically
- compare behavior vs host glibc and vs our own previous versions
- explain why a decision changed (evidence ledger)

### Hard Constraint
`/dp/asupersync` and `/dp/frankentui` are **tooling only** for glibc_rust. libc runtime must not link them.

### asupersync Role
- deterministic orchestration of conformance scenarios
- traceability primitives and stable virtual time
- scripted injection of corruption/loss patterns for evidence/FEC tests

### frankentui Role
- snapshot/diff oriented output for:
  - RuntimeKernelSnapshot
  - evidence ledger entries
  - raptorq-style decode proofs

### Artifact Contracts (Make It Mechanical)
- `RuntimeKernelSnapshot` capture format must be stable + versioned.
- Harness must be able to:
  - run scenario -> capture snapshot -> diff vs golden -> emit report
  - decode evidence stream offline -> verify -> emit proof + diff

### Definition Of Done
- One-command harness entrypoint produces deterministic report.
- Snapshot schema changes are deliberate (versioned) and show up in diffs.
- Evidence decode/proof output is readable and debuggable.

title: vDSO fastpath: defensive handling for positive rc + cross-arch version strings
description:
Review of time_abi.rs vDSO fastpath (commit 92989d2) flagged two minor issues that don't affect current correctness:

1) In raw_clock_gettime (line 102-105), if vdso_clock_gettime returns an unexpected POSITIVE rc (buggy vDSO or future ABI change), the current code computes set_abi_errno(-rc) which yields a negative errno value. Per POSIX errno must be positive. Fix: guard with rc < 0 check before negating, or treat any non-{0, -ENOSYS} result as a kernel anomaly warranting fallback.

2) resolve_vdso_symbols (line 166, 178) hardcodes c"LINUX_2.6" as the dlvsym version. x86_64's vDSO uses LINUX_2.6, but aarch64 uses LINUX_2.6.39 and riscv64 uses LINUX_4.15. Currently falls back to dlsym (unversioned) on non-x86_64 — works but costs a wasted dlvsym call. Fix: per-arch version constants.

Discovered during bd-j946 review.

title: NSS/resolver hardening: deterministic cache/retry/backoff + fixtures
description:
Background:
- NSS/resolver behavior is security and correctness sensitive, especially under retries/caching.

Scope:
- Extend files-backend path with deterministic cache, invalidation, retry/backoff policy, and resolver error handling.
- Ensure failure codes and ordering semantics are explicit.

Deliverables:
1) NSS/resolver policy tables.
2) Cache/backoff implementation and diagnostics.
3) Conformance fixtures for positive/negative lookup paths.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Covered lookup flows match declared semantics deterministically.
- Poisoning/retry instability cases are bounded and observable.

Testing/Logging:
- Unit tests for parser/cache/invalidation/backoff logic.
- E2E lookup scenarios with adversarial inputs.
- Logs: trace_id, query_type, backend, cache_state, retry_count, errno/outcome.
acceptance_criteria:

- Add deterministic unit tests for nominal, boundary, and invalid-input paths in the touched modules.

2. Integration + E2E Evidence
- Add or extend fixture-driven integration coverage in `tests/conformance` and/or `tests/integration` for this bead scope.
- Add a deterministic E2E script path (or harness command) with explicit setup/teardown and replayable seeds.
- Compare FrankenLibC outputs against host glibc fixtures (or documented replacement-level contract) for all touched symbols.

3. Logging + Traceability Evidence

4. Performance + Regression Evidence

title: [parity][bug][glob] trailing-slash pattern: file-match + dir-only wildcard + NOCHECK strips slash diverged from glibc
description:
Found by enriching glob_differential_fuzz (rich GLOB_BRACE tokens + explicit trailing slashes). fl discarded trailing-slash semantics entirely. glibc rules (probed):
- LITERAL final component + trailing slash: existence check on the slash-stripped name; matches a regular FILE too, returned WITHOUT the slash (BAR/ -> BAR); a directory is returned WITH the slash (d/ -> d/). fl: Path::new("BAR/").exists() is false (ENOTDIR) so fl returned NOMATCH.
- WILDCARD final component + trailing slash: matches ONLY directories, each marked with '/' (*/ -> [d/], never the file BAR; BA?/ -> NOMATCH). fl treated the trailing '/' as an empty next component, returning files without slashes and not filtering by dir-ness.
- NOCHECK/NOMAGIC no-match fallback returns the pattern with trailing slash(es) STRIPPED (o/ -> o, {a,b}/ -> {a,b}). fl returned it with the slash.
FIX (crates/frankenlibc-core/src/string/glob.rs): strip trailing slashes up front (strip_trailing_slashes, preserving root /), remember trailing_slash; magic-free branch appends '/' iff dir; glob_recursive detects a trailing slash on the final component and applies ONLYDIR+MARK semantics; all NOCHECK/NOMAGIC fallbacks return the stripped pattern. 40k differential-fuzz 0-div, +unit test.
close_reason: Fixed: trailing-slash glob parity (literal file-match, wildcard dir-only+mark, NOCHECK slash-strip). 40k fuzz 0-div + unit test.

title: [bug][RED][design-decision] 5 locale_abi_test arms red: fl aliases the C locale onto C.UTF-8, so setlocale(LC_ALL,"C") returns "C.UTF-8" and CODESET is UTF-8 not ANSI_X3.4-1968
description:
RED at HEAD: setlocale_query_returns_c, setlocale_set_c_locale, setlocale_set_posix_locale, nl_langinfo_codeset, nl_langinfo_l_codeset. Worker vmi1293453 and hz1, harness 'cargo test -j 1 --no-fail-fast -p frankenlibc-abi --test locale_abi_test'.

NOT environment-dependent and NOT cross-test interference — both were checked and both are refuted. setlocale_set_c_locale FAILS RUN ALONE: 'test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 51 filtered out' (worker hz2, --exact --test-threads=1). And setlocale(LC_ALL,"C") cannot depend on LANG in the first place.

LIVE ORACLE, host glibc 2.42 (ldd (Ubuntu GLIBC 2.42-0ubuntu3.1) 2.42), python3 ctypes on libc.so.6, run under the worker's own LANG=C.UTF-8:
  setlocale(LC_ALL,"C")       -> "C"        nl_langinfo(CODESET) -> "ANSI_X3.4-1968"
  setlocale(LC_ALL,"POSIX")   -> "C"
  setlocale(LC_ALL,"C.UTF-8") -> "C.UTF-8"  nl_langinfo(CODESET) -> "UTF-8"
  setlocale(LC_ALL,"")        -> "C.UTF-8"  (env-derived)
glibc's two locales are internally consistent pairs: C<->ANSI_X3.4-1968, C.UTF-8<->UTF-8.

WHAT fl DOES (crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/locale_abi.rs): C_LOCALE_NAME = "C.UTF-8", C_LOCALE_CODESET = "UTF-8", and setlocale returns C_LOCALE_NAME for EVERY accepted request — the NULL query, "C", "POSIX", "" and "C.UTF-8" all return "C.UTF-8". locale_core::is_c_locale matches b"C"|b"POSIX"|b"". So fl is ALSO internally consistent — it just ships exactly one locale, C.UTF-8, and aliases the C locale onto it. The source comment is explicit that this is intended: 'The conversion ABI is UTF-8 throughout, so every public locale report must expose the same encoding as MB_CUR_MAX and the multibyte codec.'

THIS NEEDS A DECISION, NOT A PATCH. The two ways out are not interchangeable:
  (a) Implement the real C locale (MB_CUR_MAX=1, CODESET=ANSI_X3.4-1968) and keep C.UTF-8 as a separate selectable locale. setlocale then returns the canonical name of what was selected, and needs per-category current-name state plus the LC_ALL composite-string form glibc emits for mixed categories. This is the parity answer and it reaches into mbstowcs/wctomb/printf %ls/iconv defaults — far beyond these 5 arms.
  (b) Accept that fl ships one UTF-8 locale and that a request for "C" yields C.UTF-8 semantics, and rewrite the 5 arms to assert fl's documented contract, recording a KNOWN non-parity with glibc for LC_ALL="C".
Option (b) is cheap but it is a deliberate ABI divergence on the single most commonly requested locale name, and a program doing strcmp(setlocale(LC_ALL,NULL),"C") or save/restore round-trips will see it. Option (a) is correct and large.

DO NOT close this by editing the arms without recording which option was chosen and why. Whoever decides owns the codeset consequence, not just the string.

Note the startup-query arm (setlocale_query_returns_c) additionally needs a C-program oracle, not a python one: CPython calls setlocale itself during init, so a python probe cannot observe the true pre-main locale.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
PASSED OVER DELIBERATELY, not overlooked (BlackThrush 2026-08-15). Leaving this for whoever owns the ABI call, because the halfway version is strictly worse than either endpoint.

Today fl is INTERNALLY CONSISTENT: setlocale reports C.UTF-8 and nl_langinfo reports UTF-8, and the codec really is UTF-8. The tempting cheap increment -- make setlocale return the canonical name of what was requested ('C' for C/POSIX) while leaving the codec alone -- would produce setlocale(LC_ALL,'C')=='C' with CODESET=='UTF-8', which matches NEITHER glibc NOR fl's own documented contract, and would make MB_CUR_MAX disagree with the reported locale. That is a new defect wearing a green test.

So the fork stands as this bead states it: (a) real C locale with MB_CUR_MAX=1 and ANSI_X3.4-1968, per-category current-name state and the LC_ALL composite form, reaching into mbstowcs/wctomb/printf %ls/iconv defaults; or (b) accept one UTF-8 locale and rewrite the 5 arms against fl's contract with the non-parity recorded. Nothing in between is safe to land.

Note the campaign directive (bd-2g7oyh, no-gaps) points at (a), which is also multi-turn work that should not be started and abandoned mid-way through the codec.

title: EPIC: CVE Arena Security Validation
description:
Goal: Validate FrankenLibC against real CVE exploits to prove TSM effectiveness.

Background:
The CVE Arena contains test cases for known glibc vulnerabilities. FrankenLibC's TSM should either:
1. Prevent the vulnerability from being exploitable (hardened mode)
2. Detect and report the unsafe operation (strict mode metrics)

Current CVE Arena Contents (tests/cve_arena/):

- synthetic/ - Simulated vulnerability patterns
- research/ - Investigation notes

1. Heap overflow CVEs (malloc arena corruption)

4. UAF CVEs (use-after-free patterns)
5. Buffer overflow CVEs (string operations)

- All CVE triggers run without crash in hardened mode
- TSM metrics show healing actions for each CVE pattern
- Strict mode detects (but may not prevent) unsafe operations
- Zero new vulnerabilities introduced by FrankenLibC

- Each CVE gets a dedicated test fixture
- E2E scripts capture membrane metrics during CVE trigger
- Structured logs show exact healing actions taken

title: 517d0a233 silently reverted closed bd-8f6gck: all 28 non-f128 fromfp entry points returned float again (wrong return register)
description:
517d0a233 silently reverted CLOSED bead bd-8f6gck, and the damage was NOT confined to f128.

bd-8f6gck (P1, closed 2026-06-14 on 6c1f2c9e5) is this exact defect, in its own words:
"changed all 32 entry points to return intmax_t/uintmax_t (was f64/f32 -> wrong return register
XMM0 vs RAX, lossy >width53, wrong wide-overflow clamp+spurious FE_INEXACT)". Twelve days later
517d0a233 "abi/math: C99 Annex G special values for complex exp/hyperbolic" put every one of them
back to f64/f32.

MEASURED at HEAD before the fix:
  fromfp/ufromfp/fromfpx/ufromfpx entry points returning f64 or f32   28
  entry points returning intmax_t/uintmax_t                            0
At 517d0a233's parent all 32 returned intmax_t/uintmax_t.

So this was a LIVE wrong-ABI defect on the ordinary double entry points, not an f128 curiosity:
fl returned its answer in xmm0 while every C caller reads rax. It also lost the whole error
contract — HEAD's fromfp_impl returned f64::NAN for NaN/inf/out-of-range instead of the clamped
integer, and the FE_INVALID/FE_INEXACT discipline was gone.

ORACLE, taken before changing anything (glibc 2.42, libm.so.6, fromfp@@GLIBC_2.25). Reading the
return as an integer gives the C23 answers; reading it as a double hands back the untouched
argument register, which is the signature of a wrong-return-register call:

  fromfp(3.7,  TONEAREST, 64)   as_int=4    as_double=3.7
  fromfp(-3.7, TONEAREST, 64)   as_int=-4   as_double=-3.7
  fromfp(2.5,  TONEAREST, 64)   as_int=2                     (half-to-even)
  fromfp(NaN,  TONEAREST, 64)   = i64::MAX
  fromfp(+inf) = i64::MAX     fromfp(-inf) = i64::MIN
  fromfp(3.7, TONEAREST, 0)  = 0
  fromfp(200.0, w=8) = 127    fromfp(-200.0, w=8) = -128
  ufromfp(-0.4, UPWARD) = 0   ufromfp(-3.0) = 0   ufromfp(NaN) = u64::MAX
  2.5 across all five modes: TOWARDZERO 2, UPWARD 3, DOWNWARD 2, TONEAREST 2,
                             TONEARESTFROMZERO 3

Every one matches the restored implementation's documented contract.

FIXED in 72ae1c2a2, by the same context-verified `git apply -R` used for the rest of the engine.
All 36 functions in the two hunks that carry this family were fromfp-family stubs, so no unrelated
work was touched. 32 entry points back to intmax_t/uintmax_t; 0 remain float-returning.

conformance_diff_fromfp — bd-8f6gck's own 14400-tuple gate — was DARK (would not compile) and is
now relit and GREEN. That is an independent confirmation of the oracle probe above, and it is also
the reason the reversion went unnoticed for six weeks: the gate that would have caught it could not
link, so it reported nothing. See bd-ocwiw9 and the closure rule now in AGENTS.md.

title: EPIC: Bw-Trees for Extent Indexes (Graveyard Entry 8.7)
description:
# EPIC: Bw-Trees for Extent Indexes (Graveyard Entry 8.7)

## PURPOSE
Replace traditional B-tree extent indexes with Bw-Trees (Buzzword Trees) — lock-free delta-chain trees that allow concurrent readers and writers without any reader blocking. This is a long-term performance optimization for the extent index hot path.

## BACKGROUND
From the Alien CS Graveyard entry 8.7:
- Bw-Tree (Levandoski et al., ICDE 2013): latch-free B-tree with delta chains
- Key insight: instead of in-place mutation, append delta records to page
- Readers never block: they traverse the delta chain from newest to oldest
- Writers use CAS to append deltas (no locks)
- Periodic consolidation merges delta chains back into base pages

## DESIGN

### Architecture
- Mapping table: PageId -> AtomicPtr<PageDelta>
- Delta chain: linked list of delta records (insert, delete, split, merge)
- Base page: consolidated B-tree node
- Consolidation: background thread merges delta chains when they exceed threshold

### Delta Records
```rust
enum PageDelta {
    Insert { key: ExtentKey, value: ExtentValue, next: *const PageDelta },
    Delete { key: ExtentKey, next: *const PageDelta },
    Split { split_key: ExtentKey, new_page_id: PageId, next: *const PageDelta },
    Merge { removed_page_id: PageId, next: *const PageDelta },
    Base(BTreeNode),
}
```

### Concurrency
- Lookup: traverse mapping table -> delta chain -> base page (all read-only, no locks)
- Insert/Delete: create delta, CAS into mapping table (retry on conflict)
- Split/Merge: structural modification via delta + CAS
- Consolidation: create new base page, CAS to replace delta chain

### Extent Index Integration
- Replace extent B-tree in ffs-ext4 and ffs-btrfs with Bw-Tree
- Same lookup API: find_extent(inode, logical_block) -> PhysicalExtent
- Same mutation API: insert_extent, delete_extent, split_extent

## CURRENT PRIORITY
P2 — performance optimization, not blocking correctness. Current B-tree works correctly.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Lock-free lookup: readers never block on writers
- [ ] CAS-based insert/delete: no mutex on hot path
- [ ] Delta chain consolidation prevents unbounded chain growth
- [ ] Benchmark: lookup throughput under concurrent writers vs B-tree with locks
- [ ] Correctness: all B-tree invariants maintained (sorted, balanced, split/merge correct)
- [ ] Drop-in replacement for current extent index

## Success Criteria
1. All children closed
2. E2E benchmark (bd-1mdk.4) shows improvement over locked B-tree
3. Unit tests (bd-1mdk.3) pass
4. Delta chain consolidation compacts correctly
5. Mapping table is lock-free (no mutex in hot path)

title: Implement Bw-Tree mapping table and delta chain core
description:
# Implement Bw-Tree mapping table and delta chain core

## GOAL
Implement the foundational data structures for a Bw-Tree (Levandoski et al., ICDE 2013): the mapping table (PageId -> AtomicPtr<PageDelta>) and delta chain (linked list of insert/delete/split/merge deltas appended via CAS).

## BACKGROUND
From Alien CS Graveyard entry 8.7: Bw-Trees are latch-free B-trees that replace in-place mutation with append-only delta records. Readers traverse the delta chain from newest to oldest, never blocking. Writers use compare-and-swap (CAS) to atomically append deltas. This eliminates all reader-side synchronization.

## DESIGN

### Mapping Table
```rust
struct MappingTable {
    pages: Vec<AtomicPtr<PageDelta>>,
    next_page_id: AtomicU64,
}
```
- Fixed-size array of atomic pointers (one per page/node)
- All B-tree operations go through mapping table indirection
- Enables lock-free structural modifications (split/merge update a pointer, not a tree)

### Delta Chain
```rust
enum PageDelta {
    Insert { key: ExtentKey, value: ExtentValue, next: *const PageDelta },
    Delete { key: ExtentKey, next: *const PageDelta },
    Split { separator: ExtentKey, new_sibling: PageId, next: *const PageDelta },
    Merge { removed_sibling: PageId, next: *const PageDelta },
    Base(BTreeNode),
}
```
- Each delta is a small record prepended to the chain via CAS
- Lookup: walk chain applying deltas to reconstruct current state
- Base page: consolidated snapshot of all deltas (periodic compaction target)

### CAS Append Protocol
1. Read current head pointer from mapping table
2. Create new delta with next = current head
3. CAS mapping_table[page_id] from current to new delta
4. On CAS failure: retry (another writer appended concurrently)

### Memory Management
- Delta nodes allocated via crossbeam-epoch (same EBR as MVCC versions)
- Old deltas freed after consolidation and epoch advance
- No manual memory management or unsafe deallocation

## RUST IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Use `crossbeam::epoch::{Atomic, Owned, Shared, Guard}` for all pointers
- `unsafe` blocks required for Shared pointer dereference (justified by epoch pin safety)
- #[repr(C)] for delta variants to ensure stable layout
- Consider cache-line alignment for mapping table entries to avoid false sharing

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] MappingTable supports allocate_page, get_page, cas_page operations
- [ ] Delta chain supports Insert, Delete append via CAS
- [ ] Lookup correctly traverses delta chain to find current value
- [ ] CAS retry loop handles concurrent append conflicts
- [ ] crossbeam-epoch used for all delta allocation and reclamation
- [ ] Unit tests: single-threaded insert/delete/lookup round-trip
- [ ] Unit tests: concurrent CAS append (2+ threads, verify no lost updates)
- [ ] Unit tests: delta chain traversal returns correct merged state
- [ ] Logging: tracing spans for CAS attempts, retries, and chain length at lookup time

title: Implement Bw-Tree consolidation (delta chain compaction)
description:
# Implement Bw-Tree consolidation (delta chain compaction)

## GOAL
Implement background consolidation that merges accumulated delta records back into a base page, preventing unbounded delta chain growth and maintaining lookup performance.

## BACKGROUND
From Alien CS Graveyard entry 8.7: Without consolidation, delta chains grow linearly with writes, degrading lookup from O(log n) to O(log n + chain_length). Consolidation creates a fresh base page incorporating all deltas, then atomically replaces the chain via CAS on the mapping table.

## DESIGN

### Consolidation Trigger
- Chain length threshold: consolidate when delta chain exceeds configurable max (default: 16 deltas)
- Background thread: periodic scan of all pages for chains exceeding threshold
- Opportunistic: reader that encounters long chain can trigger inline consolidation

### Consolidation Protocol
1. Pin epoch (prevent GC of chain during consolidation)
2. Traverse delta chain, collecting all Insert/Delete operations
3. Apply operations to base page, producing new consolidated base
4. CAS mapping_table[page_id] from old chain head to new base
5. On CAS success: defer_destroy old chain nodes
6. On CAS failure: discard new base, retry (new deltas appended concurrently)

### Split/Merge During Consolidation
- If consolidated page exceeds max size: split into two pages
- If consolidated page below min size and sibling below threshold: merge
- Split/Merge are themselves delta records, enabling concurrent structural modifications

### Structural Modification Protocol (SMO)
- Split: create new sibling page, append Split delta to original, append Insert delta to parent
- Merge: append Merge delta to removed page, append Delete delta to parent
- All via CAS — no locks, no latches

## RUST IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Consolidation can race with concurrent inserts: CAS handles this correctly
- crossbeam-epoch Guard must be held during entire consolidation
- New base page: Owned::new(PageDelta::Base(consolidated_node))
- Location: ffs-bwtree/src/consolidation.rs

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Consolidation merges delta chain into fresh base page
- [ ] CAS atomically replaces old chain with consolidated base
- [ ] Concurrent writers during consolidation handled (CAS retry)
- [ ] Chain length bounded by consolidation threshold
- [ ] Split triggered when consolidated page too large
- [ ] Merge triggered when consolidated page too small
- [ ] Unit tests: consolidation produces correct base page
- [ ] Unit tests: concurrent consolidation + insert race
- [ ] Benchmark: lookup latency before/after consolidation
- [ ] Logging: tracing spans for consolidation trigger, duration, chain length before/after

# Add comprehensive unit tests for Bw-Tree operations

## GOAL
Build a thorough unit test suite verifying Bw-Tree correctness: single-threaded CRUD, concurrent operations, consolidation correctness, split/merge structural modifications, and memory safety (Miri-compatible).

## TEST CATEGORIES

### 1. Single-Threaded CRUD
- Insert 1000 keys, verify all lookups return correct values
- Delete half the keys, verify deleted keys return None
- Insert duplicate keys (update semantics), verify latest value wins
- Range scan: iterate keys in sorted order, verify ordering

### 2. Concurrent Insert/Lookup
- 4 threads each inserting 1000 unique keys concurrently
- After all threads complete: verify all 4000 keys present
- During inserts: 4 reader threads continuously looking up random keys
- Readers must never see partial/corrupt state

### 3. Concurrent Insert/Delete
- 2 writer threads: one inserting, one deleting (non-overlapping ranges)
- After completion: inserted range present, deleted range absent
- Overlap test: both threads target same keys, verify no lost updates

### 4. Consolidation Correctness
- Insert 100 deltas on one page, trigger consolidation
- Verify consolidated base page contains correct merged state
- Insert during consolidation: verify new delta visible after consolidation

### 5. Split/Merge
- Insert enough keys to trigger page split
- Verify both pages contain correct key ranges
- Delete keys to trigger merge, verify single page remains
- Concurrent split: multiple threads triggering splits on adjacent pages

### 6. Memory Safety (Miri)
- Small-scale tests (100 keys) runnable under Miri
- Verify no use-after-free, no data races, no undefined behavior
- crossbeam-epoch reclamation: verify old nodes freed after epoch advance

### 7. Edge Cases
- Empty tree: lookup, delete, range scan on empty tree
- Single-element tree: all operations
- Maximum chain length: verify consolidation triggers at threshold
- CAS retry exhaustion: verify graceful handling (if implemented)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All 7 test categories implemented and passing
- [ ] Concurrent tests use deterministic seeding for reproducibility
- [ ] Miri tests pass (no UB detected)
- [ ] Test coverage: >= 80% line coverage for bwtree module
- [ ] Each test has descriptive name and documents expected behavior
- [ ] Logging: test harness captures tracing output for debugging failures

title: E2E benchmark: Bw-Tree vs locked B-tree extent index throughput
description:
# E2E benchmark: Bw-Tree vs locked B-tree extent index throughput

## GOAL
Prove that the Bw-Tree extent index provides superior concurrent throughput compared to the current locked B-tree implementation. This is the justification benchmark for the entire Bw-Tree epic.

## BENCHMARK SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Read-Heavy (95% lookup, 5% insert)
- Simulate metadata-heavy workload (readdir, stat)
- Thread counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
- Measure: lookups/sec, p50/p95/p99 lookup latency
- Expected: Bw-Tree scales linearly (readers never block); locked B-tree saturates

### Scenario 2: Write-Heavy (30% lookup, 70% insert/delete)
- Simulate file creation/deletion workload
- Thread counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
- Measure: operations/sec, CAS retry rate, consolidation frequency
- Expected: Bw-Tree outperforms at >= 4 threads (CAS contention < lock contention)

### Scenario 3: Mixed Workload (realistic filesystem)
- 50% lookup, 30% insert, 10% delete, 10% range scan
- Thread counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
- Measure: aggregate ops/sec, per-operation latency breakdown
- Expected: Bw-Tree advantage increases with thread count

### Scenario 4: Single-Threaded Baseline
- Pure sequential operations (no concurrency)
- Measure: Bw-Tree overhead vs B-tree (delta chain traversal cost)
- Expected: B-tree faster single-threaded (simpler structure); Bw-Tree within 2x

### Scenario 5: Consolidation Overhead
- Measure: consolidation frequency, duration, and impact on concurrent operations
- Stress test: maximum write rate with consolidation enabled/disabled
- Expected: consolidation adds < 10% overhead at steady state

- Operations per second (throughput)
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) per operation type
- CAS retry rate (contention measure)
- Consolidation frequency and duration
- Memory usage (peak RSS)
- Scaling efficiency: ops/sec(N threads) / ops/sec(1 thread)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Bw-Tree outperforms locked B-tree at >= 4 concurrent threads for read-heavy workload
- [ ] Bw-Tree single-threaded overhead is within 2x of locked B-tree
- [ ] CAS retry rate < 10% under realistic workloads
- [ ] Consolidation overhead < 10% at steady state
- [ ] Results stored as JSON CI artifacts for regression tracking
- [ ] Benchmark harness is deterministic and reproducible

title: Fuzz target: membrane validation pipeline
description:
Fuzz membrane validation pipeline directly.

Target Components:
- ValidationPipeline::validate()
- TLS cache operations
- Bloom filter operations
- Arena slot lookups
- Fingerprint verification
- Canary checks

Fuzzing Strategy:
1. Arbitrary pointer addresses (including edge cases)
2. Pointer arithmetic on valid allocations
3. Near-miss pointers (allocation ± small delta)
4. Concurrent validation from multiple threads
5. Mixed valid/invalid pointer sequences

State Coverage:
Exercise all SafetyState transitions:
- Valid → Valid (re-validation)
- Valid → Freed (free then validate)
- Freed → Quarantined (quarantine fill)
- Unknown → Foreign (external pointer)

Cache Coherence:
- TLS cache invalidation on free
- Bloom filter false positive paths
- Arena slot reuse after quarantine

Invariant Checks:
- Lattice monotonicity (states only become more restrictive)
- Generation counter ordering
- Cache consistency with arena state

Success Criteria:
- Zero false negatives (unsafe passed as safe)
- All SafetyState transitions exercised
- No deadlocks under concurrent load
- Bounded latency for all paths

acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

### Mandatory Verification Gate
1. Unit Test Evidence
- Add deterministic unit tests for nominal, boundary, and invalid-input paths in the touched modules.
- Include strict and hardened mode assertions when behavior differs by runtime mode.
- Include failure-mode tests covering repair/deny/default behavior with explicit expected outputs.

2. Integration + E2E Evidence
- Add or extend fixture-driven integration coverage in `tests/conformance` and/or `tests/integration` for this bead scope.
- Add a deterministic E2E script path (or harness command) with explicit setup/teardown and replayable seeds.
- Compare FrankenLibC outputs against host glibc fixtures (or documented replacement-level contract) for all touched symbols.

3. Logging + Traceability Evidence
- Emit structured logs (JSONL or deterministic text) that include bead ID, scenario ID, runtime mode, symbol family, decision path, and outcome.
- Verify logs expose repair/deny counters and reason codes so regressions are diagnosable from artifacts alone.
- Record artifact paths in bead notes (test logs, fixture diffs, benchmark outputs, conformance reports).

4. Performance + Regression Evidence
- Capture before/after baseline for latency/throughput on touched hot paths.
- Enforce no-regression threshold or document bounded tradeoff with quantitative rationale.

5. CI Gate Evidence
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --all-targets`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --all-targets`
- all bead-specific harness and E2E scripts pass with deterministic logs archived.

title: [parity][bug] printf %m renders numberless 'Unknown error' for unknown errno (ignores width/precision)
description: Found by NEW printf_m_differential_test (live glibc). The %m extension render (stdio_abi.rs) called strerror_r and only used its buffer when rc==0. But strerror_r returns EINVAL (non-zero) for an UNKNOWN errno while STILL filling the buffer with 'Unknown error N'; the %m path discarded that and pushed a hardcoded literal 'Unknown error' — dropping the number AND ignoring width/precision flags. So printf('%m') with errno=4095 gave 'Unknown error' vs glibc 'Unknown error 4095', and '%.0m' gave 'Unknown error' vs glibc '' (empty). Fix: render %m via the shared rendered_strerror_message(e) directly (yields glibc's 'Unknown error <N>' incl negatives) then format_str applies width/precision. Known errnos (0..133) were already correct. ⚠️TEST NOTE: fl %m reads fl's OWN __errno_location (separate symbol from glibc's in a debug test binary) — set frankenlibc_abi::errno_abi::__errno_location for the fl call. stdio_abi_test(255)+strerror_scan+printf_positional green. Also adds fgets_differential_test (7 cases, CLEAN: binary-safe thru embedded NUL, n=1 lone-NUL, n=0 NULL, EOF).

title: Performance: regression prevention system
description:
Performance regression prevention system.

Goal: Automated detection of performance regressions.

Baseline Establishment:
- Criterion benchmark results
- Per-function timing thresholds
- Memory allocation baselines
- Syscall count baselines

Regression Detection:
- Compare PR results against main branch
- Statistical significance testing
- Threshold: 5% slowdown triggers warning
- Threshold: 20% slowdown blocks merge

Benchmarks:
1. Membrane validation latency
2. Allocator operations (malloc/free cycle)
3. String operations (memcpy throughput)
4. Runtime math kernel decisions
5. E2E application benchmarks

CI Integration:
- Run benchmarks on every PR
- Store historical results
- Generate trend reports
- Alert on degradation

Reporting:
- Before/after comparison
- Flame graph diff
- Allocation profile diff
- Syscall trace diff

Success Criteria:
- No undetected performance regressions
- Historical trend tracking
- Actionable regression reports

## Acceptance Criteria
See `acceptance_criteria` field.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria
Implementation must preserve all existing functionality and claims while adding deterministic verification coverage.

### Mandatory Verification Gate
- Comprehensive unit tests are required for all touched logic: positive, negative, adversarial, and regression.
- Deterministic e2e scripts are required for all externally visible behavior in strict and hardened mode where relevant.
- Structured logs are mandatory for unit/e2e runs with fields: `trace_id`, `mode`, `api_family`, `symbol`, `decision_path`, `healing_action`, `errno`, `latency_ns`, `artifact_refs`.
- Closure evidence must include exact test commands, expected outputs/thresholds, and representative failure signatures.
- CI must persist logs, diffs, and reports with deterministic naming and retention for replay/triage.
- Tooling contract: deterministic orchestration/traceability uses `/dp/asupersync`, and deterministic diff/snapshot/TUI evidence uses `/dp/frankentui`.
notes:
### Mandatory Test/E2E Logging Checklist
- Test command set is documented in bead notes before closure (unit + e2e + perf where applicable).
- Expected output and pass/fail thresholds are documented per command.
- Failure triage snippets are documented (top failure classes + where to inspect artifacts).
- Evidence index entry links logs, parity diffs, and benchmark/proof artifacts.

description:
# Review finding

Workspace gate `rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_frankenfs_cod cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` stops in `ffs-tui` on a warning promoted to error.

## Failure
- File: `crates/ffs-tui/src/lib.rs:474`
- Item: `fn build_system_health_text(snap: &DashboardSnapshot) -> Text`
- Lint: `mismatched-lifetime-syntaxes`
- Suggested fix from compiler: return `Text<'_>` instead of bare `Text`

## Why this is high severity
This single signature keeps the whole workspace clippy gate red under `-D warnings`, so no one can currently use the mandated workspace lint gate as a merge signal.

## Repro
`rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_frankenfs_cod cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`

## Expected fix direction
Apply the explicit lifetime to the `Text` return type and rerun workspace clippy to ensure there are no additional red-gate warnings behind it.
close_reason: Fixed: crates/ffs-tui/src/lib.rs:474 now reads 'fn build_system_health_text(snap: &DashboardSnapshot) -> Text<'_>' with explicit elided lifetime. title: [MEDIUM] review: printf executor hardcodes LP64 vararg widths
description:
[MEDIUM] review: printf conformance executor hardcodes LP64 vararg widths

Recent printf executor work widened promotion and dispatch handling, but the promotion layer still bakes in LP64 assumptions:
- `crates/frankenlibc_conformance/src/lib.rs:2492-2496` defines `PrintfArg::Long(c_longlong)` and `PrintfArg::Ulong(c_ulonglong)`.
- `crates/frankenlibc_conformance/src/lib.rs:2502-2585` treats `%l`, `%j`, `%z`, `%t`, and `%q` as a single `long_like` bucket and rewrites integer args into those 64-bit slots.

That matches today's 64-bit Linux host, but it is not a target-width model for all supported ABIs. `%ld`, `%zd`, and `%td` are width-sensitive and can diverge from `long long` / `unsigned long long` on non-LP64 targets, which risks false conformance results and executor-side mis-marshalling.

Review ask:
- split `long`, `long long`, `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, and `intmax_t` promotion by actual ABI width instead of one 64-bit bucket
- gate this through target metadata so the executor stays correct if the conformance matrix expands past the current host ABI
close_reason: LP64 assumption now explicit: PrintfArg module docs the invariant and three compile-time size_of asserts fail the build on any target where c_long/size_t/ptrdiff_t is narrower than c_longlong. The full split-by-ABI-width refactor stays scoped for the moment a non-LP64 target is added to the matrix — the assertion message points back to this bead. Committed b624a988.

title: gets fortify overflow abort coverage
description: __gets_chk aborts when stdin supplies more bytes than the real destination buffer can hold, but fortify_abi_test has no fork-isolated coverage for that stdin-driven overflow path. Add a pipe-backed child-process regression so the guard stays pinned without mutating parent stdin.
close_reason:
ALREADY SATISFIED — closing on run tests matched to this bead's contract.

COVERING TEST: gets_chk_line_over_real_buffer_aborts_child_process — writes an over-long line into a
pipe wired to stdin, calls __gets_chk with a 4-byte buffer, and requires the child to die on
SIGABRT. That is exactly the overflow-abort contract this bead names.

EVIDENCE. crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/fortify_abi_test.rs, run just now:
  cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --test fortify_abi_test
  -> test result: ok. 152 passed; 0 failed; 0 IGNORED; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
Zero ignored matters here: a sibling bead last round nearly closed on a suite that reported 24
ignored, where the arm in question could have been one of them.

WHY THE ABORT ARMS CANNOT PASS VACUOUSLY — I checked the harness rather than trusting the test
names. assert_child_sigabrt forks, and if the child RETURNS NORMALLY it calls _exit(127); the parent
then asserts WIFSIGNALED(status) and WTERMSIG(status) == SIGABRT. So a fortify wrapper that failed to
abort would exit 127, WIFSIGNALED would be false, and the assertion would fail. The sentinel exit is
what makes these real tests rather than 'we called it and nothing happened'.

NOT CITED BY BEAD ID. None of the eight fortify beads is named anywhere in the test tree, so the
bead->gate mapping that settled earlier batches returned NONE for all of them. Coverage was
established by matching each bead's CONTRACT to a named executing test instead. Bead-ID citation is
a convenience, not the definition of coverage — and its absence is not evidence of absence.

No code change was needed or made for this bead.

title: HTM fast-path for hot libc functions (section 4.2, Score 3.0)
description:
Implement Hardware Transactional Memory (HTM) fast-path for the hottest libc functions on Intel TSX-capable processors. Concept: Use Intel RTM (Restricted Transactional Memory) instructions (XBEGIN/XEND/XABORT) to speculatively execute hot functions without acquiring locks. If the transaction commits, the function executed atomically without any synchronization overhead. If the transaction aborts (due to conflict, capacity, or interrupt), fall back to the standard lock-based path. Target functions: (1) malloc/free — speculative allocation from thread-local cache without arena lock. If cache is sufficient, commit. If not, abort and take the slow path. (2) memcpy for small sizes (<256 bytes) — speculative copy that avoids cache-line locking overhead. (3) pthread_mutex_lock — speculative lock elision (execute the critical section transactionally, skip the lock entirely). Implementation: (a) Runtime CPUID check for RTM support. (b) Adaptive retry logic — track abort rate per call site. If abort rate > threshold (e.g., 30%), disable HTM for that site for a cooldown period. (c) Fallback path must be functionally identical to HTM path. (d) TSM integration — TSM validation must be idempotent (safe to re-execute on transaction retry). Caveat: Intel deprecated TSX on some SKUs. This is a performance opportunity on supported hardware, not a required feature.

**Alien CS Reference:** Section 4.2 of the graveyard. HTM (Intel TSX / IBM POWER HTM) provides speculative lock elision. Key papers: Herlihy & Moss (1993) original HTM proposal; Intel TSX Programming Guide. The graveyard Score 3.0 reflects hardware deprecation risk but high payoff on supported SKUs.

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- Use core::arch::x86_64::{_xbegin, _xend, _xabort, _xtest} intrinsics behind #[cfg(target_feature = "rtm")].
- Wrap in HtmFastPath<F: Fn() -> R> that encapsulates the speculative-try/fallback pattern.
- Per-call-site abort counter: AtomicU32 with relaxed ordering, sampled every 64 invocations to amortize overhead.
- Cooldown: exponential backoff (1ms, 2ms, 4ms, ... up to 1s) before re-enabling HTM at a disabled site.
- All TSM state reads inside the transaction must be from immutable/const data to avoid transactional capacity aborts.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. HtmFastPath compiles on non-RTM targets as a no-op passthrough (zero overhead).
2. On RTM-capable hardware, malloc fast-path commit rate >70% under low contention (1-4 threads).
3. Abort rate tracking is correct: synthetic abort injection yields accurate per-site counters.
4. Fallback path produces bit-identical results to HTM path for all inputs.
5. Adaptive disable/re-enable logic verified by test that forces >30% abort rate, confirms disable, waits cooldown, confirms re-enable.
6. All operations emit structured tracing: tracing::trace!(target: "htm", site, outcome, abort_reason).
7. Benchmark: malloc/free microbenchmark shows >15% throughput improvement on RTM hardware vs lock-based baseline at 4+ threads.

**Logging Requirements:**
- Every HTM transaction attempt logs: call_site_id, attempt_number, outcome (commit/abort/fallback), abort_code (if abort).
- Periodic (every 1000 ops) summary log: per-site commit rate, abort rate, disabled sites, cooldown remaining.
- All logs use tracing crate with target = "htm" for filterable structured output.

title: Integrate journal replay into OpenFs mount flow
description:
# Integrate journal replay into OpenFs mount flow

## GOAL
Make ext4 journal replay a first-class, option-controlled part of `OpenFs` open/mount flows.

Today `OpenFs::from_device()` will attempt JBD2 replay for ext4 images (via `maybe_replay_ext4_journal()`), but:
- there is no explicit "read-only" / "simulate" mode
- CLI `inspect`/RO mount should not mutate the on-disk image

This bead makes journal replay behavior explicit and testable.

## SCOPE
1. Add an explicit journal replay mode to `ffs-core::OpenOptions`:
   - `Apply`: perform replay and write through to the underlying device
   - `SimulateOverlay`: perform replay into an in-memory overlay so reads see replayed state but the image file is unchanged
   - `Skip`: do not replay; report that the journal was present
2. Wire CLI flows:
   - `ffs inspect`: use `SimulateOverlay` (never mutate)
   - `ffs mount` (read-only today): use `SimulateOverlay`
   - future RW mount: use `Apply`
3. Preserve observability:
   - `OpenFs.ext4_journal_replay` should contain replay stats when replay was attempted

## IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- `OpenFs` already stores the replay outcome in `ext4_journal_replay`.
- The missing piece is the device behavior during replay.

Preferred approach:
- Introduce a small `ByteDevice` overlay wrapper (copy-on-write at byte ranges) that:
  - stores `write_all_at()` calls into an in-memory map keyed by offset
  - serves `read_exact_at()` from the overlay when present, otherwise from the underlying device
- Use `ByteDeviceBlockAdapter` on top of this wrapper during replay.

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit/integration tests in `crates/ffs-harness/tests/ext4_journal_recovery.rs`:
   - Add a new scenario that opens with replay mode `SimulateOverlay` and asserts:
     - replay outcome reports committed sequences
     - the underlying device bytes at `TARGET_BLOCK` are unchanged
     - a read through the overlay device returns the replayed bytes
2. Add/extend CLI-level tests (if a CLI test harness exists) or add a harness test that:
   - runs `OpenFs::open_with_options()` on a synthetic image and verifies mode selection

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. `OpenOptions` exposes an explicit ext4 journal replay mode.
2. `ffs inspect` and read-only mount paths do not mutate image files.
3. Replay stats remain available for diagnostics.
4. All new behavior is covered by tests (no “vibes”).

title: Implement ext4 allocator bitmap reading
description:
# Implement ext4 allocator bitmap reading

## GOAL
Implement **read-only** access to ext4 block/inode allocation bitmaps so FrankenFS can:
- report free space accurately (df-like)
- validate group-descriptor free counts
- prepare for write-path work (allocator state must be observable before mutation)

## CONTEXT
- `ffs-core::OpenFs` already provides ext4 primitives (`read_group_desc`, `read_inode`, extent mapping, etc.).
- `ffs-alloc` already contains bitmap helpers (`bitmap_get`, `bitmap_count_free`, etc.) and group stats parsing, but it is not yet surfaced as a read-only inspection API.

## SCOPE
1. Add an ext4 free-space inspection API on `OpenFs` (in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs`):
   - read raw block bitmap for a group (using `bg_block_bitmap` from `Ext4GroupDesc`)
   - read raw inode bitmap for a group
   - compute per-group and global totals
2. Wire CLI:
   - extend `ffs inspect --json` output (in `crates/ffs-cli/src/main.rs`) to include:
     - `free_blocks_total`
     - `free_inodes_total`
     - optional: mismatches vs superblock/group-desc counters

## IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Use the ext4 block size from the parsed superblock.
- For group N:
  - locate its group descriptor via `OpenFs::read_group_desc(cx, group)`
  - read the bitmap block(s) via the existing device read helpers
- Counting strategy:
  - blocks: count free bits in each group bitmap (respect the last group’s partial size)
  - inodes: count free bits similarly

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Pure unit tests (no external tools):
   - cover `ffs-alloc` bitmap helpers (some already exist; extend if needed)
   - add tests for edge cases: partial final byte, wrap-around search, bounds
2. Harness integration tests (skip if kernel tools missing):
   - generate a small ext4 image with `mkfs.ext4`
   - compare free counts from:
     - `dumpe2fs -h` or `tune2fs -l`
     - FrankenFS bitmap-derived totals

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. `OpenFs` can read ext4 block + inode bitmaps for any group without panics.
2. Reported free counts are consistent with kernel tool output for a generated image.
3. `ffs inspect --json` surfaces free-space summary.
4. FEATURE_PARITY.md is updated accordingly.

## NOTE
This bead is READ-ONLY. Allocation/deallocation mutation is part of bd-huh.

title: Implement ext4 orphan inode list reading
description:
# Implement ext4 orphan inode list reading

## GOAL
Implement **read-only** detection + traversal of ext4’s orphan inode list for diagnostics.

For V1 read-only mount, we do not perform orphan recovery; we only:
- detect if an orphan list is present
- traverse it safely (cycle detection, bounds)
- report orphan count + sample in diagnostics / `ffs inspect --json`

## CONTEXT
- ext4 orphan list head is stored in the superblock (`s_last_orphan` in kernel naming).
- individual orphan inodes chain via a field in the inode (kernel uses `i_dtime` as next pointer during orphan processing).
- `ffs-ondisk::Ext4Superblock` does not currently expose `s_last_orphan`, so this work requires parsing that field.

## SCOPE
1. On-disk parsing:
   - extend `crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs` `Ext4Superblock` to parse and expose `last_orphan` (naming can be `last_orphan` or `orphan_head`).
2. Core traversal:
   - add an `OpenFs` method in `crates/ffs-core/src/lib.rs`:
     - `read_ext4_orphan_list(cx) -> OrphanList` (or similar)
   - implement traversal:
     - stop at 0
     - cycle detection (cap iterations at `inodes_count`)
     - validate inode numbers are in range
3. CLI:
   - extend `ffs inspect --json` to include orphan diagnostics:
     - count
     - optional: first N inode numbers

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit tests for superblock parsing:
   - construct a minimal superblock buffer and set the orphan head field
   - assert the parsed value matches
2. Unit/integration tests for traversal logic:
   - use a small in-memory `ByteDevice` with a mocked inode table containing an orphan chain
   - verify:
     - correct traversal order
     - cycle detection triggers a clear error
     - out-of-range inode numbers are rejected

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. `ffs inspect` reports orphan presence/count without panicking.
2. Traversal is safe against cycles and malformed pointers.
3. Read-only workflows do not mutate the image.
4. FEATURE_PARITY.md is updated accordingly.

title: Implement journal replay write-back to device
description:
# Implement journal replay write-back to device

## GOAL
After JBD2 journal replay parses committed transactions, actually write the recovered blocks back to the filesystem image so that the image state reflects the journal commits.

## BACKGROUND
Currently replay_jbd2() in ffs-journal parses journal blocks and identifies committed transactions, but the recovered block data is never written to the device. This is "Phase 2" of journal replay.

## CURRENT STATE
- replay_jbd2() returns ReplayOutcome with committed_sequences ✅
- Journal descriptor/commit/revoke parsing works ✅
- Block data from committed transactions is available ✅
- **Missing**: Writing recovered blocks to their target locations on the device

## DELIVERABLES
1. `apply_replay(cx, dev, outcome) -> Result<ApplyStats>`
   - For each committed transaction in order:
     - For each data block in the transaction:
       - Write the data block to its target location on the device
   - Skip blocks in the revoke table
   - Verify written data by re-reading and comparing
2. `clear_journal(cx, dev)` - mark journal as clean after successful replay
3. Crash safety: if interrupted, next mount replays again (idempotent)

## TESTS
1. Replay + apply: dirty journal → clean image with correct data
2. Revoke list respected: revoked blocks not written
3. Idempotency: apply twice gives same result
4. Verify: re-read written blocks matches journal data
5. Interrupted apply: restart replays from scratch

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
Every journal write-back operation MUST emit structured logs with:
- `[JBD2:Apply]` - apply start/end: `info!(target: "ffs::jbd2", txn_count=N, total_blocks=B, "journal_apply_start")`
- `[JBD2:Write]` - each block write: `trace!(target: "ffs::jbd2", seq=S, target_block=B, size=SZ, "journal_block_write")`
- `[JBD2:Revoke]` - revoke skip: `debug!(target: "ffs::jbd2", seq=S, target_block=B, "journal_block_revoked_skip")`
- `[JBD2:Verify]` - write verification: `debug!(target: "ffs::jbd2", target_block=B, match=bool, "journal_write_verify")`
- `[JBD2:Clear]` - journal clear: `info!(target: "ffs::jbd2", last_seq=S, cleared=bool, "journal_clear")`
- `[JBD2:Error]` - any failure: `error!(target: "ffs::jbd2", seq=S, target_block=B, error=E, "journal_apply_error")`

Log levels:
- TRACE: every individual block write
- DEBUG: revoke skips and verifications
- INFO: apply start/end summaries, journal clear
- ERROR: any write or verify failure

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Journal replay produces correct filesystem state
2. Idempotent (safe to replay multiple times)
3. All writes go through BlockDevice (respects cache)
4. All operations logged for post-mortem analysis

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: CRASH SAFETY: Journal write-back MUST be idempotent. If interrupted mid-apply, the next mount will replay the entire journal again. This means writes must be safe to repeat. The key insight: journal data blocks are written to their final locations, so re-writing the same data is harmless. After successful apply, clear the journal by writing a clean commit block.

title: Implement structured logging with JSON output
description:
# Implement structured logging with JSON output

## GOAL
Implement production-grade structured logging for operational visibility and debugging.

## BACKGROUND
From AGENTS.md: "Deterministic audit logs for explainability."
From spec: "Evidence ledger (what evidence drove what decision)."

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

### 1. Structured Log Events
```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
pub struct LogEvent {
    pub timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    pub level: Level,
    pub target: String,
    pub message: String,
    pub fields: BTreeMap<String, Value>,
    pub span: Option<SpanInfo>,
}
```

### 2. Domain-Specific Fields
```rust
// MVCC events
log_event!(level: INFO, 
    message: "transaction_commit",
    txn_id: txn.id,
    commit_seq: cs,
    write_set_size: txn.write_set.len(),
    duration_us: duration.as_micros(),
);

// Cache events
log_event!(level: DEBUG,
    message: "cache_eviction",
    block: block_num,
    reason: reason,
    t1_len: cache.t1_len(),
    t2_len: cache.t2_len(),
);
```

### 3. Span Context
```rust
let span = span!(Level::INFO, "mount", 
    image = %path, 
    mode = %if ro { "ro" } else { "rw" }
);
let _guard = span.enter();
// All logs within have span context
```

### 4. Output Formats
- Human-readable for development
- JSON for production/aggregation
- Configurable via env var or config

### 5. Log Rotation
- Size-based rotation
- Time-based rotation
- Compression of old logs

## TESTS
1. Unit: JSON output valid
2. Unit: Fields correctly serialized
3. Integration: Span context propagated
4. Integration: Rotation works

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. All significant events logged
2. JSON parseable by log aggregators
3. Span context maintained
4. Performance overhead < 1%

title: Implement multi-threaded FUSE dispatch with Send+Sync state
description:
# Implement multi-threaded FUSE dispatch with Send+Sync state

## GOAL
Enable concurrent FUSE request handling using fuser multi-threaded mode, as mandated by spec §1.7 Mechanical Sympathy.

## BACKGROUND
The spec states: "MUST use multi-threaded dispatch. All `Filesystem` state MUST be `Send + Sync`. `parking_lot` locks for concurrency."

Single-threaded FUSE dispatch is a severe bottleneck:
- 5-10μs per kernel/userspace round-trip
- Sequential ops block on I/O
- CPU underutilization on multi-core

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

### 1. FuseBackend State Architecture
```rust
pub struct FuseBackend {
    // Arc-wrapped for multi-threaded access
    inner: Arc<FuseInner>,
}

struct FuseInner {
    fs: RwLock<OpenFs>,           // parking_lot RwLock
    cache: Arc<ArcCache>,          // Already Send+Sync
    mvcc: Arc<MvccStore>,          // Already Send+Sync
    config: MountConfig,           // Immutable after mount
    metrics: AtomicMetrics,        // Lock-free counters
}
```

### 2. Thread Pool Configuration
- Default: min(num_cpus, 8) threads
- Configurable via MountConfig
- Each thread has its own I/O budget tracking

### 3. Lock Granularity
- ArcCache: Internal fine-grained locking (already done)
- MvccStore: Per-block version chain locks
- OpenFs: Per-operation RwLock (readers concurrent, writers exclusive)
- Metrics: Atomic counters (no locks)

### 4. Avoid False Sharing
- Align hot counters to cache line (64 bytes)
- Separate read-heavy and write-heavy state

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit test: FuseBackend is Send + Sync (compile-time)
2. Integration: 100 concurrent read requests complete without deadlock
3. Integration: 10 concurrent write + 90 concurrent read complete
4. Stress: 10 threads x 1000 ops each, verify no data corruption

## LOGGING
- Log thread pool initialization (thread count)
- Log per-thread request dispatch (trace level)
- Log lock contention events (warn level)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. `cargo test` confirms FuseBackend: Send + Sync
2. Concurrent benchmark shows >4x throughput vs single-threaded
3. No deadlocks in 1-hour stress test
4. Metrics show balanced load across threads

title: Implement MVCC version persistence layer
description:
# Implement MVCC version persistence layer

## GOAL
Persist MVCC version chains so **committed** versions survive process restart (crash/restart durability for the MVCC layer).

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
- `crates/ffs-mvcc/src/lib.rs` contains an in-memory `MvccStore` with:
  - `Transaction { writes, reads }`
  - `commit()` and `commit_ssi()`
  - version chains stored as `BTreeMap<BlockNumber, Vec<BlockVersion>>`

On restart, all committed version history is lost.

## DESIGN OPTIONS
### Option A: Append-only WAL (recommended)
- Write-ahead log of MVCC commits.
- On startup: replay WAL into `MvccStore`.
- Periodic checkpoint compacts WAL into a base snapshot.

### Option B: Separate version-store file + index
- Append-only log + periodic index rebuild.

### Option C: Inline inside filesystem image
- Too invasive for V1.

## RECOMMENDED: WAL (Option A)
### WAL invariants
- Replay is idempotent.
- Partial/truncated tail entries are detected and ignored safely.
- Commit boundary is explicit.
- Every on-disk record is checksummed (crc32c or blake3) so corruption is detectable.

### I/O authority
All filesystem I/O must be `&asupersync::Cx`-aware (AGENTS.md: no ambient authority).

## DELIVERABLES
1. A persistence module for ffs-mvcc (new files are OK):
   - `crates/ffs-mvcc/src/wal.rs` (binary format + encode/decode)
   - `crates/ffs-mvcc/src/persist.rs` (integration glue)
2. A persistent constructor and integration points:
   - `MvccStore::open_persistent(cx, wal_path, options)` (or a wrapper type that owns `MvccStore`)
   - On `commit`/`commit_ssi`, append commit records.
3. Checkpointing:
   - a compacted snapshot format
   - atomic replacement (temp file + rename)

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Crash-restart:
   - commit some writes
   - drop store
   - reopen from WAL
   - verify latest committed versions are present
2. Uncommitted not restored:
   - write without commit, drop
   - reopen
   - verify no uncommitted versions exist
3. Truncation handling:
   - corrupt/truncate WAL tail
   - replay stops safely and does not panic

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. WAL is created and replay works deterministically.
2. Committed versions persist; uncommitted do not.
3. Checkpointing reduces WAL growth and is crash-safe.
4. All behavior is covered by tests with clear logging on failure.

title: Cross-crate integration: MVCC commit log feeds evidence ledger
description:
# Cross-crate integration: MVCC commit log feeds evidence ledger

## GOAL
Wire MVCC commit/abort events into the EvidenceLedger so that all transaction decisions are recorded for post-hoc audit. This bridges ffs-mvcc and ffs-repair/evidence subsystems.

## BACKGROUND
bd-2jk.11 extends the EvidenceLedger for MVCC decisions, but there is no bead that wires the actual MVCC commit path to produce ledger entries. Every commit, abort, and SSI conflict must emit a structured evidence record.

## DELIVERABLES
1. MvccStore::commit() emits EvidenceEntry::TransactionCommit { txn_id, commit_seq, write_set_size, duration_us }
2. MvccStore::abort() emits EvidenceEntry::TransactionAbort { txn_id, reason, read_set_size, write_set_size }
3. SSI conflict detection emits EvidenceEntry::SerializationConflict { txn_id, conflicting_txn, conflict_type }
4. Evidence entries are append-only JSONL, machine-parseable

title: Implement version chain compression
description:
# Implement version chain compression

## GOAL
Reduce memory overhead of MVCC version chains without breaking snapshot visibility semantics.

## CURRENT REALITY (CODE)
- `MvccStore` stores full `Vec<u8>` for every `BlockVersion`.
- Hot blocks can accumulate long chains (high memory overhead).

## STRATEGIES (PHASED)
1. **Dedup identical versions** (low-risk, high-win)
   - if a staged write produces bytes identical to the latest visible version, store a reference instead of duplicating
2. **Safe chain compaction / capping**
   - prune versions older than the oldest active snapshot (already partially supported via `active_snapshots` + `prune_versions_older_than`)
   - add policy knobs for max chain length
3. **Delta encoding** (higher complexity)
   - store small diffs against a base version
   - ensure reconstruction is bounded and fast

## DELIVERABLES
1. Define a compressed representation for block version data (new module recommended):
   - `crates/ffs-mvcc/src/compression.rs`
2. Integrate into `MvccStore` so callers can still `read_visible`/`read_latest` semantics (whatever the existing read API is or will be).
3. Add microbenchmarks (optional but recommended) and documentation of tradeoffs.

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Reconstruction correctness:
   - for a chain of edits, reconstruct each version and assert byte-equality
2. Snapshot safety:
   - ensure compaction never removes a version needed by any registered active snapshot
3. Performance sanity:
   - reconstruction time is bounded for typical chain lengths (add a unit test with a reasonable upper bound)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Demonstrable memory reduction on a representative "hot block" workload.
2. No observable behavior changes (goldens + MVCC invariants).
3. Compression behavior is configurable and documented.

title: Wire MVCC version store into block read/write path
description:
# Wire MVCC version store into block read/write path

## GOAL
Connect the in-memory MvccStore to actual block I/O so that:
1. Read operations see snapshot-consistent block versions
2. Write operations stage new block versions through MVCC transactions
3. The ARC cache interacts correctly with versioned blocks

## BACKGROUND
Currently, MvccStore works in isolation (tested with synthetic data). The read path in ffs-core bypasses MVCC entirely, reading raw blocks from the device. This bead connects the two.

From the write path in README:
```
ffs-core: begin write transaction
  → ffs-mvcc: create new block versions (COW)
    → ffs-block: write through cache
  → ffs-mvcc: commit (SSI validation)
```

## DESIGN
```rust
/// MVCC-aware block device wrapper
pub struct MvccBlockDevice<D: BlockDevice> {
    inner: D,
    store: Arc<MvccStore>,
}

impl<D: BlockDevice> MvccBlockDevice<D> {
    pub fn read(&self, block: BlockNumber, snapshot: Snapshot, cx: &Cx) -> Result<BlockBuf> {
        // 1. Check MvccStore for version visible to snapshot
        // 2. If found, return versioned data
        // 3. If not, fall back to inner device
    }
    
    pub fn write(&self, block: BlockNumber, data: &[u8], txn: &mut Transaction, cx: &Cx) -> Result<()> {
        // 1. Stage new version in transaction write-set
        // 2. Don't write to device yet (COW)
    }
}
```

## DELIVERABLES
1. `MvccBlockDevice<D: BlockDevice>` struct in ffs-mvcc or ffs-core
2. Transaction wrapper with begin/commit/abort lifecycle
3. Integration into OpenFs read path (snapshot reads)
4. Cache coherence: dirty blocks from MVCC go through cache write-back
5. Tests proving snapshot isolation with real block I/O

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit: Two concurrent readers see consistent snapshots
2. Unit: Writer creates new version, reader on old snapshot doesn't see it
3. Unit: FCW conflict correctly aborts second committer
4. Unit: Committed writes visible to subsequent transactions
5. Unit: Abort discards staged writes
6. Integration: Read-modify-write cycle with snapshot isolation
7. Integration: ARC cache hit for versioned block
8. Benchmark: No performance regression >5% on read path

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
### Read path logging
- mvcc_read_start (trace): block, snapshot
- mvcc_version_hit (trace): block, version_commit_seq
- mvcc_version_miss (trace): block, snapshot (falling back to device)
- mvcc_read_complete (trace): block, source (mvcc/device), duration_us

### Write path logging
- mvcc_write_stage (trace): block, txn_id, data_len
- mvcc_write_conflict (debug): block, txn_id, conflicting_commit_seq

### Transaction logging
- txn_begin (debug): txn_id, snapshot_seq
- txn_commit_start (debug): txn_id, write_set_size, read_set_size
- txn_commit_success (info): txn_id, commit_seq, duration_us
- txn_commit_conflict (warn): txn_id, conflict_type (fcw/ssi), conflicting_block
- txn_abort (debug): txn_id, reason

### Cache coherence logging
- cache_invalidate (trace): block, reason (mvcc_commit)
- cache_writeback (trace): block, version_commit_seq

### Performance logging
- slow_txn_commit (info): txn_id, duration_ms (if > 100ms)
- large_write_set (debug): txn_id, write_set_size (if > 1000)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. All existing read-path tests still pass
2. MVCC snapshot isolation verified with block-level I/O
3. No performance regression >5% on read path
4. Cache coherence maintained
5. Logging sufficient for debugging isolation violations
