title: Implement FUSE write operations dispatch (create/mkdir/write/unlink/rename)
description:
# Implement FUSE write operations dispatch

## GOAL
Add write operation handlers to FrankenFuse so that mounted filesystems support mutation operations.

## BACKGROUND
Currently ffs-fuse only handles read operations (getattr, lookup, readdir, read, readlink). Write operations need:
1. FUSE protocol handlers in FrankenFuse
2. Delegation to FsOps trait methods
3. Transaction wrapping (begin → operation → commit)
4. Error mapping for write-specific errors (ENOSPC, EROFS, EEXIST, etc.)

## DELIVERABLES
### Phase 1: File creation and writing
1. `create(parent, name, mode, umask, flags)` → create file + open
2. `write(ino, fh, offset, data, flags)` → write data to file
3. `setattr(ino, mode, uid, gid, size, atime, mtime)` → chmod/chown/truncate

### Phase 2: Directory operations  
4. `mkdir(parent, name, mode, umask)` → create directory
5. `unlink(parent, name)` → remove file
6. `rmdir(parent, name)` → remove directory
7. `rename(parent, name, newparent, newname, flags)` → move/rename

### Phase 3: Link operations
8. `link(ino, newparent, newname)` → hard link
9. `symlink(parent, name, link)` → symbolic link
10. `mknod(parent, name, mode, rdev)` → device/fifo/socket

### Each handler must:
- Check read-only mode → EROFS
- Begin MVCC transaction
- Delegate to FsOps implementation
- Commit or abort transaction
- Map errors to errno
- Log operation at appropriate level

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit: create + write + read roundtrip
2. Unit: mkdir + create file inside + readdir
3. Unit: unlink reduces link count
4. Unit: rmdir on non-empty → ENOTEMPTY
5. Unit: rename across directories
6. Unit: EROFS on read-only mount
7. Unit: ENOSPC when disk full (simulated)
8. Integration: 100 concurrent file creates
9. Property: Random create/delete sequences maintain consistency

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
### Operation-level logging (all at debug unless error)
- create (debug): parent_ino, name, mode, result_ino
- write (trace): ino, offset, len, written_bytes (not data content)
- setattr (debug): ino, changed_fields (mode/size/time), old_values, new_values
- mkdir (debug): parent_ino, name, mode, result_ino
- unlink (debug): parent_ino, name, target_ino, remaining_links
- rmdir (debug): parent_ino, name, target_ino
- rename (debug): old_parent, old_name, new_parent, new_name, flags

### Transaction logging
- txn_begin (trace): txn_id, operation, inode(s)
- txn_commit (trace): txn_id, commit_seq, duration_us
- txn_abort (debug): txn_id, reason

### Error logging
- write_error (warn): operation, ino, errno, error_context
- permission_denied (info): operation, ino, uid, required_mode
- disk_full (warn): operation, requested_blocks, available_blocks

### Performance logging
- slow_operation (info): operation, ino, duration_ms (if > 100ms)

## POSIX COMPLIANCE NOTES
- create: EEXIST if exists and O_EXCL, ENOSPC if disk full
- mkdir: EEXIST, EACCES for permission
- unlink: EISDIR (use rmdir instead), ENOENT
- rmdir: ENOTEMPTY, ENOTDIR
- rename: atomic replace semantics (POSIX.1-2017)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. All 10 FUSE write operations implemented
2. Transaction wrapping correct (commit on success, abort on error)
3. Read-only mount correctly rejects writes with EROFS
4. Errno mapping matches POSIX expectations
5. All operations logged with sufficient context for debugging

title: Implement crash recovery on mount after unclean shutdown
description:
# Implement crash recovery on mount after unclean shutdown

## GOAL
When FrankenFS mounts a filesystem image that was not cleanly unmounted (crash, SIGKILL, power loss), it must detect the unclean state and perform recovery before serving any requests.

## BACKGROUND
Unclean shutdown can leave:
- Uncommitted MVCC transactions (partial writes in version chains)
- Stale RaptorQ symbols (dirty groups not refreshed)
- Incomplete journal transactions (JBD2 write path)
- Dirty inode/block caches not flushed to disk

Without crash recovery, mounting after a crash could expose partially-written data, stale versions, or inconsistent metadata.

## DESIGN

### Unclean Shutdown Detection
- Superblock dirty flag: set on mount, cleared on clean unmount
- If dirty flag is set on mount: unclean shutdown detected
- Journal recovery: check for uncommitted journal transactions

### Recovery Steps (ordered)
1. Journal replay: apply committed but unflushed journal transactions
2. MVCC rollback: abort any in-flight transactions (no commit record = abort)
3. Version chain cleanup: remove uncommitted versions from chains
4. RaptorQ symbol validation: mark all groups as needing re-verification
5. Trigger immediate scrub of metadata-critical groups (superblock, GDT, inode tables)
6. Clear superblock dirty flag after recovery completes
7. Log all recovery actions to evidence ledger

### Integration Points
- ffs-cli mount command: detect unclean state before serving FUSE
- Journal replay (bd-1xe.4): already handles ext4 journal replay
- MVCC subsystem: needs abort/rollback API for in-flight transactions
- Scrub daemon: needs priority queue for post-recovery metadata verification

### Error Handling
- If recovery fails (journal corrupt, metadata unreadable): refuse to mount, log detailed error
- If recovery partial (some transactions recovered, others not): mount read-only, log warning
- Never silently ignore unclean state

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Unclean shutdown detected via superblock dirty flag
- [ ] Journal transactions replayed correctly on recovery mount
- [ ] In-flight MVCC transactions aborted cleanly
- [ ] RaptorQ symbols re-verified after crash recovery
- [ ] Evidence ledger records all recovery actions
- [ ] Mount refuses if recovery fails completely
- [ ] Read-only fallback if recovery is partial
- [ ] Unit tests: mock unclean state, verify recovery steps

title: E2E test: mount, write 10000 files, unmount, remount, verify all files
description:
# E2E test: mount, write 10000 files, unmount, remount, verify all files

## GOAL
Verify that FrankenFS correctly persists data across mount/unmount cycles. This is the fundamental persistence correctness test.

## TEST SCENARIO

### Phase 1: Write
1. Create fresh 512MB ext4 image with FrankenFS
2. Mount via FUSE (read-write mode)
3. Create directory tree: 100 directories, 100 files each = 10000 files
4. Each file: deterministic content based on path (e.g., BLAKE3(path) repeated to fill 4KB)
5. Compute BLAKE3 checksum manifest for all 10000 files
6. Unmount cleanly

### Phase 2: Verify
7. Remount the same image (read-only mode)
8. Walk entire directory tree, verify all 10000 files present
9. Read each file, verify BLAKE3 checksum matches manifest
10. Verify directory structure (ls each directory, check file count)
11. Unmount

### Phase 3: Read-Write Cycle
12. Remount read-write
13. Modify 1000 random files (new deterministic content)
14. Delete 500 random files
15. Create 500 new files
16. Update manifest
17. Unmount, remount, verify updated manifest

### Timing Requirements
- Phase 1: < 30s for 10000 files on SSD
- Phase 2: < 15s for verification
- Phase 3: < 20s for modifications + verification

### Failure Modes to Detect
- File content corruption (checksum mismatch)
- Missing files (not persisted to disk)
- Extra files (stale data from previous test)
- Directory entry corruption (wrong file count)
- Permission/ownership corruption

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All 10000 files survive mount/unmount cycle with correct content
- [ ] Directory structure exactly matches expected layout
- [ ] Read-write-modify cycle preserves all changes
- [ ] Test is deterministic (same seed = same result)
- [ ] Test completes in < 120s total
- [ ] Test passes in CI without root (FUSE with allow_other or user mount)
close_reason: done

title: E2E test: SIGKILL during write, remount, verify consistency
description:
# E2E test: SIGKILL during write, remount, verify consistency

## GOAL
Verify that FrankenFS maintains consistency guarantees after an unclean shutdown (SIGKILL during active writes). The filesystem must be mountable, crash recovery must work, and all committed data must be intact.

## TEST SCENARIO

### Phase 1: Setup
1. Create fresh 256MB ext4 image
2. Mount via FUSE, write baseline dataset (500 files, checksums recorded)
3. fsync all files, verify baseline is durable
4. Begin continuous write workload (background thread writing new files)

### Phase 2: Crash
5. After 2 seconds of active writing, send SIGKILL to FUSE process
6. Record which files had fsync called vs which were in-flight

### Phase 3: Recovery
7. Remount the filesystem image
8. Crash recovery should trigger automatically (journal replay, MVCC rollback)
9. Record evidence ledger output

### Phase 4: Verification
10. All baseline files (pre-crash) must be intact with correct checksums
11. Files that had fsync completed must be intact
12. Files that were in-flight at SIGKILL time: acceptable to be missing or truncated, but:
    - Must NOT contain garbage data
    - Must NOT corrupt other files
    - Directory must be consistent (no dangling entries)
13. No filesystem-level corruption (fsck-equivalent check passes)

### Invariants
- Atomicity: a file write either fully committed or fully absent
- No cross-file corruption: crash during file A write must never affect file B
- Metadata consistency: directory entries match existing inodes
- Journal consistency: no partial journal transactions visible

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Filesystem mounts after SIGKILL without errors
- [ ] All pre-crash baseline files intact with correct checksums
- [ ] All fsync'd files intact
- [ ] In-flight files are either complete or cleanly absent (no partial garbage)
- [ ] No cross-file corruption
- [ ] Evidence ledger records crash recovery actions
- [ ] Test is reproducible (deterministic write pattern)
- [ ] Test completes in < 60s

- SIGTERM triggers clean unmount sequence
- Double-unmount is idempotent (no panic)
- Mount with invalid image returns descriptive error

### 3. Errno Mapping Tests
- Every FfsError variant maps to correct errno
- Unknown errors map to EIO
- Cancelled maps to EINTR
- CorruptData maps to EIO
- NoSpace maps to ENOSPC
- PermissionDenied maps to EACCES

### 4. State Tests
- FsOps state is Send + Sync (compile-time test)
- Concurrent getattr calls do not race
- Cache access under lock is bounded (no starvation)

title: EPIC: SOS Barrier Certificate Expansion [Score 10.0]
description:
Expand SOS barrier certificates to new invariants. 2 invariants currently live in production. Pattern proven: MOSEK/SCS offline synthesis generates Sum-of-Squares polynomial decomposition, producing Gram matrix Q. Runtime evaluates the certificate in O(d^2) time at <30ns. Need to extend to: (1) allocator fragmentation bounds — prove that fragmentation ratio stays within polynomial envelope, (2) thread-safety invariants for concurrent allocation — prove mutual exclusion and ordering properties as polynomial constraints, (3) memory pressure guards — prove that allocation headroom satisfies safety margin as SOS certificate, (4) size-class admissibility — prove that requested sizes map to valid size classes with bounded waste. Each new certificate follows the same pipeline: formulate the safety property as a polynomial optimization problem, solve offline via MOSEK or SCS semidefinite programming, extract the Gram matrix Q, compile the result as &'static const data with SHA-256 proof hash for integrity verification. The certificates provide formal mathematical guarantees that specific invariants hold, replacing runtime checks with compile-time-proven bounds. This is the highest-value alien pattern in the project (Score 10.0) because it eliminates entire classes of runtime failure modes with zero runtime overhead beyond the O(d^2) evaluation.

title: SOS certificate: allocator fragmentation bound
description: Formulate allocator fragmentation ratio as a polynomial optimization problem. The fragmentation bound ensures that the ratio of wasted memory to allocated memory stays within a provably safe envelope. Steps: (1) Model fragmentation as polynomial f(x) where x = (allocation_count, free_count, size_class_vector, arena_utilization). (2) Formulate the invariant: f(x) <= threshold for all reachable states. (3) Solve offline via MOSEK SDP to find SOS decomposition: threshold - f(x) = sigma(x) where sigma is SOS. (4) Extract Gram matrix Q from the SOS decomposition. (5) Compile Q as &'static const [f64; N*N] with SHA-256 hash of the matrix bytes. (6) Runtime evaluation: compute monomial basis z(x), evaluate z^T * Q * z in O(d^2). Target: <30ns evaluation, zero heap allocation during check. The certificate replaces the current runtime fragmentation heuristic with a mathematically proven bound.
design:
**Alien CS Reference:** Section 14.1 / graveyard Score 10.0. SOS barrier certificates from Prajna & Jadbabaie (2004). MOSEK SDP solver for offline Gram matrix synthesis. Runtime evaluation follows the polynomial certificate evaluation pattern from Parrilo (2003).

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- Define SosCertificate<const D: usize> struct holding gram_matrix: [[f64; D]; D], proof_hash: [u8; 32], monomial_degree: u32.
- Compile Gram matrix Q as &'static SosCertificate<D> via const evaluation or build.rs code generation from MOSEK output.
- Runtime evaluate() method: compute monomial basis z(x) for state vector x, return z^T * Q * z. Must be #[inline(always)] on hot path.
- SHA-256 integrity check at startup: verify proof_hash matches sha256(gram_matrix_bytes).
- All matrix operations use fixed-size arrays (no heap allocation) for the <30ns target.
acceptance_criteria:
1. SosCertificate<D> struct compiles with const D up to 16 (covering polynomial degree up to 4 for 4-variable state).
2. evaluate() returns correct value for known test vectors (hand-computed from small Gram matrices).
3. evaluate() latency <30ns at p99 measured by criterion with --measurement-time=10.
4. SHA-256 integrity check passes for valid certificates and rejects tampered matrices.
5. Build.rs pipeline reads MOSEK .task output and generates const SosCertificate literal.
6. Fragmentation ratio stays within certified envelope under sawtooth allocation benchmark (10K alloc/free cycles).
7. Certificate evaluates to negative value when fragmentation ratio artificially exceeds threshold (inject via test hook).
notes:
**Logging Requirements:**
- Certificate evaluation results logged at tracing::trace!(target: sos_barrier, certificate=fragmentation, value, state_vector).
- Negative certificate evaluations logged at tracing::warn!(target: sos_barrier, certificate=fragmentation, violation, value, state_vector).
- Startup integrity check logged at tracing::info!(target: sos_barrier, certificate=fragmentation, hash_valid, matrix_dim).

title: SOS certificate: thread-safety invariant for concurrent allocation
description:
Formulate thread-safety for concurrent allocation as polynomial constraints amenable to SOS certification. The invariant ensures that concurrent allocator operations maintain mutual exclusion on shared arena metadata and ordering properties on free-list pointers. Steps: (1) Model the concurrent state as polynomial variables: thread_count, lock_state (0/1 encoded), arena_owner, free_list_head, allocation_epoch. (2) Formulate safety property: no two threads simultaneously modify the same arena's free list — encode as polynomial inequality. (3) Solve offline via MOSEK/SCS to find SOS witness. (4) Extract Gram matrix Q. (5) Compile as &'static const data with SHA-256 proof hash. (6) Runtime: evaluate certificate at allocation entry points. If certificate evaluation yields negative value, the allocation path has entered an unsafe concurrent state and the TSM membrane triggers hardened-mode escalation. This provides a mathematical proof that the allocator's concurrency invariants hold, replacing lock-based reasoning with algebraic certificates.

## Acceptance Criteria
See `acceptance_criteria` field.
design:
**Alien CS Reference:** Section 14.1 / graveyard Score 10.0. SOS barrier certificates from Prajna & Jadbabaie (2004). Concurrent safety modeled as polynomial constraints on lock-state encoding, following Lasserre (2001) moment hierarchy for polynomial optimization.

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- Reuse SosCertificate<D> from bd-2ste.1. State vector: (thread_count, lock_state_encoded, arena_owner_id, free_list_gen, alloc_epoch).
- Certificate evaluation inlined at allocator entry points via #[inline(always)] wrapper.
- Negative evaluation triggers TSM hardened-mode escalation via tsm::escalate(ViolationKind::ConcurrentUnsafe).
- All polynomial variables derived from existing allocator state -- no additional memory reads required.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria
1. Thread-safety certificate evaluates correctly for single-threaded allocation (always positive).
2. Certificate detects simulated concurrent modification (two threads touching same arena free list).
3. Evaluation latency <30ns at p99 under 8-thread contention.
4. TSM escalation triggers within 1 operation of certificate violation detection.
5. No false positives under normal concurrent allocation patterns (16 threads, 100K alloc/free cycles).
6. SHA-256 proof hash verified at startup alongside fragmentation certificate.
7. Evidence ledger records every escalation with thread IDs, arena ID, and certificate value.

- Tooling contract: deterministic orchestration/traceability uses `/dp/asupersync`, and deterministic diff/snapshot/TUI evidence uses `/dp/frankentui`.

title: SOS certificate: memory pressure guard
description:
Formulate memory pressure detection as a polynomial optimization problem with SOS certification. The guard ensures that allocation headroom (available memory relative to peak demand) satisfies a safety margin before allowing new allocations. Steps: (1) Model pressure state as polynomial variables: heap_used, heap_capacity, recent_alloc_rate, recent_free_rate, mmap_count, arena_count. (2) Formulate invariant: headroom(x) = capacity - used - projected_demand(rate, window) >= margin, expressed as polynomial inequality. (3) Solve offline via SDP: find SOS decomposition proving headroom >= margin over the reachable state polytope. (4) Extract Gram matrix Q, compile as const data with SHA-256 hash. (5) Runtime: evaluate z^T*Q*z at each allocation. If certificate value drops below zero, trigger backpressure (refuse allocation, return ENOMEM) before actual OOM. This replaces heuristic pressure detection with a formally proven bound, ensuring the system never enters unrecoverable OOM states within the certified envelope.

## Acceptance Criteria
See `acceptance_criteria` field.
design:
**Alien CS Reference:** Section 14.1 / graveyard Score 10.0. Memory pressure as polynomial optimization from Prajna & Jadbabaie (2004). Headroom computation follows the SOS feasibility framework from Parrilo (2003).

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- State vector: (heap_used: u64, heap_capacity: u64, alloc_rate_ema: f64, free_rate_ema: f64, mmap_count: u32, arena_count: u32).
- EMA (exponential moving average) for rates computed with alpha=0.1, updated on each alloc/free.
- Certificate evaluation at allocation entry: if negative, return ENOMEM immediately (backpressure).
- Backpressure path must NOT allocate (no error formatting, no logging that allocates).
- Use fixed-point arithmetic if f64 evaluation exceeds 30ns budget.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria
1. Certificate correctly predicts OOM when heap_used approaches heap_capacity under linear allocation.
2. Backpressure (ENOMEM) triggers before actual kernel OOM killer would fire.
3. No false ENOMEM under normal allocation patterns (p99.9 false positive rate < 0.01%).
4. Evaluation latency <30ns including EMA rate update.
5. System recovers after backpressure: when free operations reduce pressure, certificate becomes positive and allocations resume.
6. Stress test: 64 threads allocating at maximum rate with bounded heap -- zero OOM kills with certificate active.
7. Certificate value correlates with actual headroom (R-squared > 0.95 on synthetic workload).

### Mandatory Verification Gate
- Comprehensive unit tests are required for all touched logic: positive, negative, adversarial, and regression.
- Deterministic e2e scripts are required for all externally visible behavior in strict and hardened mode where relevant.
- Structured logs are mandatory for unit/e2e runs with fields: `trace_id`, `mode`, `api_family`, `symbol`, `decision_path`, `healing_action`, `errno`, `latency_ns`, `artifact_refs`.
- Closure evidence must include exact test commands, expected outputs/thresholds, and representative failure signatures.
- CI must persist logs, diffs, and reports with deterministic naming and retention for replay/triage.
- Tooling contract: deterministic orchestration/traceability uses `/dp/asupersync`, and deterministic diff/snapshot/TUI evidence uses `/dp/frankentui`.
notes:
**Logging Requirements:**
- tracing::trace!(target: sos_barrier, certificate=memory_pressure, value, heap_used, heap_capacity, alloc_rate) per evaluation.
- tracing::warn!(target: sos_barrier, certificate=memory_pressure, backpressure_triggered, value, heap_used) on ENOMEM.
- Periodic summary every 10K ops: pressure_level, headroom_pct, backpressure_count.

### Mandatory Test/E2E Logging Checklist
- Test command set is documented in bead notes before closure (unit + e2e + perf where applicable).
- Expected output and pass/fail thresholds are documented per command.
- Failure triage snippets are documented (top failure classes + where to inspect artifacts).
- Evidence index entry links logs, parity diffs, and benchmark/proof artifacts.
- Overload behavior logging is required when applicable: pressure signal, degradation mode, selected policy, guard decision, rollback trigger.

title: SOS certificate: size-class admissibility
description:
Formulate size-class mapping admissibility as a polynomial optimization problem with SOS certification. The certificate proves that every requested allocation size maps to a valid size class with bounded internal fragmentation (waste). Steps: (1) Model as polynomial: requested_size, mapped_class_size, waste = mapped_class_size - requested_size. (2) Formulate invariant: for all valid requested_size in [1, MAX_ALLOC], waste/requested_size <= max_waste_ratio AND mapped_class_size is in the valid size-class set. Encode the size-class set membership as polynomial indicator constraints. (3) Solve offline via MOSEK: find SOS decomposition proving the waste bound holds over the entire input domain. (4) Extract Gram matrix Q, compile as &'static const with SHA-256 hash. (5) Runtime: evaluate certificate for each allocation request to verify the size-class mapping is admissible. Target: <30ns evaluation. This eliminates the possibility of size-class mapping bugs silently causing excessive fragmentation, providing a mathematical guarantee on the allocator's space efficiency.

## Acceptance Criteria
See `acceptance_criteria` field.
design:
**Alien CS Reference:** Section 14.1 / graveyard Score 10.0. Size-class admissibility as polynomial feasibility from Prajna & Jadbabaie (2004). Waste bound certification uses SOS decomposition over bounded integer domains.

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- State vector: (requested_size: usize, mapped_class_size: usize). Both cast to f64 for polynomial evaluation.
- Certificate encodes: waste_ratio = (mapped_class_size - requested_size) / requested_size <= MAX_WASTE_RATIO.
- Size-class set membership encoded as polynomial indicator: product of (size - valid_class_i) terms.
- Precompute certificate for all valid size classes at build time; runtime is a table lookup + certificate check.
- MAX_WASTE_RATIO configurable at compile time (default 0.25 = 25% waste).
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria
1. Certificate validates all current size classes produce waste ratio <= MAX_WASTE_RATIO.
2. Certificate rejects artificially bad size-class mapping (e.g., 17-byte request mapped to 256-byte class).
3. Evaluation latency <30ns including size-class lookup.
4. All allocation sizes from 1 to MAX_ALLOC (default 64KB for small allocations) covered by certificate.
5. Build-time generation produces certificate for configurable size-class tables.
6. Regression test: adding a new size class requires certificate regeneration (CI enforces).
7. Waste ratio measurement under real workload matches certificate prediction (within 5% tolerance).

### Mandatory Verification Gate
- Comprehensive unit tests are required for all touched logic: positive, negative, adversarial, and regression.
- Deterministic e2e scripts are required for all externally visible behavior in strict and hardened mode where relevant.
- Structured logs are mandatory for unit/e2e runs with fields: `trace_id`, `mode`, `api_family`, `symbol`, `decision_path`, `healing_action`, `errno`, `latency_ns`, `artifact_refs`.
- Closure evidence must include exact test commands, expected outputs/thresholds, and representative failure signatures.
- CI must persist logs, diffs, and reports with deterministic naming and retention for replay/triage.
- Tooling contract: deterministic orchestration/traceability uses `/dp/asupersync`, and deterministic diff/snapshot/TUI evidence uses `/dp/frankentui`.

title: Property-based testing framework
description:
Property-based testing for algorithmic correctness.

Goal: Use property testing to verify implementation invariants.

Properties by Category:

String Operations:
- strlen(s) == position of first null byte
- strcmp(a, a) == 0 (reflexivity)
- strcmp(a, b) == -strcmp(b, a) (antisymmetry)
- memcpy(dst, src, n); memcmp(dst, src, n) == 0

Allocator:
- malloc(n) returns aligned pointer or null
- malloc(n) followed by free(p) leaves consistent state
- realloc preserves content up to min(old_size, new_size)

Math:
- sin²(x) + cos²(x) ≈ 1
- exp(log(x)) ≈ x for x > 0
- abs(x) >= 0
- copysign(abs(x), y) == copysign(x, y) when x >= 0

Membrane:
- validate(p) after malloc(p) returns Valid
- validate(p) after free(p) returns Freed or Quarantined
- SafetyState lattice join is commutative

Infrastructure:
- proptest crate for Rust
- Custom strategies for libc types
- Shrinking for minimal counterexamples

Success Criteria:
- Properties defined for all major function families
- 10000+ test cases per property
- All properties pass

title: PCC at FFI boundary (section 11.9, Score 3.0)
description:
Implement Proof-Carrying Code (PCC) at the FFI boundary between FrankenLibC and calling programs. PCC attaches a machine-checkable proof to code that crosses a trust boundary. For FrankenLibC, the FFI boundary is where untrusted C code calls into the libc. PCC can prove: (1) Calling convention compliance — the caller has set up the stack frame, registers, and arguments correctly according to the System V ABI. (2) Pointer validity — pointer arguments passed to libc functions point to valid, accessible memory regions. (3) Size consistency — buffer size arguments match actual buffer sizes. Implementation: (a) At the FFI entry point, the PCC verifier checks the proof attached to the call. If the proof verifies, skip TSM runtime checks (they are proven unnecessary). If no proof or invalid proof, fall through to full TSM validation. (b) Proof generation: the calling program's compiler (or a post-compilation pass) generates proofs for each libc call site. (c) Proof format: use a compact proof representation (e.g., Foundational PCC with LF type theory). (d) Performance target: proof verification <5ns (faster than full TSM validation at 20ns). Net effect: PCC-verified call sites get near-zero overhead, unverified call sites get full TSM protection.

**Alien CS Reference:** Section 11.9 of the graveyard (Score 3.0). PCC originated from Necula (1997). Foundational PCC (Appel & Felten 2001) uses LF type theory for compact proofs. The pattern maps to FrankenLibC's FFI trust boundary where untrusted C code enters the libc.

**Rust Implementation Guidance:**
- Define ProofToken as an opaque ZST (zero-sized type) constructed only by the PCC verifier.
- FFI entry points check thread-local Option<ProofToken> (not ABI-visible parameter) for backward compatibility.
- Proof format: minimal bytecode verified by a stack-based checker in <5ns.
- PccVerifier struct with verify(proof_bytes: &[u8], call_site: CallSiteDescriptor) -> Option<ProofToken>.
- If proof verification fails or no proof present, full TSM validation runs (graceful degradation).

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. PccVerifier implemented with stack-based proof checker supporting: pointer-in-bounds, size-matches-allocation, alignment-correct proof obligations.
2. Proof verification latency <5ns for simple proofs (stack buffer with known size) measured by criterion.
3. At least 3 FFI entry points (memcpy, snprintf, malloc) instrumented with PCC fast-path.
4. When proof present and valid: TSM validation is skipped, measurable latency reduction (>10ns savings).
5. When proof absent or invalid: full TSM validation runs, no behavior change vs current (regression test).
6. Proof format specification document committed to docs/pcc_proof_format.md.
7. Evidence ledger records PCC decisions: call_site, proof_present, proof_valid, action (fast_path or full_tsm).

**Logging Requirements:**
- Every PCC verification: call_site, proof_size_bytes, verification_result, verification_time_ns via tracing::debug!(target: "pcc").
- Periodic summary (every 10K calls): PCC hit rate, average verification time, TSM bypass count.
- Proof failures at WARN level with truncated proof bytes for debugging.

notes:
## Purpose (North Star)
FrankenLibC is a clean-room Rust libc targeting:
- drop-in ABI compatibility with glibc for declared targets (symbols + versions + calling conventions + errno + observable side effects),
- full POSIX coverage plus GNU/glibc extensions where real software depends on them,
- memory safety achieved structurally via a Transparent Safety Membrane (TSM) at the C ABI boundary,
- evidence-driven correctness and performance via deterministic conformance fixtures, E2E scenarios, and regression gates.

This epic is the master closure DAG for reaching a *releaseable* end-state at the currently declared replacement level, and for defining what “finished” means as we graduate to L1/L2/L3.

## Non-Negotiable Contracts (Project Law)
These are not aspirational; they must be enforced by tests/gates:
1. Full POSIX coverage target with GNU compatibility where expected by real software.
2. ABI compatibility is mandatory (symbols, versions, calling conventions, errno behavior).
3. Runtime mode switch is mandatory: `FRANKENLIBC_MODE=strict|hardened` (default `strict`), process-level, immutable after init.
4. Clean-room porting: spec-first; never line-by-line translate legacy glibc.
5. `/dp/asupersync` and `/dp/frankentui` are mandatory build/test tooling (NOT runtime libc deps).
6. Mandatory methods:
   - alien-artifact-coding: formal / lattice / evidence / guarantees; but compiled to simple runtime artifacts.
   - extreme-software-optimization: profile-first; behavior proofs; one lever per change.

## Replacement Levels (What “Finished” Means)
Replacement level definitions and artifacts are part of the release contract:
- L0 (Interpose): `LD_PRELOAD` on host glibc; allowed taxonomy includes `GlibcCallThrough` and `Stub`.
- L1 (Hardened Interpose): L0 but hardened is the default runtime mode; hard-parts and evidence gates become stricter.
- L2 (Partial Replace): no host glibc required for a declared subset of programs/surfaces; CRT/syscall glue and core pthread primitives are required.
- L3 (Full Replace): no host glibc required for general dynamic programs; rtld/loader hard-parts must be real.

Current claim (see README + `tests/conformance/replacement_levels.json`): L0.

## Mode Contract (Strict vs Hardened)
Strict mode:
- objective: maximize ABI-compatible observational equivalence on defined inputs.
- repairs are NOT admissible; invalid/undefined inputs must not be “helpfully rewritten”.

Hardened mode:
- objective: prevent memory-unsafe outcomes via deterministic repair/deny actions.
- every repair/deny path must emit auditable evidence.

Mode selection must be deterministic and immutable for the process lifetime.

## TSM Contract (Transparent Safety Membrane)
The ABI boundary is treated as an untrusted input surface.
Every entrypoint performs mode-aware validation and then routes:
`ABI -> membrane (validate/sanitize/repair/audit) -> core (safe kernels) | raw syscalls | controlled callthrough (L0 only)`.

TSM pipeline is explicitly performance-budgeted:
- strict overhead target: <20ns/call for membrane-gated hot paths
- hardened overhead target: <200ns/call for membrane-gated hot paths

## Evidence-Driven Completion (What Closes Beads)
No feature is “done” without:
- fixture-based conformance evidence (strict + hardened where relevant),
- benchmark evidence (baseline + delta; plus isomorphism/behavior proof for optimizations),
- deterministic E2E coverage for representative real programs (LD_PRELOAD smoke/stress/fault/stability),
- structured logs that are joinable across artifacts (trace_id, mode, gate, symbol/api_family, outcome, timing, artifact refs).

The closure program is centered around:
- `bd-5fw`: release-exit contract + deterministic closure protocol.
- `bd-33p`: evidence/logging unification and compliance gates.
- `bd-b5a`: deterministic E2E suite.
- `bd-15n` + `bd-2tq`: conformance expansion and POSIX suite.
- `bd-30o`: optimization closure with proofs.
- `bd-29b`: runtime config/env truth and drift prevention.

## Phase Map (From PLAN_TO_PORT_GLIBC_TO_RUST.md, but Self-Contained Here)
This is the canonical phase model for the port, expressed as bead workstreams:

Phase 0: Spec Lock + Scope Matrix
- Deliver: explicit scope ledger (what we claim), strict/hardened semantics per family, and traceability anchors.
- Evidence: matrix rows for critique beads; fixtures reference POSIX/C/TSM specs; no hidden exclusions.
- Primary beads: `bd-2vv` (surface classification), `bd-15n` (fixtures), `bd-29b` (runtime knobs), `bd-3rw` (docs drift gates).

Phase 1: ABI Spine + Mode Gate
- Deliver: a stable ABI veneer + immutable mode initialization + per-call context propagation.
- Evidence: unit/e2e tests proving strict/hardened routing and trace propagation.
- Primary beads: `bd-33p` (trace/evidence contract), plus ABI/core/membrane integration beads under symbol families.

Phase 2: Provenance Fabric + Allocator Safety Core
- Deliver: provenance/lifetime metadata, quarantine, and allocator boundary correctness.
- Evidence: strict allocator fixtures + hardened healing oracle + CVE corpus scenarios.
- Primary beads: `bd-1m5` (CVE arena), `bd-1oz` (fuzz), conformance tasks under `bd-15n`.

Phase 3: Bootstrap API Completion (String/Memory)
- Deliver: mem*/str* family correctness and performance with strict/hardened split.
- Evidence: fixtures + benchmarks + hot-kernel behavior proofs.
- Primary beads: conformance/benchmark work under `bd-15n` and `bd-30o`.

Phase 4: Full POSIX Expansion

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Guidelines Complete (GentleOwl)

Document: crates/glibc-rs-membrane/src/runtime_math/controller_registration_guidelines.md

### 8-Step Checklist:

1. **Create module file** — exports: State enum (0..3), Summary struct, Controller struct with new/observe_and_update/state/summary. Required invariants: deterministic init, O(1) updates, saturating arithmetic.
2. **Declare pub mod** — alphabetical order in mod.rs declarations + use imports.
3. **Add Mutex<Controller> field** — to RuntimeMathKernel struct.
4. **Add cached AtomicU8** — cached_<name>_state for hot-path severity reads.
5. **Initialize in new()** — Mutex::new + AtomicU8::new(0).
6. **Wire into observe_validation_result()** — Tier A (cadence-gated meta on base_severity) or Tier B (domain-specific base). CRITICAL: no Mutex in fusion severity literal.
7. **Add to fusion severity vector** — increment META_SEVERITY_LEN, update fusion::SIGNALS, add cached load at next index.
8. **Add snapshot fields** — additive only, document units/range, wire in snapshot() method.

### Key Constraints Documented:
- No Mutex locks in fusion severity aggregation literal (enforced by compile-time test)
- No float math on strict decide() hot path (use integer ppm)
- Snapshot schema is additive-only (never remove/rename)
- Conservative merge: new controllers can only escalate, never de-escalate
- All controllers must impl Default
- State enum values must be contiguous 0..3

### Reference Implementation:
- alpha_investing as the canonical example (468 lines, full integration verified)

## Acceptance Criteria
Implementation must preserve all existing functionality and claims while adding deterministic verification coverage.

### Mandatory Verification Gate
- Comprehensive unit tests are required for all touched logic: positive, negative, adversarial, and regression.
- Deterministic e2e scripts are required for all externally visible behavior in strict and hardened mode where relevant.

title: Symbol expansion: stdio family (phased approach)
description:
Complete stdio family coverage - the largest and most complex subsystem.

Current State:
- FILE* operations: mostly GlibcCallThrough
- printf family: partial Implemented (format engine exists)
- scanf family: likely stubs
- fopen/fclose/fread/fwrite: GlibcCallThrough

Target Architecture:
FrankenLibC needs its own FILE structure and buffering:
1. FILE state machine (read/write/append modes)
2. Buffer management (fully buffered, line buffered, unbuffered)
3. Error and EOF flag handling
4. Wide character support (fwide, fwprintf)

Implementation Phases:
Phase 1: Core FILE operations
- fopen, fclose, fflush
- fread, fwrite
- fgetc, fputc, fgets, fputs

Phase 2: Formatted I/O
- printf family (fprintf, sprintf, snprintf, asprintf)
- scanf family (fscanf, sscanf)

Phase 3: Positioning
- fseek, ftell, fgetpos, fsetpos
- rewind

Phase 4: Misc
- freopen, fdopen, fileno
- setvbuf, setbuf
- clearerr, feof, ferror

Testing:
- Unit: each FILE operation in isolation
- Integration: multi-step file processing workflows
- Concurrency: thread-safe FILE operations
- Hardened: handling of invalid FILE pointers

Complexity Warning:
This is ~20% of glibc by LOC. Needs phased approach.

Success Criteria:
- All stdio.h functions classified Implemented
- Zero glibc call-through for stdio
- Python hello world works (heavy stdio user)

## Acceptance Criteria
See `acceptance_criteria` field.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria
Implementation must preserve all existing functionality and claims while adding deterministic verification coverage.

### Mandatory Verification Gate
- Comprehensive unit tests are required for all touched logic: positive, negative, adversarial, and regression.
- Deterministic e2e scripts are required for all externally visible behavior in strict and hardened mode where relevant.
- Structured logs are mandatory for unit/e2e runs with fields: `trace_id`, `mode`, `api_family`, `symbol`, `decision_path`, `healing_action`, `errno`, `latency_ns`, `artifact_refs`.
- Closure evidence must include exact test commands, expected outputs/thresholds, and representative failure signatures.
- CI must persist logs, diffs, and reports with deterministic naming and retention for replay/triage.
- Tooling contract: deterministic orchestration/traceability uses `/dp/asupersync`, and deterministic diff/snapshot/TUI evidence uses `/dp/frankentui`.
notes:

- Test command set is documented in bead notes before closure (unit + e2e + perf where applicable).
- Expected output and pass/fail thresholds are documented per command.
- Failure triage snippets are documented (top failure classes + where to inspect artifacts).
- Evidence index entry links logs, parity diffs, and benchmark/proof artifacts.
- Overload behavior logging is required when applicable: pressure signal, degradation mode, selected policy, guard decision, rollback trigger.

title: Stdio Phase 1: FILE structure and basic I/O
description:
Stdio Phase 1: Core FILE structure and basic operations.

Goal: Implement FrankenLibC's own FILE structure with basic I/O.

FILE Structure Design:
- File descriptor (int fd)
- Buffer pointer and size
- Buffer position (read/write)
- Flags (read/write/append/binary)
- Error and EOF flags
- Lock for thread safety
- Wide orientation flag

Phase 1 Functions:
- fopen, fclose, fflush
- fread, fwrite
- fgetc, fputc, ungetc
- fgets, fputs
- fileno

title: Stdio Phase 2: Printf family
description:
Stdio Phase 2: Printf family implementation.

Goal: Complete printf format engine.

Printf Functions:
- printf, fprintf, sprintf, snprintf
- vprintf, vfprintf, vsprintf, vsnprintf
- asprintf, vasprintf (GNU extensions)
- dprintf, vdprintf

Format Specifiers:
- Integer: d, i, u, o, x, X, b (C23)
- Float: f, F, e, E, g, G, a, A
- Character: c, s, p, n, %
- Width and precision: *, digit
- Flags: -, +, space, #, 0
- Length modifiers: hh, h, l, ll, j, z, t, L

Implementation Strategy:
Format engine in frankenlibc-core/src/stdio/printf.rs:
1. Parse format string
2. Extract arguments from va_list
3. Format each specifier
4. Output to destination

Complexity Points:
- Floating-point formatting (Ryu or Dragonbox)
- Positional arguments ($)
- Wide character output (wprintf family)

Testing:
- Unit: each specifier in isolation
- Edge cases: width overflow, precision truncation
- Locale: decimal separator (depends on locale)
- Security: %n restrictions in hardened mode

Success Criteria:
- All specifiers implemented
- Output matches glibc format
- Hardened mode restricts %n

title: Symbol expansion: math family with precision validation
description:
Complete math family coverage with correct rounding.

Current State:
- Basic functions (sin, cos, exp, log): likely Implemented via libm
- Special functions (gamma, bessel): likely stubs
- Float variants (sinf, sinl): partial
- FP environment (fenv): partial

Implementation Strategy:
Most math can delegate to Rust's libm crate or system libm.
Key is ensuring:
1. Correct rounding modes
2. NaN/Inf handling
3. errno setting (EDOM, ERANGE)
4. Exception flags (FE_DIVBYZERO, etc.)

Target Functions:
- Trig: sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2
- Hyperbolic: sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh
- Exponential: exp, exp2, expm1, log, log2, log10, log1p
- Power: pow, sqrt, cbrt, hypot
- Special: lgamma, tgamma, erf, erfc, j0, j1, jn, y0, y1, yn
- Rounding: ceil, floor, trunc, round, nearbyint, rint
- Remainder: fmod, remainder, remquo
- FP manipulation: frexp, ldexp, modf, scalbn, copysign
- Classification: fpclassify, isnan, isinf, isfinite, isnormal
- FP environment: fegetround, fesetround, feclearexcept, etc.

Testing:
- Unit: boundary values (±0, ±Inf, NaN, denormals)
- Precision: compare with mpfr for accuracy
- Rounding modes: test all four modes
- Errno: verify correct errno setting

Notes:
- float/double/long double variants (f, l suffixes)
- Some functions are macros in glibc (type-generic)

Success Criteria:
- All math.h functions classified Implemented
- Precision within 1 ULP of reference
- Correct errno/exception behavior

title: Membrane: TLS cache invalidation on free (prevent CachedValid UAF)
description:
Problem: ptr_validator TLS cache can return CachedValid after free because entries are never invalidated across threads, breaking UAF detection guarantees.

Acceptance:
- Add regression test: validate() -> CachedValid, free(), validate() must NOT return CachedValid and must deny read/write.
- Implement deterministic invalidation mechanism that works cross-thread (epoch/stamp) without allocations.
- Keep strict fast-path overhead minimal (single atomic load/compare per TLS lookup).
notes: Fixed TLS cache stale-hit-after-free bug by adding a global invalidation epoch stamp. Cache entries are tagged with epoch at insert and only hit when epochs match; AllocationArena::free bumps epoch for known pointers. Added regression test tls_cache_does_not_allow_uaf_after_free in ptr_validator.rs. Ran: rustfmt on touched files; cargo test -p glibc-rs-membrane.
close_reason: Added epoch-stamped TLS cache entries and bump-on-free invalidation to prevent stale CachedValid hits after free; added regression test; cargo test -p glibc-rs-membrane passes.

title: [test-hygiene] Tests that hardcode unprivileged behaviour are permanently RED on the root rch fleet
description:
A defect CLASS, found while clearing the unistd_abi_test REDs (LIBC45-47). Filed so the pattern is
searchable rather than rediscovered a fourth time.

THE MECHANISM. rch workers run as root (visible as root@<ip> in every run log). Any test that
asserts a privileged operation FAILS is therefore red on the entire fleet while the code under test
is perfectly correct. These are not flaky: they fail 100% of the time remotely and pass 100% locally,
which is the worst possible signature — it looks like a real regression to anyone running remotely
and like a clean tree to anyone running locally.

FOUR INSTANCES FIXED SO FAR (daaed5036, and the acct pair in the commit citing this bead):
  kexec_load_unprivileged_returns_known_errno        — kexec_load(0,0,NULL,0) is the UNLOAD op and
                                                       SUCCEEDS as root; test asserted rc == -1
  mount_setattr_empty_path_preserves_unprivileged... — asserted the HOST must return -1
  diff_acct_unprivileged_returns_eperm               — acct(path) succeeds as root
  diff_acct_null_filename_returns_eperm_for_unpriv.  — acct(NULL) succeeds as root

THE FIX SHAPE, which is what makes this worth recording. Do NOT simply delete the assertion. In every
case the test already had, or could cheaply gain, a fl-vs-host comparison that holds in BOTH
environments; the privilege-specific assertion is then guarded on geteuid() != 0. Applied that way
each of these tests came out STRONGER than before:
  - kexec_load had NO oracle at all and now compares return+errno against libc::syscall.
  - mount_setattr compared only errno; it now compares the return value too.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH KNOWING. As root these tests really do perform the privileged operation. acct(2)
switches process accounting ON for the whole machine, so the acct gate now disables it again when
privileged. Anyone extending this family should check whether the operation they are testing mutates
global system state before letting it run as root.

VERIFIED CLEAN in this class (ran as root, all green, so they were written tolerantly already):
  conformance_diff_adjtimex 5 passed, conformance_diff_keyctl 7 passed,
  conformance_diff_nice_eperm 1 passed, conformance_diff_set_host_domainname 5 passed.

REMAINING TO AUDIT: the fsopen/fsmount '_preserves_unprivileged_eperm_like_host' family in
stdlib_abi_test.rs (~6 tests). Their '_like_host' naming suggests they compare rather than hardcode,
which would make them safe, but that was NOT verified — stdlib_abi_test was not run in this sweep.
Search term for the whole class: 'unprivileged' or '_eperm' in a test fn name.
close_reason:
FIXED across the whole class. Commits daaed5036 (kexec_load, mount_setattr), 0b94bd68a (acct pair), ac96c75cc (the 11 mount-API tests).

FIFTEEN tests in total were permanently RED on the rch fleet while the code under test was correct:
  kexec_load_unprivileged_returns_known_errno
  mount_setattr_empty_path_preserves_unprivileged_eperm_like_host
  diff_acct_unprivileged_returns_eperm, diff_acct_null_filename_returns_eperm_for_unprivileged
  fsopen x3, fsmount x3, fspick x2, move_mount x3

THE LAST BATCH IS THE ONE WORTH READING. I closed the previous round by flagging the
fsopen/fsmount family as NOT audited, and explicitly refused to infer from the '_like_host' naming
that they compared against the host. That caution was correct: 11 of them were red, and the naming
was simply wrong — fsopen_nonzero_flags_with_valid_fsname_preserves_eperm_like_host had no host arm
at all, only a hardcoded -1/EPERM. Had I trusted the name I would have left a live red family behind
and reported the class as closed.

  before -> test result: FAILED. 6 passed; 11 failed
  after  -> test result: ok. 17 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 469 filtered out (twice)

TWO SUB-SHAPES, both from the same cause: as root fsopen('tmpfs',1) SUCCEEDS and returns a
descriptor, while the NULL-path variants get past the privilege check and report EFAULT(14) instead
of EPERM(1).

WHAT MADE THE BULK TRANSFORM SAFE, since transforming 10 tests at once is exactly how you damage
passing ones: the 10 shared a byte-identical assertion block, and that block CONTAINS EPERM, which
is what kept it off the 13 structurally identical blocks belonging to privilege-independent (EINVAL)
tests. Verified afterwards rather than assumed — 13 bare pairs remain, 0 unguarded EPERM blocks,
EINVAL reference count unchanged at 143.

A MISTAKE I MADE AND CAUGHT: my first version of the fsopen fix compared fd NUMBERS. These tests run
on parallel threads, so another can claim the descriptor between the host call and fl's; it passed
once and failed on the very next run. Comparing fd identity was never the contract. It now compares
success-vs-failure and only compares errno on the failure path, and I ran the gate TWICE to confirm
the race is gone. Worth remembering: any differential test over an fd-returning call must compare
the outcome, not the number.

REAL RESOURCE AND SIDE-EFFECT FIXES, not just assertion guards:
  - fsopen leaked a descriptor on every privileged run; both call sites now close it.
  - the acct gate switches process accounting ON for the whole machine as root, and now switches it
    back off.
  - the fsmount loop takes 'continue' not 'return', so a privileged run still covers the remaining
    flag values instead of silently skipping them.
Three of these tests came out STRONGER than before: kexec_load and fsopen had no oracle at all and
now compare against the kernel; mount_setattr compared only errno and now compares the return value.

VERIFIED CLEAN in the same class (already tolerant): conformance_diff_adjtimex 5 passed,
conformance_diff_keyctl 7 passed, conformance_diff_nice_eperm 1 passed,
conformance_diff_set_host_domainname 5 passed.

Search term for anyone extending this: 'unprivileged' or '_eperm' in a test fn name. And do not
trust a '_like_host' suffix to mean the test actually has a host arm — one of these did not.

title: EPIC: Testing & Fault Injection
description:
# EPIC: Testing & Fault Injection

## PURPOSE
Build a comprehensive fault injection and stress testing framework for FrankenFS. A filesystem that cannot prove it handles failures correctly is not production-worthy. This epic covers: WAL interruption, partial repair, metadata corruption, I/O throttling, crash-replay testing, fsx-style stress, and xfstests compatibility.

## BACKGROUND
Kernel filesystems (ext4, btrfs, XFS) have decades of testing infrastructure: xfstests, fsx, blktests, syzkaller. FrankenFS must build equivalent coverage, with the added dimension of testing its unique features (MVCC, RaptorQ self-healing).

## SCOPE
1. Fault injection primitives (pluggable I/O layer with configurable failures)
2. WAL interruption tests (crash during journal write)
3. Partial repair tests (incomplete RaptorQ symbols)
4. Metadata corruption tests (corrupt specific metadata structures)
5. I/O throttling tests (slow I/O, deadline misses)
6. Crash-replay suite (deterministic crash schedules)
7. fsx-style stress (random operations + verification)
8. xfstests compatibility (run standard FS test suites)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Fault injection layer can inject failures at any I/O point
- [ ] All fault injection tests are deterministic and CI-executable
- [ ] Crash-replay covers 500+ random schedules
- [ ] fsx-style stress runs for configurable duration with corruption checking
- [ ] xfstests generic + ext4 subsets pass

## Success Criteria
1. All children closed
2. Fault injection framework reusable across all scenarios
3. xfstests subset passes (bd-32yn.7)
4. Crash-replay suite covers 500+ schedules
5. CI-executable without hardware dependencies

title: Fault injection: WAL interruption (crash mid-fsync)
description:
# Fault injection: WAL interruption (crash mid-fsync)

## GOAL
Test filesystem behavior when a crash occurs during WAL/journal write (mid-fsync). This is the most critical crash scenario — partial journal records must be handled correctly.

## SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Crash during WAL entry write (before fsync)
- Begin transaction, write WAL entries, crash before fsync
- Expected: on recovery, transaction is cleanly aborted (no partial data)

### Scenario 2: Crash during fsync (partial write to disk)
- WAL entry partially written (torn write)
- Expected: CRC32C detects torn entry, entry discarded, transaction aborted

### Scenario 3: Crash after fsync but before commit record
- WAL data entries durable, but commit record not written
- Expected: transaction aborted (no commit = no visibility)

### Scenario 4: Crash during commit record write
- Commit record partially written
- Expected: CRC32C of commit record fails, transaction aborted

### Scenario 5: Crash after commit record (before cache flush)
- Transaction committed in WAL, but dirty cache blocks not flushed
- Expected: WAL replay reconstructs committed state

## IMPLEMENTATION
- Pluggable I/O layer with injectable failure points
- Failure injection: fail_at_byte(offset) — crash after writing N bytes
- Deterministic: same seed produces same crash point
- Recovery verification: mount after crash, verify filesystem consistent

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All 5 scenarios produce correct recovery behavior
- [ ] No data corruption from partial WAL writes
- [ ] No silent data loss
- [ ] Deterministic and CI-executable
- [ ] Evidence records logged for all recovery actions

title: Fault injection: partial repair symbols (incomplete RaptorQ)
description:
# Fault injection: partial repair symbols (incomplete RaptorQ)

## GOAL
Test filesystem behavior when RaptorQ repair symbols are partially available — some symbols corrupted, some missing, or insufficient symbols for full recovery.

## SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Some repair symbols corrupted
- Corrupt 20% of repair symbols in a block group
- Inject data corruption within RaptorQ decode capacity
- Expected: repair succeeds using remaining symbols

### Scenario 2: Repair symbols insufficient
- Corrupt enough repair symbols that decode fails
- Inject data corruption that now cannot be repaired
- Expected: graceful failure, evidence record logged, no silent data loss

### Scenario 3: Symbol metadata corrupted
- Corrupt the symbol header (checksums, group descriptors)
- Expected: symbols detected as invalid, repair falls back to re-encode or fails gracefully

### Scenario 4: Stale symbols (data changed after symbol generation)
- Write new data to blocks, do NOT refresh repair symbols
- Corrupt the new data blocks
- Expected: repair restores OLD data (stale), system detects version mismatch via BLAKE3

### Scenario 5: Symbol storage I/O errors
- Inject I/O errors when reading repair symbol blocks
- Expected: repair fails gracefully, evidence logged, no panic

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Partial symbol corruption: repair succeeds when capacity allows
- [ ] Insufficient symbols: graceful failure with evidence
- [ ] Stale symbols: version mismatch detected
- [ ] I/O errors: no panic, graceful degradation
- [ ] All scenarios deterministic and CI-executable

title: Fault injection: metadata corruption (superblock, GDT, inodes)
description:
# Fault injection: metadata corruption (superblock, GDT, inodes)

## GOAL
Test filesystem behavior when critical metadata structures are corrupted. Metadata corruption is catastrophic — it can make the entire filesystem unreadable.

## SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Superblock corruption
- Corrupt primary superblock fields (magic number, block count, inode count)
- Expected: mount fails with clear error, backup superblock used if available

### Scenario 2: Group Descriptor Table corruption
- Corrupt GDT entries (block bitmap location, inode bitmap, inode table)
- Expected: affected block groups inaccessible, other groups still readable

### Scenario 3: Inode corruption
- Corrupt individual inode fields (size, block count, extent tree root)
- Expected: affected file inaccessible, other files intact

### Scenario 4: Inode bitmap corruption
- Corrupt inode allocation bitmap
- Expected: allocation inconsistency detected, defensive read behavior

### Scenario 5: Block bitmap corruption
- Corrupt block allocation bitmap
- Expected: allocation inconsistency detected, read-only degradation

### Scenario 6: Extent tree internal node corruption
- Corrupt B-tree internal node in extent tree
- Expected: file partially readable (extents before corruption accessible)

### Recovery Testing
- For each scenario: verify RaptorQ repair (if metadata has 2x overhead) can recover
- If repair impossible: verify graceful degradation and clear error reporting

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Each metadata corruption type produces appropriate error response
- [ ] No panics from corrupted metadata
- [ ] Checksums detect corruption before use (no silent data misinterpretation)
- [ ] RaptorQ metadata repair works for recoverable cases
- [ ] Evidence ledger records all detected corruption
- [ ] All scenarios deterministic and CI-executable

title: Fault injection: I/O throttling (slow I/O, deadline misses)
description:
# Fault injection: I/O throttling (slow I/O, deadline misses)

## GOAL
Test filesystem behavior under degraded I/O performance — simulating slow disks, network storage latency, or I/O congestion.

## SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Uniform slow I/O
- Add 50ms latency to every read/write operation
- Expected: filesystem remains functional, FUSE operations complete (slowly)
- Measure: FUSE operation timeout handling, queue depths

### Scenario 2: Intermittent I/O stalls
- Random 500ms-2s stalls on 5% of I/O operations
- Expected: no deadlocks, backpressure activates, operations eventually complete

### Scenario 3: I/O bandwidth limit
- Limit to 10MB/s read, 5MB/s write (simulating NAS or USB)
- Expected: FlushDaemon adapts, no OOM from dirty block accumulation

### Scenario 4: I/O timeout
- I/O operations that take > 30s return ETIMEDOUT
- Expected: operation fails gracefully, no resource leak

### Scenario 5: Progressive degradation
- Start with normal I/O, gradually increase latency over 60s
- Expected: backpressure system activates, evidence ledger records degradation

## IMPLEMENTATION
- Pluggable I/O layer with configurable delay, bandwidth limit, timeout
- Delay injection: uniform, gaussian, or bimodal distribution
- Integration: inject at ffs-block I/O boundary

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] No deadlocks under any I/O degradation scenario
- [ ] Backpressure correctly activates under I/O stalls
- [ ] No OOM from unbounded dirty block accumulation during slow I/O
- [ ] Operations fail gracefully on timeout (no resource leak)
- [ ] All scenarios CI-executable with deterministic delays

title: Crash-replay test suite: 500 random schedules with injected crashes
description:
# Crash-replay test suite: 500 random schedules with injected crashes

## GOAL
Run 500 deterministic crash-replay scenarios: each generates a random sequence of filesystem operations, injects a crash at a random point, recovers, and verifies consistency.

## DESIGN

### Operation Generator
- Random sequence of: create, write, read, rename, unlink, mkdir, rmdir, fsync
- Operations parameterized: file size, directory depth, name length
- Deterministic: seeded PRNG produces reproducible sequences
- Length: 100-1000 operations per schedule

### Crash Point Selection
- For each schedule, select 1-3 random crash points
- Crash point = operation index + I/O sub-operation (e.g., crash during 3rd block write of operation #47)
- Ensures coverage of: mid-write, mid-fsync, mid-rename, mid-unlink crashes

### Recovery and Verification
After each crash:
1. Mount filesystem (triggers crash recovery)
2. Full filesystem walk: verify all accessible files are readable
3. Consistency check: no dangling inodes, no double-allocated blocks
4. Committed data check: all fsync'd data intact
5. Evidence ledger check: recovery actions logged

### Reporting
- Per-schedule: pass/fail, crash point, recovery time, evidence summary
- Aggregate: pass rate, mean recovery time, most common failure mode
- Any failure: save full reproducer (seed, schedule, crash point)

## IMPLEMENTATION
- Test harness: Rust test binary with configurable seed range
- Parallelizable: each schedule is independent (run on multiple cores)
- CI: run all 500 schedules on every PR (target: < 10 minutes total)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] 500 schedules generated and executed
- [ ] 100% pass rate (zero consistency violations after recovery)
- [ ] All fsync'd data preserved after crash
- [ ] Failure reproducers saved for any failing schedule
- [ ] Total runtime < 10 minutes on CI hardware
- [ ] Every schedule deterministic (same seed = same result)

title: Conformance: fsx-style stress test with corruption injection
description:
# Conformance: fsx-style stress test with corruption injection

## GOAL
Implement an fsx-style (File System eXerciser) stress test that performs random file operations while continuously verifying data integrity. Extended with FrankenFS-specific corruption injection to test self-healing under stress.

## BACKGROUND
fsx (from LTP/xfstests) is the gold standard for filesystem stress testing. It performs random reads, writes, truncates, and mmaps on a file, maintaining an in-memory reference copy. After each operation, it verifies the file matches the reference. Any mismatch is a bug.

## DESIGN

### Operations (weighted random selection)
- write(offset, length, data): 40%
- read(offset, length) + verify: 25%
- truncate(length): 10%
- fsync(): 10%
- fallocate(offset, length): 5%
- punch_hole(offset, length): 5%
- close + reopen: 5%

### Verification
- In-memory reference buffer tracks expected file content
- After each read: compare against reference
- Periodically: close file, reopen, read entire file, compare against reference
- After unmount + remount: verify entire file against reference

### Corruption Injection Extension
- Every N operations (configurable, default 1000): inject random block corruption
- Wait for scrub daemon to detect and repair
- Verify file still matches reference after repair
- Evidence ledger check: repair logged correctly

### Parameters
- File size: configurable (default 64MB)
- Operation count: configurable (default 100000)
- Seed: deterministic
- Duration mode: run for N seconds instead of N operations

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Zero data mismatches across 100K operations
- [ ] Survives corruption injection + repair cycles
- [ ] Deterministic with seed (reproducible failures)
- [ ] Runs in < 5 minutes for default parameters
- [ ] Clear failure report with exact operation that triggered mismatch

title: E2E test: xfstests generic and ext4 subsets
description:
# E2E test: xfstests generic and ext4 subsets

## GOAL
Run the standard Linux filesystem test suite (xfstests/fstests) against FrankenFS FUSE mount to verify compatibility with expected filesystem semantics.

## BACKGROUND
xfstests (github.com/kdave/xfstests) is the authoritative filesystem test suite used by all major Linux filesystems. It contains:
- generic/: tests applicable to all POSIX filesystems (~600 tests)
- ext4/: tests specific to ext4 semantics (~100 tests)

## APPROACH

### Phase 1: Generic Subset
Run xfstests generic/ tests that apply to FUSE filesystems. Exclude tests requiring:
- Direct I/O (O_DIRECT) — FUSE may not support
- Filesystem-specific ioctls
- Quota management
- ACLs (unless we implement them)
- Kernel-specific features (fiemap, etc.)

Expected pass rate: start with identifying which tests pass, create tracking for regressions.

### Phase 2: ext4 Subset
Run xfstests ext4/ tests. Many require mkfs.ext4 features we may not support yet.
Subset: tests covering basic file operations, directory operations, extent handling.

### Infrastructure
- xfstests requires: TEST_DEV (FrankenFS FUSE mount), SCRATCH_DEV (second mount for temp data)
- Wrapper script: configure xfstests for FrankenFS, run selected tests, capture results
- CI integration: run on every PR, track pass/fail count over time

### Known Exclusions
- Tests requiring root (CAP_SYS_ADMIN)
- Tests requiring kernel features not available in FUSE
- Tests for features we explicitly don't implement (quotas, ACLs, etc.)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] xfstests infrastructure configured for FrankenFS
- [ ] Generic test subset identified and documented
- [ ] ext4 test subset identified and documented
- [ ] CI integration: test results tracked per commit
- [ ] Pass rate monotonically increases over time
- [ ] Regression: any previously passing test that fails blocks merge

title: Add unit tests for fault injection framework harness
description:
# Add unit tests for fault injection framework harness

## GOAL
Provide unit test coverage for the Testing and Fault Injection epic (bd-32yn). The epic has many E2E/integration test beads (bd-32yn.1 through bd-32yn.7) but NO unit tests for the fault injection framework itself -- the pluggable I/O layer, failure point registration, deterministic replay, and crash-point scheduling.

## TEST PLAN

### Pluggable I/O Layer Tests
1. FaultInjector wraps BlockDevice transparently (no faults = passthrough)
2. fail_at_byte(offset) triggers fault at exact byte
3. fail_on_read(block) returns injected error
4. fail_on_write(block) returns injected error
5. Fault cleared after trigger (one-shot mode)
6. Persistent fault mode (fault on every access)

### Deterministic Replay Tests
7. Same seed produces same fault sequence
8. Fault sequence is reproducible across runs
9. Fault log captures all injected faults with timestamps

### Crash Point Tests
10. Crash point registered at specific operation
11. Crash point fires at correct moment (before/after fsync)
12. Recovery after crash point: filesystem mounts cleanly

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
All 12 tests above. Deterministic.

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Fault injected (debug): fault_type, target_block, operation
- Crash point fired (info): crash_point_id, operation_in_flight

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. All 12 tests pass
2. Framework is reusable across all fault injection beads
3. Deterministic replay verified

title: Evidence/logging unification v2: schema, joins, and artifact index integrity
description:
Background:
- Existing logging contracts are solid, but closure quality depends on consistent evidence across unit/e2e/perf/release workflows.

Goal:
- Ensure one canonical structured evidence schema is emitted by all verification surfaces and can be machine-joined across artifacts.

Deliverables:
1) Unified schema profile for unit/e2e/perf/release events.
2) Cross-artifact correlation keys (trace_id, bead_id/work-item, mode, api_family/symbol).
3) Artifact index verifier ensuring every failed test points to concrete diagnostics.
4) CI gate that validates schema conformance and required field completeness.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Every failing path in CI emits parseable evidence with linkable artifacts.
- Schema validator catches missing/invalid fields deterministically.
- Downstream reports can aggregate by trace_id without lossy joins.

Test and Logging Requirements:
- Unit tests for schema serialization/validation and index generation.
- E2E tests that intentionally trigger representative failures and verify evidence completeness.
- Mandatory detailed logs for both success and failure paths.

Alien-artifact Explainability Requirements:
- Evidence records must support decision explainability (which controller/gate/action and why), not just pass/fail telemetry.
close_reason: All child deliverables validated; structured-log fixture/gate regression fixed and evidence compliance/tests passing.

title: Cross-crate trace propagation + runtime decision explainability fields
description:
Background:
- Even valid events are low-value if they cannot be correlated end-to-end.

Scope:
- Ensure trace and context propagation across ABI boundary, membrane runtime decision law, harness runners, and report generators.
- Add explicit decision explainability fields (controller, gate, action, risk inputs).

Deliverables:
1) Context propagation contract across crates.
2) Explainability field set and semantics.
3) Fallback behavior when context is missing.

Acceptance Criteria:
- A single failing symbol can be traced from entrypoint to final report.
- Decision reason fields are always present for runtime actions.

Rationale:
- Enables postmortem-grade diagnostics without re-running workloads.

Testing/Logging:
- Unit tests for propagation APIs and field defaults.
- E2E failure path test verifying full trace chain.
- Logs: trace_id, span_id, symbol, decision, risk_inputs, controller_id.
close_reason: Delivered cross-crate trace propagation + runtime decision explainability contract with fallback and validation/report coverage

- E2E tests with injected telemetry defects.
- Logs include violation_code, offending_event, expected_fields, remediation_hint.

title: ffs-ondisk: missing kernel-canonical EXT4_FT_* file-type constants and EXT4_FT_MAX
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, fourth visit,
different target): the Linux kernel header `fs/ext4/ext4.h`
declares 8 well-known directory-entry file-type constants
(EXT4_FT_UNKNOWN through EXT4_FT_SYMLINK), the boundary EXT4_FT_MAX,
and the dir-tail checksum sentinel EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM. Our Rust port
exposes the values **only as `Ext4FileType` enum discriminants**
(crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:3020) and a **private** const
EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM (l. 3048).

Concrete gaps:

  1. **No public, named pub-const constants** — code outside the
     ondisk crate cannot grep for `EXT4_FT_REG_FILE` or
     `EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM`. The values are hidden behind enum match
     arms, which obscures the kernel-reference origin and makes
     cross-crate use awkward.

  2. **No EXT4_FT_MAX = 8 constant** — the boundary above which any
     raw u8 file_type value is invalid (or the dir-tail sentinel).
     Currently the from_raw method has the boundary check inline as
     a `_ => Unknown` fallback with no name.

  3. **No kernel-conformance test** pinning the enum discriminants
     to the kernel's EXT4_FT_* macro values. A regression that, e.g.,
     swapped EXT4_FT_DIR (2) and EXT4_FT_REG_FILE (1) would not be
     caught — readdir would silently expose every directory as a
     regular file.

  4. **EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM is private** — but the dir-block checksum
     pipeline in ffs-core/ffs-cli needs to recognise this sentinel.
     Currently it's accessible only via implicit byte comparisons.

Acceptance: 9 new pub consts mirroring the kernel header values,
one kernel-conformance unit test pinning the enum discriminants
to the constants and verifying the from_raw boundary behaviour
(every raw u8 in [0, EXT4_FT_MAX) round-trips through the enum;
values >= EXT4_FT_MAX (except EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM) decode to Unknown).
notes: Shipped: 9 pub-const ext4 file-type constants (EXT4_FT_UNKNOWN through EXT4_FT_SYMLINK + EXT4_FT_MAX) added to crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs, plus EXT4_FT_DIR_CSUM=0xDE promoted from private to pub. Ext4FileType enum discriminants now reference the named constants. Kernel-conformance unit test ext4_file_type_constants_match_kernel_header pins each value, the enum/constant equality, the from_raw round-trip across [0, EXT4_FT_MAX), the boundary fallback to Unknown for values >= EXT4_FT_MAX (including 0xDE which is handled by the dir-tail pipeline, not from_raw), and a strict-monotonic ordering cross-check. Verified via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-ondisk --lib ext4_file_type_constants_match_kernel_header + cargo check (Finished in 5.10s).

title: [bug] cuserid was a hardcoded root/user stub — passwd lookup deleted by e634aff2a
description:
FOUND AND FIXED while clearing the unistd_abi_test REDs (LIBC45/46). Filed so the defect itself has
a record separate from the test-repair work in the same commit.

fl's cuserid did not consult the passwd database AT ALL. Its entire body was:
    let name = if uid == 0 { "root" } else { "user" };
That is the FALLBACK branch of the real implementation, left inline after e634aff2a deleted the
lookup around it. Classic silent-deletion signature: the fallback survives, the logic vanishes, and
the function keeps returning plausible-looking answers.

DELETED HELPERS, recovered verbatim from e634aff2a^:
  cuserid_name_for_uid(uid) -> pwd_abi::lookup_passwd_by_uid(uid).map(pw_name)
                               .filter(non-empty).unwrap_or(root/user fallback)
  copy_cuserid_name(dst, name)
CUSERID_BUFSIZE and with_cuserid_buf survived, as did pwd_abi::lookup_passwd_by_uid, so this was
purely re-wiring.

ALSO FIXED IN PASSING: the stub truncated a caller-supplied buffer at a bare .min(8) instead of
CUSERID_BUFSIZE - 1, so any login name longer than 8 bytes was silently cut.

This is the FOURTH distinct fix this session traced to the 2026-06-26 deletions (after the
fmod-family exact-op guard, significand, and the C23 inverse pi-trig f32 routing). The sweep that
keeps paying out is 'git log -S <helper name> --all' on names taken from the campaign memories.

GATE: cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --test unistd_abi_test -- cuserid
  before -> cuserid_resolves_current_uid_from_passwd_backend FAILED, left=[114,111,111,116] ('root')
            right=[102,114,97,110,107,101,110,99,117,115,101,114,105,100] ('frankencuserid')
  after  -> test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 629 filtered out

NOTE this bead is the DEFECT. bd-l1xxt3 separately asks for a host-glibc differential gate for
cuserid and is NOT satisfied by this fix — the existing test drives fl through
FRANKENLIBC_PASSWD_PATH rather than comparing against the host. Left open deliberately.
close_reason:
FIXED. Commit daaed5036. Gate: cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --test unistd_abi_test -- cuserid
  before -> cuserid_resolves_current_uid_from_passwd_backend FAILED (returned 'root', wanted 'frankencuserid')
  after  -> test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 629 filtered out
Also covered by the crate-scoped batch: 'test result: ok. 10 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured;
621 filtered out'.

Restored cuserid_name_for_uid and copy_cuserid_name verbatim from e634aff2a^. Everything else the
implementation needs had survived the deletion (CUSERID_BUFSIZE, with_cuserid_buf,
pwd_abi::lookup_passwd_by_uid), so this was purely re-wiring the two call sites.

Also fixed the truncation the stub introduced: it capped a caller-supplied buffer at a bare .min(8)
instead of CUSERID_BUFSIZE - 1, silently cutting any login name longer than 8 bytes. That was NOT in
the original and would have been easy to carry forward unnoticed while 'restoring'.

WHY THIS WAS INVISIBLE. The stub returned 'root' for uid 0 and 'user' otherwise — always a
plausible-looking answer, never an error. Nothing crashed and nothing looked wrong; only a test that
pinned the value against a KNOWN passwd entry could catch it. That is the general hazard with this
deletion class: the surviving fallback is by construction the branch that looks most reasonable.

FOURTH fix this session traced to the 2026-06-26 deletions, after the fmod-family exact-op guard
(bd-wq67e2), significand (bd-jyvpp3) and the C23 inverse pi-trig f32 routing (bd-9jvokf).

bd-l1xxt3 REMAINS OPEN and is not satisfied by this: it asks for a host-glibc DIFFERENTIAL gate for
cuserid, whereas the existing test drives fl through FRANKENLIBC_PASSWD_PATH and never compares
against the host. Fixing the implementation does not supply the oracle that bead wants.

title: [RC-WS1] Allocator LAST_THREAD_CACHE reentry slot unsound under sequential TCB + tid reuse
description:
Residual soundness defect in committed allocator fix 97848ecf ([bd-35hjg.3] Guard allocator cache by thread key), crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/malloc_abi.rs. Surfaced in cross-review (Agent Mail msg 36446, SilentFalcon; re-confirmed by FrostyOx 2026-05-21).

ROOT CAUSE: AllocatorReentrySlot is keyed by two independently kernel/glibc-reused identifiers that can desync across thread lifecycles. Fast path current_allocator_reentry_slot() keys on thread_key = TCB self pointer (fs:[0] / tpidr_el0); glibc recycles the TCB address for a new thread after an old one exits. Slow path allocator_reentry_slot_for_tid() keys on tid (gettid); the kernel also recycles tids. Slots are write-once (tid set via compare_exchange 0->tid, never reset) with no thread-exit unbind hook.

TRIGGER: thread A (tid=100, key=K) claims slot S. A exits. Thread B reuses A TCB => key=K, tid=200; B fast path matches slot_matches_thread_key(S,K) and adopts S WITHOUT rebinding (fast path never calls bind_slot_to_thread_key). Independently the kernel reuses tid 100 for thread C (fresh TCB, key K2); C slow path probes by tid, finds S (S.tid==100), and bind_slot_to_thread_key steals S for C. Two concurrently live threads then mutate the same slot native_guard_bits / allocator_depth -> per-thread reentry isolation broken -> AtomicU32 depth fetch_sub underflow can pin a thread permanently in-reentry, exhausting the finite bootstrap bump allocator.

NOTE FOR FIXER: the obvious mitigation -- slow path refuses to steal the globally cached slot -- is INSUFFICIENT. A fast-path thread holds &slot in a live NativeAllocatorReentryGuard across its whole allocation; a third thread can move LAST_THREAD_CACHE off that slot mid-allocation, after which the slow path sees it uncached and steals it while still in use (TOCTOU). A sound fix needs single-owner slot identity independent of reusable tid/TCB values: a monotonic per-thread generation counter, real per-thread TLS for the slot, or a thread-exit unbind hook.

DONE-WHEN: a stress test exercising sequential TCB reuse + tid reuse cannot make two live threads share one AllocatorReentrySlot; reentry depth/guard accounting stays per-thread. Validate via the WS-0 adversarial smoke lane.

title: scanf scan_char: unchecked pos+n add panics / undefined on huge width
description: crates/frankenlibc-core/src/stdio/scanf.rs:965 computes 'if pos + n > input.len()' where n is spec.width.unwrap_or(1). If the format specifies an enormous width (fuzzer crafted, or pathological user input), pos + n overflows usize. In debug mode this panics (fuzz_scanf surfaced it); in release mode it's UB — could wrap around and skip the bounds check, reading past input. Fix: use pos.checked_add(n) and return None on overflow.
notes: Fixed in 6d29fb13: scan_char uses pos.checked_add(n) with early-return None on overflow. Protects against fuzzer/pathological spec.width values.

title: verify_ext4_integrity reports false-positive inode checksum failures for unallocated inodes
description: verify_ext4_integrity() checks inode checksums for ALL inodes that read_inode succeeds on, including unallocated inodes with stale data. On a clean mkfs'd ext4_small.img (16MB), it reports 55 failures and 18 passes, marking the image as unhealthy. The function should consult the inode bitmap to skip unallocated inodes. This is a correctness bug in the integrity CLI subcommand.
