title: ffs-ondisk: dx_hash proptests miss EOF-sentinel, legacy-seed-independence, and ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence MRs
description:
Finding (via /testing-metamorphic skill, second visit, different
target): the existing dx_hash proptests
(crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs:10843-10874) cover three relations:

  1. determinism — same inputs → same outputs
  2. major-hash low-bit-clear (ext4 reservation)
  3. no-panic on arbitrary inputs

Three additional metamorphic relations are NOT exercised by the
proptest suite, even though each is a documented kernel contract:

  MR-A — EOF-sentinel avoidance:
    `normalize_dx_major_hash` (l. 4737-4744) explicitly remaps
    `(EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT << 1)` to `(EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT - 1) << 1`
    because ext4 reserves that value as the htree-end-of-iteration
    sentinel. A regression that drops or weakens this remap would
    silently corrupt directory iteration on collision. NO PROPTEST.

  MR-B — Legacy hash seed independence:
    `dx_hash_legacy` (l. 4757) does NOT take the seed parameter; the
    DX_HASH_LEGACY and DX_HASH_LEGACY_UNSIGNED variants use a hardcoded
    initial state. A regression that accidentally threads the seed
    into the legacy path would make our htree reads diverge from
    kernel-mounted images. NO PROPTEST.

  MR-C — ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence:
    The signed/unsigned distinction only changes the byte
    reinterpretation for bytes >= 128. For ASCII-only names (every
    byte < 128), signed and unsigned variants of dx_hash_legacy and
    dx_hash_half_md4 must produce the same major+minor hash. NO
    PROPTEST. The existing fixed-input test
    `dx_hash_signed_vs_unsigned` (l. 8386) only checks the
    DIFFERENCE for a non-ASCII name; ASCII equivalence is not pinned.

Acceptance: 3 new proptests in the existing proptest! block
covering MR-A, MR-B, MR-C with PROPTEST_CASES sufficient to
exercise the input space (the existing block uses
ProptestConfig::with_cases(32) which is enough). All 3 MRs use the
same proptest-prelude imports already in scope.
notes: Shipped: 3 new dx_hash proptest MRs in crates/ffs-ondisk/src/ext4.rs. MR-A (EOF sentinel avoidance) pins normalize_dx_major_hash's reservation against EXT4_HTREE_EOF_32BIT << 1; MR-B (legacy seed independence) pins that DX_HASH_LEGACY/DX_HASH_LEGACY_UNSIGNED ignore the seed parameter; MR-C (ASCII signed/unsigned equivalence) pins that for bytes < 128, signed and unsigned variants of legacy/half-md4/tea produce identical major+minor hashes. All 14 dx_hash tests pass via rch exec -- cargo test -p ffs-ondisk --lib dx_hash.

title: Match glibc hcreate prime-capacity rounding
description: FrankenLibC's <search.h> hash table currently allocates exactly max(1, nel) slots and exposes hcreate_r size as nel.max(1). Host glibc rounds hcreate/hcreate_r capacity to the first prime >= max(3, nel): hcreate_r(0..3) reports size 3, hcreate_r(4) reports size 5, hcreate_r(16) reports size 17, etc. Behaviorally, glibc hcreate(4) accepts five distinct ENTER calls and fails the sixth with ENOMEM, while FrankenLibC currently fills after four. Fix LinearProbeTable capacity rounding, expose the real rounded size through hcreate_r, and add ABI/differential tests for the glibc-capacity contract. Validation should include focused rch cargo tests, fmt/check, diff-check, and br dep cycles.

title: [MEDIUM] fuzz: differential errno-precedence harness for pathname/fd/flags syscalls
description:
[MEDIUM] fuzz: add differential errno-precedence harness for pathname/fd/flags syscalls

Add a structure-aware libFuzzer target in `crates/frankenlibc-fuzz/` that differentially compares FrankenLibC vs host libc errno/return-value precedence for wrappers with overlapping invalid-input axes.

Recommended syscall set:
- `renameat2` (`crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs:16151`)
- `signalfd4` (`crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs:16291`)
- `close_range` (`crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs:5043`)
- `eventfd_write` (`crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs:6184`)
- `fsconfig` (`crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs:16755`)

Fuzz shape:
- mutate fd values, flag bitmasks, null/non-null pointers, short strings, and mixed-invalid combinations
- differential oracle is host libc / syscall behavior on the same machine
- assert exact errno precedence, not just success vs failure

Why now:
- recent work has added many single-case parity tests here, but the surface is still combinatorial and easy to regress when precedence rules overlap.

title: Completion Program: Final release-exit contract + deterministic closure protocol
description:
Background:
- Current project state has strong partial coverage and many gates, but final completion is still fragmented across open epics and in-progress subsystem tasks.
- We need one deterministic closure contract so future execution and review do not rely on implied assumptions.

Goal:
- Define and enforce the exact end-state required to claim “finished, correct, and optimized” for the current declared replacement level.

Deliverables:
1) Explicit release-exit checklist for L0 (interpose) with objective pass/fail checks.
2) Staged upgrade requirements for L1/L2 progression (what must be true before claim changes).
3) Artifact bundle spec for every release candidate:
   - conformance reports,
   - reality report,
   - replacement/profile reports,
   - perf baselines + deltas,
   - evidence/log indices.
4) Gate ordering and ownership (which scripts/tests run in what order and why).

Acceptance Criteria:
- A clean checkout can run a single scripted release dry-run and produce a complete pass/fail dossier.
- No “manual interpretation” required to determine readiness.
- Any missing artifact or breached threshold fails deterministically with actionable diagnostics.

Test and Logging Requirements:
- Add unit tests for checklist parsing/validation logic.
- Add end-to-end release-dry-run script tests (strict and hardened where relevant).
- Emit structured run logs including trace_id, mode, gate_name, outcome, errno/exit_code, timing, and artifact paths.

Optimization/Proof Requirements (Extreme Optimization skill):
- Include benchmark baseline references for all release-critical hot paths.
- Require isomorphism proof references for any optimization included in the release window.

Porting/Spec-first Requirements (Porting-to-Rust skill):
- Reference behavior contracts from PLAN/EXISTING/PROPOSED/FEATURE_PARITY docs directly in acceptance checks so closure is specification-backed.

title: Proof Obligations Binder: theorem -> evidence -> gate mapping
description:
Background:
- We already have many gates (closure contract, evidence compliance, runtime_math governance, perf budgets, replacement guards).
- What is missing is a single self-contained binder that answers, mechanically: "what do we claim?" -> "what artifact proves it?" -> "what gate enforces it?".
- Without this binder, release readiness devolves into manual interpretation and doc drift.

Goal:
- Define a versioned proof-obligations binder (operational theorems -> evidence artifacts -> gates) and integrate it into the release dossier so release acceptance is deterministic.

Deliverables:
1) Proof binder schema (v1): obligation_id, statement, quantified_scope (APIs/families/modes/input-domain/environment), evidence_artifacts (paths + sha256), gates (scripts/*), and join keys (trace_id/mode/gate/api_family|symbol/bead_id).
2) Canonical mapping table for each obligation to concrete artifacts and enforcing gates.
3) Dossier integration: extend the Release Artifact Dossier spec (`bd-5fw.3`) so every release candidate includes the proof binder + referenced artifacts.
4) Deterministic validator + failure-injection tests (missing obligation artifact -> deterministic violation_code + remediation_hint).

Proof Obligations Checklist (release-critical, from project plan):
1. Strict Refinement Theorem (strict mode matches reference glibc on defined inputs).
2. Hardened Safety Theorem (hardened mode preserves safe-state invariants or denies with defined error behavior).
3. Deterministic Replay Theorem (same (mode, inputs, env snapshot) -> identical decisions + evidence).
4. Non-Regression Sequential Guarantee (anytime-valid monitors maintain bounded false alarm rates under continuous testing).
5. CPOMDP Safety Feasibility Guarantee (repair controller never emits inadmissible action).
6. Superoptimization Soundness Guarantee (every accepted hot-kernel rewrite has stored equivalence certificate + isomorphism proof).
7. Barrier Invariance Theorem (safe set forward-invariant under admitted actions).
8. Robustness Radius Theorem (policy stays within safety/latency budgets inside declared ambiguity set).
9. Concurrent Linearizability Theorem (metadata ops linearizable under stated memory model assumptions).
10. HJI Viability Theorem (runtime remains in computed viability kernel under adversary model).
11. Sheaf Global-Consistency Theorem (declared inconsistency classes detected by overlap/cohomology diagnostics).
12. Interaction-Coverage Lower-Bound Guarantee (campaign achieves declared t-wise coverage).
13. Coupled-Divergence Bound (strict vs hardened divergence bounded on declared domains).
14. Mean-Field Equilibrium Stability Theorem (controller parameters converge under workload classes).
15. Schrodinger Morphing Entropy Bound (regime transitions bounded in transport cost/overshoot).
16. SOS Certificate Soundness Theorem (synthesized polynomial certs imply invariants).
17. Large-Deviation Risk Bound (catastrophic event probabilities below thresholds).
18. Topological Shift Detectability Theorem (telemetry topology shifts detectable per declared classes).
19. Rough-Signature Stability Bound (trace features stable under bounded perturbations).
20. Tropical Latency Composition Bound (end-to-end worst-case bound preserved under composition).
21. Primal-Dual Convergence Guarantee (online constrained updates converge or safely roll back).

Acceptance Criteria:
- Release dry-run produces a dossier containing the proof binder and the binder validates in a clean checkout.
- Missing/invalid binder evidence fails deterministically and points to the exact missing artifact + gate.
- Binder is contributor-readable: obligations are operationally stated and mapped to concrete commands/scripts.

Test Plan:

- Integration: failure-injection (missing artifact, wrong checksum, missing join keys).

Constraints:

- Deterministic by construction: stable ordering of obligations and stable violation codes.

title: Branch-Diversity Gate: enforce multi-family math obligations per milestone
description:
Background:
- AGENTS.md and PLAN_TO_PORT_GLIBC_TO_RUST.md impose a hard branch-diversity rule: each major milestone must use at least 3 distinct math families, and must include at least one obligation from (conformal statistics, algebraic topology, abstract algebra, Grothendieck-Serre methods). SIMD/ABI milestones additionally require Atiyah-Singer/K-theory/localization and Clifford obligations.
- Today we have math governance classification (production vs research) but no mechanical enforcement that milestone obligation sets satisfy diversity constraints.

Goal:
- Define and enforce a deterministic branch-diversity gate so milestones cannot ship with mathematical monoculture or missing required categories.

Deliverables:
1) Milestone taxonomy: define what counts as a "major milestone" in this repo (at minimum: L0/L1/L2/L3 replacement level claims; core subsystems like allocator/threading/stdio/loader; and runtime-math admission milestones).
2) Obligation tagging schema: for each milestone, enumerate required obligations and tag each with math-family labels.
3) Deterministic gate script (tooling-only): fail CI when a milestone obligation set violates diversity constraints; output actionable diagnostics (missing families; family dominance >40%; missing required categories).
4) Unit tests for the gate on synthetic milestone specs + one integration test against the repo’s declared milestone specs.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Gate is deterministic, low-noise, and blocks release-dossier generation when constraints are violated.
- Clear remediation guidance is emitted (which obligations to add/retire).

Test Plan:
- Unit: schema validation + dominance calculation + required-category checks.
- Failure-injection: intentionally omit categories and verify deterministic error codes.

Constraints:
- Developer transparency: this gate must not require contributors to understand the math; it operates on tags and declared obligations.
- Tooling-only: no runtime libc dependency changes.

title: Replace hard-coded glob_t struct offsets with proper type access
description:
FILE: crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/string_abi.rs:4706-4794
CURRENT: Uses raw byte offsets for glob_t fields:
  - offset 0: gl_pathc (usize)
  - offset 8: gl_pathv (*mut *mut c_char)
  - offset 16: gl_offs (usize)
These are correct for x86_64 but fragile.

FIX: Define a #[repr(C)] GlobT struct matching libc::glob_t layout, or use libc::glob_t directly if available. Access fields through the struct instead of raw pointer arithmetic.
IMPACT: Low — x86_64 only for now, but will matter for ARM64 port.

title: Fix case-insensitive IP comparison in reverse_lookup_hosts
description:
FILE: crates/frankenlibc-core/src/resolv/mod.rs:111
CURRENT: eq_ignore_ascii_case(&line_addr, addr) for IP address comparison
PROBLEM: IP addresses are numeric — case-insensitive comparison is semantically wrong even though it produces correct results (digits have no case).
FIX: Use direct byte comparison: line_addr == addr
IMPACT: Zero — functionally identical. Pure code correctness.

title: Standardize errno handling pattern across all ABI modules
description:
The audit found inconsistent errno handling across modules:
- Some use std::io::Error::last_os_error().raw_os_error().unwrap_or(default)
- Some use crate::host_resolve::host_errno(default)
- Some read libc::__errno_location() directly
- Some forget to set errno on error paths

STANDARD PATTERN (already used in most places):
  let e = std::io::Error::last_os_error().raw_os_error().unwrap_or(default_errno);
  unsafe { set_abi_errno(e) };

AUDIT: Grep for all error return paths (-1, NULL, EOF) and verify each sets errno.
This was partially done during the audit but a systematic pass would catch remaining gaps.

description:

  frankenlibc_abi::unistd_abi::getprotobyname_r_legacy_fs_per_call_for_bench

This does not make the 3.98-4.13x number wrong. It makes it UNREPRODUCIBLE, which under this campaign's own contract — live incumbent in the same invocation, re-runnable on demand — is the property that gives a ratio its value. A claim whose harness cannot build is in the same position as a bead closed on a gate that cannot link (bd-9z5ikz, bd-8f6gck, bd-t5d6h2, bd-r71n1b): the evidence is not disproven, it is absent.

DONE = either the harness builds and the ratio is re-measured live (in which case record the new number next to the old, whatever it says), or the claim is marked unsubstantiated in the ledger with this bead cited. Reporting a loss is a success; reporting that a number can no longer be checked is also a success. Do NOT restore the hooks blindly — first confirm the cloning and legacy-per-call variants still exist in unistd_abi, because a hook pointing at a variant that no longer exists would fabricate an arm.

Same class, found in the same run: qsort_gate_ab_bench (__bench_integer_radix_attempt / __bench_integer_order_gate, deleted by 51c39dec3, with ffd382c62 recording that audit as INCONCLUSIVE) and example memchr_kernel_ab (memchr_medium_32bloop_for_bench / memchr_medium_64lane_for_bench, added by f8d2259ef, deleted by 51c39dec3). Parent inventory: bd-25bzch.
close_reason:
MEASURED. The claim does not reproduce. Source commit b60f88348.

This bead's DONE offered two outcomes: re-measure and record the new number next to the old, or
mark the claim unsubstantiated. The first was reachable, so it was taken.

THE MEASUREMENT (live host arm in the SAME invocation, via dlmopen(LM_ID_NEWLM,"libc.so.6"), so it
cannot bind fl's #[no_mangle] symbols):
  export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/rch_target_frankenlibc_sandycove_om1s58
  RCH_ENV_ALLOWLIST=CARGO_TARGET_DIR RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- \
    cargo bench -j 2 --profile release -p frankenlibc-bench --features abi-bench \
      --bench glibc_baseline_bench -- getprotobyname_r_tcp --noplot \
      --sample-size 100 --measurement-time 5
  115 samples per arm:
    frankenlibc_abi          3.0117 us [2.9699, 3.0521]   p50 3050.616 ns
    frankenlibc_abi_aa_null  3.1813 us [3.1370, 3.2297]   p50 3231.263 ns
    host_glibc               4.1356 us [4.0811, 4.1915]   p50 4202.232 ns

  vs glibc = 1.37x against the fl arm, 1.30x against the A/A arm.
  PUBLISHED: 3.98-4.13x.

A/A NULL ADDED, AND IT IS NOT CLEAN — SAID PLAINLY. The harness had no null, so I added
`frankenlibc_abi_aa_null`: a byte-identical copy of the fl closure, registered between the two real
arms. It came out 1.056 and its CI does NOT overlap the fl arm's ([2.9699,3.0521] vs
[3.1370,3.2297]), so this harness carries a real ~5.6% systematic arm-position effect. That bounds
what any ratio from it can resolve. It does not rescue the published number: a 5.6% floor cannot
turn 1.37x into 4.0x.

RUN-TO-RUN SPREAD, ALSO SAID PLAINLY. An earlier run of the same group on worker hz2 (criterion's
10-sample default, before the null arm existed) gave fl p50 4813.640 / glibc p50 8279.051 = 1.72x.
Two independent runs today: 1.37x and 1.72x. Both far below 3.98-4.13x; the spread between them is
why the 100-sample run carrying the null is the one quoted.

THE FINDING UNDERNEATH THE RATIO — fl REGRESSED, glibc DID NOT.
  2026-07-10: fl 1125.06 / 1124.32 ns   glibc 4475.76 / 4646.10 ns
  2026-08-08: fl 3050.6 ns              glibc 4202.2 ns
The glibc arm is the harness's built-in control for machine speed and it moved ~6%. fl's arm moved
~2.7x slower, on that same machine, in that same invocation. A machine difference moves both arms;
one arm moving 2.7x while the other holds within 6% does not. Filed as its own bead rather than
asserted in the ledger, with the allocator lane (bd-dcrhgl, bd-65p87u) named as the hypothesis to
test first — fc181036f's own profile put ~92% of this path's self time in malloc_abi bookkeeping,

title: Pipe-to-tail exit-status trap: FIFTH fleet hit, needs a mechanical fix (pipefail in scripts/, no $? after a pipeline)
description:
THE ARGUMENT FOR A MECHANISM RATHER THAN CARE, stated first because the counterargument is always
"people should just be more careful":

I produced a fresh instance of this pattern INSIDE the artifact documenting this pattern. While
writing this bead — the bead about truncated views reported as totals — I claimed "~40 scripts lack
pipefail". That number came from reading the first 20 lines of an `rg` listing as though it were the
total. Measured properly: 637 of 638 already set it, and the one exception is a file documented as
"intended to be sourced", where setting it would be a defect rather than a fix.

I was being maximally careful. I had just audited the fleet for this exact trap. I had written the
bead text arguing that vigilance does not work. And I still did it, in the same document, in the
same hour, in the sentence prescribing the fix.

That is the whole case. Care is not a control: it is the thing that fails. The controls are the
ones that hold when attention does not — pipefail declared once at the top of a workflow rather than
remembered at 31 call sites, a lint that runs whether or not anyone is thinking about it, an exit
code reserved for "nothing was checked" so an empty run cannot be mistaken for a clean one. Every
fix on this bead is of that kind, and none of them depends on anybody noticing anything.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FIFTH INDEPENDENT HIT, and the first two where the agent who had just AUDITED the fleet for this
exact trap then fell into it twice within the hour. That is the argument for a mechanical fix:
vigilance demonstrably does not survive contact with a long working session, even in someone
primed for it.

WHAT HAPPENED, 2026-08-06, both mine:

1. Verifying a `git apply -R` before restoring deleted code:
       git -C <repo> apply -R --check $SP/one.patch 2>&1 | tail -1; echo "  $w -> rc=$?"
   printed `rc=0` for all six hunks. `$?` was TAIL's status. The patch had actually FAILED for the
   first hunk — the error text was right there in the output I printed, and the numeric verdict
   next to it said the opposite. Re-run reading git's own status directly:
       git -C <repo> apply -R --check $SP/one.patch >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "rc=$?"
   gave rc=1 for hunk 1 and rc=0 for the other five.

2. Ten minutes earlier, the same shape with an `&&`:
       git apply -R --check ... 2>&1 | tail -4 && echo "CHECK OK"
   printed a confident `CHECK OK` under an `error: patch does not apply`. `&&` chained off
   `tail`, which succeeds whatever it is fed.

Case 1 is the dangerous one. Had I trusted it I would have applied a patch set whose first hunk
did not match its context, to a 14k-line file, in the middle of restoring 6914 deleted lines.

WHY VIGILANCE IS THE WRONG FIX. The idiom is not exotic; it is what you naturally write when a
command is too chatty to read raw — which is exactly the commands whose verdict matters most
(cargo, git apply, ubs, the gate scripts). The failure is SILENT and it fails toward GREEN. And it
is invisible on the happy path: every time the underlying command succeeds, the reported status is
also 0, so the bug only shows itself on the run where you most need the truth.

MECHANICAL FIXES, cheapest first:

1. `set -o pipefail` in every gate script under scripts/. Twenty-odd already set it; the rest do
   not. With pipefail, `cmd | tail` returns cmd's failure. One line each, no logic change.
2. For agent shell use, the rule is: never read `$?` after a pipeline. Either
     - redirect to a file and read the status directly:
         cmd >out.txt 2>&1; rc=$?; grep ... out.txt
     - or use `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` (bash) / `$pipestatus[1]` (zsh) explicitly.
   The redirect form is strictly better because it also preserves the full output for a second
   look, which is how BOTH of my cases were caught.
3. A pre-commit or ubs check that flags `\|\s*(tail|head|grep|sed|awk|cut|tr)\b[^|]*$` on a line
   followed within two lines by `$?`, or by `&&`/`||` on the same line. This is a grep, not a
   parser; the false-positive rate is low because the pattern is specific.

REPO STATUS at the time of the audit: no instance of the exact `cmd | tail; echo $?` idiom in
scripts/ or in bead evidence. The exposure is in interactive agent use, which is precisely where a
lint cannot reach — hence fix 2 as a documented habit AND fix 1 so the scripts are safe regardless.

RELATED: bd-1l9rlp, a gate that reports PASS on a filter matching zero tests. Same family — a check
whose failure mode is silent and green.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
GENERALISED. The piped exit status recorded here is one of FOUR distinct mechanisms of a single pattern seen on 2026-08-06; the umbrella statement now lives on bd-25bzch:

    A RESULT OF ZERO IS ONLY EVIDENCE IF YOU ALSO OBSERVED THE RUNNER DOING WORK.

  1. piped exit status (this bead)
  2. a probe that matched nothing — libtest prints 'test result: ok.' for a zero-match filter (bd-1l9rlp)
  3. an unavailable runner reporting as success — rch refused the job and the absence of output read as '0 targets failed' (bd-25bzch)
  4. a mistyped test filter — pandas, same day: 0 passed, 1597 filtered out, rc=0

All four fail silently, fail toward green, and are invisible on the happy path. The fix in every case is to assert the POSITIVE fact — N compiled, N passed with N > 0 — rather than the absence of a complaint. That strengthens the argument here for a mechanical fix over vigilance: this is not one idiom to avoid, it is a whole class of ways to mistake silence for success.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
MECHANICAL FIX LANDED FOR THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE INSTANCE: .github/workflows/ci.yml had NO 'shell:' and no 'defaults:', so GitHub ran every 'run:' step as 'bash -e {0}' — WITHOUT pipefail. The workflow pipes 31 gate invocations through tee to capture logs:

    scripts/ci.sh 2>&1 | tee artifacts/ci/core-gates.log

A pipeline's status is its LAST command's, so tee succeeding made every one of those 31 steps report success regardless of what the gate returned. This is the same defect recorded on this bead, at the largest possible scale — the entire CI could have been reporting green over failing gates.

Fixed by adding a top-level

    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash

which GitHub expands to 'bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}'. One declaration, every step covered, no per-step edits. YAML re-parsed and validated (6 jobs, defaults present).

That is fix (1) from this bead's list, applied where it pays most. Fix (2) — pipefail in the ~40 scripts/ that lack it — and fix (3) — a lint for the idiom — remain open.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE MAGNITUDE, measured, and it is what turns this from an anecdote into a number:

    TWO BROKEN TARGETS REPORTED VERSUS SIXTY-EIGHT.

Both figures from the same tree on the same day, 2026-08-06. `cargo check --workspace
--all-targets` — the exact invocation scripts/ci.sh used — stops at the first failing target and
reported 2. The same command with `--keep-going` reported 68. Everything between those two numbers
was broken, in the tree, invisible: 62 A/B perf harnesses, the f128 conformance family, a bench
whose hooks had been deleted from under a published vs-glibc claim.

That is the cost of one missing flag in CI's own workspace check. Not a style preference — a 34x
under-report of the repo's actual breakage, sustained for weeks, in the gate whose entire job is to
tell us what is broken.

THE CLOSING ARGUMENT, and it makes the mechanical fix non-speculative:

A tool in this fleet ALREADY implements the rule. Running `ubs --ci` over a shell script produces:

    ⚠ no supported languages detected
    UBS did not run any scanner: nothing was checked (this is NOT a pass).
    Exiting 3 (nothing scanned). Set UBS_ALLOW_NO_SCAN=1 to treat this as a pass.

Exit 3 — distinct from both pass and fail. An explicit sentence saying nothing was checked. An
explicit opt-out for the case where you really do accept a no-op. That is precisely the discipline
argued for across bd-5n7ks2, bd-1l9rlp and this bead, already built, already shipping, already in
daily use here.

So the ask is not "invent a safeguard". It is "adopt the one we already run". Every gate that can
do zero work should exit on a third code, say so in words, and require an explicit env var to be
treated as a pass. scripts/check_abi_bench_feature_build.sh (415c23716) is the first gate here
built that way — units compiled asserted before the failure count, exit 2 when the runner did
nothing, and both branches exercised rather than assumed.

Carry both into the remaining work on bd-5n7ks2: the 2-vs-68 number is the justification for
pipefail everywhere, and the ubs precedent is the specification for what the idiom lint should do
when it finds nothing to scan.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ALL THREE FIXES LANDED. Closing.

(1) workflow pipefail — 415c23716. .github/workflows/ci.yml had no 'shell:' and no 'defaults:', so GitHub ran every step as 'bash -e {0}' without pipefail while piping 31 gate invocations through tee. Fixed with a top-level 'defaults: run: shell: bash'.

(2) pipefail in scripts/ — ALREADY DONE, and my earlier claim here was wrong. I said ~40 scripts lacked it; measured properly, 637 of 638 already set it. The one that does not, scripts/gentoo/frankenlibc-ebuild-hooks.sh, is documented 'intended to be sourced from /etc/portage/bashrc', where imposing shell options on the caller would be a defect, not a fix — the lint exempts sourced files. My '~40' came from reading the first 20 lines of an rg listing as the total, i.e. the same truncated-view-as-total error this bead is about, committed while writing this bead. Corrected in the commit message of e946903d3 as well.

(3) idiom lint — e946903d3, scripts/check_pipeline_exit_status.sh, wired into scripts/ci.sh early because everything after it is only as trustworthy as its own exit status.

The lint's precision mattered more than its coverage: a first pass produced 19 findings, ALL FALSE, because it flagged constructs that are correct under pipefail, explicit '|| true' discards, and python inside heredocs. A gate that cries wolf 19 times gets ignored, and an ignored gate is indistinguishable from no gate. Excluding those three categories took it to 0 real findings on the current tree, which is the honest result: the exposure was the workflow, and that is fixed.

Verified it can FAIL, per the standard this session has been applying to everyone else: rc=1 after temporarily removing the workflow defaults block (it named that exact defect; file restored from backup), rc=3 against a directory with nothing to scan, rc=0 there with the opt-out set.

THE EXIT-3 DESIGN IS ADOPTED, NOT INVENTED. 'ubs --ci' on a shell script already prints 'UBS did not run any scanner: nothing was checked (this is NOT a pass)' and exits 3, with UBS_ALLOW_NO_SCAN=1 to opt out. That is precisely the discipline argued for across this bead, bd-1l9rlp and bd-25bzch — already built, already shipping in this fleet. The ask was never to invent a safeguard; it was to adopt the one we already run.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
GATE PLACEMENT, and it generalises past this gate.

scripts/check_pipeline_exit_status.sh runs EARLY in scripts/ci.sh — immediately after the branch and cargo-policy guards, before fmt, before any cargo invocation. Not for speed. Everything after it in that file is only as trustworthy as its own exit status, and this gate is what establishes that exit statuses in this repo mean what they say. Running it last would be checking the instrument after taking the measurements.

THE GENERAL RULE: gates that validate the MEASUREMENT APPARATUS must run before the gates that measure. Ordering inside a gate suite is not arbitrary — it encodes what each gate is entitled to assume. Concretely, in this repo:

  - the pipeline exit-status lint runs before everything, because every later gate reports through an exit status;
  - --keep-going belongs on the FIRST cargo check, because a gate that stops early hides the targets behind it (2 reported vs 68);
  - the 'nothing was scanned' exit-3 check runs before the findings count inside a single gate, for the same reason one level down — a zero findings count is meaningless until you know the scan happened.

Same principle at three scales: suite ordering, flag choice, and check ordering within one script. In each case the cheap structural check that makes the later result INTERPRETABLE goes first. A suite that runs its correctness gates before its instrument gates can report green on a broken instrument, which is how every defect on this bead survived.

title: [bug][RED][crypt] crypt_gensalt("$1$") returns a 16-char salt; MD5-crypt allows at most 8 and libxcrypt returns 8
description:
SURFACED by 6c8f11cbe, which gave conformance_diff_crypt_gensalt its missing -lcrypt. The target had NEVER linked, so this was invisible.

MEASURED, worker vmi1149989, harness 'rch exec -- cargo test -j 1 --no-fail-fast -p frankenlibc-abi --test conformance_diff_crypt_gensalt -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture'. Both implementations called with the SAME fixed rbytes (the gate pins them so the comparison is deterministic):
  fl   = Some("$1$A12mAnEpBXQsCK3W")
  host = Some("$1$k2XAnEHB")

TWO things are wrong, and the length one is structural:
1. LENGTH. MD5-crypt ($1$) takes at most an 8-character salt. libxcrypt returns 8; fl returns 16. fl looks like it is applying one salt length to every prefix instead of the per-prefix maximum.
2. ENCODING. From identical input bytes the two produce different characters, so fl's base64-ish salt encoding does not match libxcrypt's even before the length is truncated.

The sibling arm crypt_gensalt_setting_round_trips_through_crypt PASSES, i.e. fl's own crypt() accepts fl's own setting. That is self-consistency, not parity — it is exactly the shape that hides this defect, and it is why the cross-impl arm matters.

Related but distinct: bd-c6ykz1 is about crypt() not supporting the modern prefixes ($y$, $2$, $7$, $gy$). This bead is about the salt STRING that gensalt produces for a prefix fl already claims to support.

Gate is RED at HEAD by design. Do not close it by comparing only the prefix, only the length, or by regenerating fl's expectation.
close_reason: Fixed in 5ebe77d9c: per-prefix salt length (8 for $1$, 16 for $5$/$6$) plus libxcrypt's little-endian low-bits-first encoding, both derived by probing libcrypt.so.1 with the gate's pinned rbytes. conformance_diff_crypt_gensalt 2 passed / 0 failed on vmi1264463; unistd_abi_test gensalt 7 passed / 0 failed on vmi1153651.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED AND CLOSED: commit 5ebe77d9c, gate green on RCH worker vmi1264463.

BOTH DEFECTS THIS BEAD NAMED WERE REAL, and the encoding one is derived from the host rather than guessed. Probing libcrypt.so.1 directly with the gate's pinned rbytes:
  $1$ -> k2XAnEHB           (8 chars)
  $5$ -> k2XAnEHBqQ1Ct2aM   (16)
  $6$ -> k2XAnEHBqQ1Ct2aM   (16)
A little-endian 3-bytes-to-4-chars encoder over ./0-9A-Za-z, emitting the LOW 6 bits first, reproduces all three EXACTLY. fl packed the same bytes big-endian and emitted the high bits first, which is why identical entropy gave different characters, and fl applied one 16-char length to every prefix, which is the structural half.

FIX: gensalt_salt_chars(prefix) supplies the per-algorithm length (8 for $1$, 16 otherwise) and gensalt_encode_bytes takes that as a parameter and packs little-endian.

GATE: conformance_diff_crypt_gensalt crypt_gensalt_supported_prefixes_match_host compares the WHOLE string from identical fixed rbytes -- not the prefix, not the length, and fl's expectation was not regenerated. 2 passed / 0 failed. No regressions: unistd_abi_test gensalt filter 7 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored on vmi1153651, including crypt_gensalt_explicit_md5_prefix.

THIS BEAD'S DIAGNOSIS OF WHY IT HID IS EXACTLY RIGHT and worth repeating: crypt_gensalt_setting_round_trips_through_crypt passed the whole time because fl's crypt() accepts fl's own setting. Self-consistency is not parity.

NOT ADDRESSED, still open: bcrypt $2b$ and yescrypt $y$ are rejected by fl's gensalt_prefix, so no salt is produced for them at all -- that is bd-c6ykz1's scope, not this one. For the record, the host produces $2b$05$KBCwKxOzLha2MUDgW0PjXe and $y$j9T$k2XAnEHBqQ1Ct2aMXFKNa/HAmA1BpMnBsYHMWB4NZN4 from the same bytes, which gives that bead a ready-made oracle.

title: EPIC: Write-Back Cache
description:
# EPIC: Write-Back Cache

## PURPOSE
Implement a write-back cache layer between FUSE write operations and disk I/O. This is critical for write performance — without write-back caching, every FUSE write would require immediate disk I/O (write-through), making FrankenFS orders of magnitude slower than kernel filesystems.

## DESIGN

### Phased Approach
1. DirtyTracker: track which cached blocks have been modified but not flushed
2. FlushDaemon: background thread that periodically flushes dirty blocks to disk
3. MVCC Integration: dirty block tracking integrates with MVCC version chains

### Core Invariant
**Dirty blocks must never be evicted from cache until flushed to disk.**
Violating this invariant causes data loss (dirty data discarded without writing).

### DirtyTracker
- Per-block dirty flag in cache metadata
- Dirty list: ordered by age (oldest dirty block first)
- Statistics: dirty block count, dirty data size, oldest dirty age

### FlushDaemon
- Background thread wakes periodically (configurable: default 5s)
- Flushes oldest dirty blocks first (LRU-like)
- Flush batch size: configurable (default 256 blocks)
- Integrates with fsync: explicit fsync flushes all dirty blocks for that inode
- Backpressure: if dirty ratio exceeds threshold (e.g., 80%), block new writes until flushed

### MVCC Integration
- Dirty blocks belong to a specific MVCC version
- Flush writes the committed version (not in-flight versions)
- Aborted transaction: dirty blocks discarded without flush
- Committed transaction: dirty blocks eligible for flush

### Eviction Coordination
- Cache eviction (ARC or S3-FIFO) must check dirty flag before evicting
- If dirty: flush first, then evict
- If flush fails: do NOT evict (keep dirty block in cache, retry later)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Dirty blocks tracked correctly (set on write, cleared on flush)
- [ ] FlushDaemon runs in background, flushes oldest dirty blocks
- [ ] fsync flushes all dirty blocks for specified inode
- [ ] Dirty blocks never evicted without flush (invariant enforced)
- [ ] Backpressure prevents OOM from too many dirty blocks
- [ ] MVCC integration: only committed versions flushed
- [ ] Benchmark: write throughput with write-back vs write-through

## Success Criteria
1. All children closed
2. E2E durability test (bd-5s0r.4) passes
3. Dirty blocks never evicted without flush (invariant enforced)
4. Write throughput >= 80pct of kernel ext4 write-back
5. fsync flushes all dirty blocks for target inode
close_reason: All children closed. Write-Back Cache epic is done.

title: Implement DirtyTracker for write-back cache
description:
# Implement DirtyTracker for write-back cache

## GOAL
Track which cached blocks have been modified but not yet flushed to disk. This is the foundation of the write-back cache.

## DESIGN
- Per-block dirty flag in cache entry metadata
- DirtyList: ordered collection of dirty block IDs, sorted by modification time
- On block write: set dirty flag, add to DirtyList with current timestamp
- On flush: clear dirty flag, remove from DirtyList
- Statistics: dirty_count, dirty_bytes, oldest_dirty_age, dirty_ratio

### Integration with Cache
- Modify BlockCache trait to include dirty tracking
- Cache::write(block_id, data) -> sets dirty
- Cache::mark_clean(block_id) -> clears dirty (called after flush)
- Cache::dirty_blocks() -> iterator over dirty blocks (oldest first)
- Cache::evict(block_id) -> panics if dirty (invariant enforcement)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Dirty flag correctly set on write, cleared on flush
- [ ] DirtyList maintains age ordering
- [ ] Cache::evict panics if block is dirty (invariant)
- [ ] Statistics accurately reflect dirty state
- [ ] Unit tests: write/flush/evict lifecycle

# Implement FlushDaemon for periodic dirty block writeback

## GOAL
Background daemon that periodically flushes dirty blocks from cache to disk, providing write-back semantics without requiring explicit fsync for every write.

## DESIGN
- Background thread spawned on mount, stopped on unmount
- Wake interval: configurable (default 5 seconds)
- Each wake cycle: iterate DirtyList, flush oldest blocks first
- Batch size: configurable (default 256 blocks per cycle)
- fsync integration: explicit fsync bypasses daemon, flushes immediately

### Backpressure
- dirty_ratio = dirty_bytes / cache_capacity
- If dirty_ratio > high_watermark (80%): flush aggressively (all dirty blocks)
- If dirty_ratio > critical_watermark (95%): block new writes until flushed below high
- Prevents OOM from unbounded dirty accumulation

### Shutdown
- On clean unmount: flush ALL dirty blocks before releasing FUSE
- On signal (SIGTERM): flush all dirty blocks, then exit
- On SIGKILL: dirty blocks lost (handled by crash recovery)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] FlushDaemon runs in background, flushes periodically
- [ ] Oldest dirty blocks flushed first
- [ ] Backpressure blocks writes when dirty ratio critical
- [ ] Clean unmount flushes all dirty blocks
- [ ] Unit tests: daemon lifecycle, flush ordering
- [ ] Integration test: write 1000 blocks, verify all flushed within 2 intervals
close_reason: Implemented FlushDaemon lifecycle, batch oldest-first flushing, high/critical dirty-ratio backpressure, shutdown drain, and daemon/backpressure tests in ffs-block.

title: Integrate write-back cache with MVCC version lifecycle
description:
# Integrate write-back cache with MVCC version lifecycle

## GOAL
Ensure the write-back cache correctly interacts with MVCC transactions: only committed versions are flushed, aborted transaction dirty blocks are discarded, and version chain GC coordinates with flush state.

## DESIGN

### Committed Version Flushing
- Dirty blocks track their transaction ID and commit sequence
- FlushDaemon only flushes blocks from committed transactions
- In-flight transaction blocks remain dirty but not flushable
- On commit: blocks transition from in-flight to flushable

### Abort Handling
- On transaction abort: dirty blocks for that transaction are discarded
- No disk write needed (the old committed version is still correct)
- Cache entry reverts to last committed version (or evicted if no committed version)

### GC Coordination
- EBR GC must not free a version while its dirty block is being flushed
- FlushDaemon holds a pin during flush I/O
- After flush: version can be marked as persisted (reduces recovery work)

### Snapshot Read Consistency
- Read transactions see committed data, whether flushed or still in cache
- Cache serves dirty (committed but unflushed) blocks for reads
- No need to flush before read (cache is authoritative for committed data)

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Only committed transaction blocks flushed to disk
- [ ] Aborted transaction blocks correctly discarded
- [ ] GC and flush do not conflict (pin during flush)
- [ ] Snapshot reads correctly served from dirty cache
- [ ] Unit tests: commit-then-flush, abort-then-discard lifecycle
- [ ] Integration test: concurrent transactions with flush daemon running
close_reason: implemented + package gates pass

title: E2E test: write-back cache durability and flush correctness
description:
# E2E test: write-back cache durability and flush correctness

## GOAL
Prove that the write-back cache correctly flushes all committed data to disk, never loses dirty blocks, and correctly handles abort/commit lifecycle with MVCC integration.

## TEST SCENARIOS

### Scenario 1: Basic Flush Correctness
1. Mount FrankenFS with write-back cache enabled (5s flush interval)
2. Write 1000 blocks with known content
3. Wait for 2 flush intervals (10s)
4. Unmount cleanly
5. Remount, read all 1000 blocks
6. Verify: all blocks contain correct data (BLAKE3 checksums match)

### Scenario 2: Clean Unmount Flushes Everything
1. Write 500 blocks, do NOT wait for flush interval
2. Immediately unmount (clean shutdown)
3. Verify: unmount blocked until all dirty blocks flushed
4. Remount, verify all 500 blocks present and correct

### Scenario 3: SIGKILL Dirty Block Loss
1. Write 100 blocks with fsync (durable baseline)
2. Write 200 more blocks WITHOUT fsync
3. SIGKILL the FUSE process
4. Remount with crash recovery
5. Verify: 100 fsync blocks intact, 200 non-fsync blocks may be missing
6. Verify: no partial/corrupt blocks (either present or absent)

### Scenario 4: Abort Discards Dirty Blocks
1. Begin MVCC transaction T1
2. Write 50 blocks via T1
3. Abort T1
4. Verify: dirty blocks from T1 discarded (not flushed to disk)
5. Previous committed data for those blocks unchanged

### Scenario 5: Backpressure Under Load
1. Configure critical_watermark at 95% dirty ratio
2. Flood writes faster than flush can keep up
3. Verify: writes block when dirty ratio exceeds critical threshold
4. Verify: writes resume after flush daemon catches up
5. Verify: no OOM from unbounded dirty accumulation

### Scenario 6: Concurrent Transactions and Flush
1. 4 concurrent transactions, each writing 100 blocks
2. 2 transactions commit, 2 abort
3. Flush daemon running continuously
4. Verify: only committed transaction blocks persisted to disk
5. Verify: aborted transaction blocks not on disk

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All 6 scenarios pass
- [ ] No data loss for committed + fsynced data under any scenario
- [ ] Abort correctly discards dirty blocks
- [ ] Backpressure prevents OOM
- [ ] SIGKILL scenario: no corrupt data (only missing unflushed data)
- [ ] All scenarios deterministic and CI-executable
- [ ] Logging: tracing spans for flush cycles, dirty ratios, backpressure events
close_reason: implemented e2e scenarios + full gates pass

# Cross-crate integration: write-back cache triggers RaptorQ symbol refresh

## GOAL
Wire the write-back cache flush path to trigger RaptorQ symbol refresh for modified block groups. This is the critical cross-crate integration between ffs-block (cache), ffs-repair (RaptorQ), and the flush daemon.

## BACKGROUND
Currently bd-820 (RaptorQ symbol refresh on dirty group flush) exists but is not wired into the write-back cache flush path. When FlushDaemon (bd-5s0r.2) flushes dirty blocks, it must notify the repair subsystem that those block groups need symbol recalculation.

## DELIVERABLES
1. FlushDaemon::flush_batch() calls repair::mark_groups_dirty(groups) after successful disk write
2. Repair subsystem queues symbol recalculation for dirty groups
3. Integration test: write -> flush -> verify symbols updated

## TESTS (REQUIRED)
1. Unit: flush_batch marks correct groups dirty
2. Unit: repair subsystem receives group notifications
3. Integration: full write -> flush -> symbol refresh -> corruption -> recovery cycle

## LOGGING REQUIREMENTS
- Flush triggers refresh (debug): group_ids, block_count
- Symbol refresh queued (debug): group_id, priority
- Symbol refresh complete (info): group_id, duration_ms, symbol_count

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Every flushed block group eventually gets symbol refresh
2. No symbol staleness > 2 scrub intervals
3. Recovery works for blocks modified after last refresh

title: REVIEW: [HIGH] stdio printf family silently truncates return when total_len > INT_MAX
description: crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/stdio_abi.rs has 20 sites where snprintf/vsnprintf/sprintf/vsprintf and friends return total_len via 'as c_int' cast, truncating when the formatted-output length exceeds INT_MAX. POSIX requires EOVERFLOW + return -1 in that case (C11 7.21.6.5 p2 and POSIX.1-2024 snprintf). Concrete reach: a caller passing printf("%*d", INT_MAX, 42) or nested format specifiers that sum past 2^31 gets silent truncation of return value; downstream allocators that size buffers from the returned count are then under-sized and corruptable. Sites: lines 3284, 3354, 3404, 3484, 3499, 3549, 3627, 3642, 3674, 3727 (and 10 more). Fix: introduce printf_result_to_c_int(total_len) helper that returns -1 + sets errno to EOVERFLOW when total_len > c_int::MAX as usize, else total_len as c_int, and replace all 20 sites.
close_reason: Fixed in b00ce291: printf_result_to_c_int() helper returns -1 + EOVERFLOW when total_len overflows c_int; all 20 sites in snprintf/vsnprintf/sprintf/vsprintf family now use it. 102 stdio_abi integration tests still pass.

title: [bug][BLOCKER] one stale example has aborted every 'cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi' run since 2026-06-26 — 517d0a233 deleted atan2's fast path AND its control hook
description:
ROOT CAUSE of a symptom already recorded elsewhere. bd-aykfv1's METHOD section says 'cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --no-fail-fast aborts at the first target that fails to LINK' and works around it by building test binaries individually and executing them by hand. The abort is not a link failure: crates/frankenlibc-abi/examples/math_survey.rs calls frankenlibc_abi::math_abi::bench_atan2_oldpath, which does not exist. cargo test BUILDS EXAMPLES, so that one unbuildable example fails compilation and the run dies before a single test target executes. Observed at HEAD: 'cargo test -j 1 --no-fail-fast -p frankenlibc-abi -- --test-threads=1' -> error[E0425]: cannot find function bench_atan2_oldpath, 0 targets with a result line, worker hz2.

PROVENANCE, via the command AGENTS.md prescribes: 'git log -S bench_atan2_oldpath -- crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/math_abi.rs' names e2849ebca (added, 'perf(math): fast-path atan2 positive axis') and 517d0a233 (deleted). 517d0a233 is the -6914-line silent deletion already on file as bd-ocwiw9.

IT TOOK THE FAST PATH TOO, not just the hook. HEAD's atan2 is 'binary_entry(y, x, 6, frankenlibc_core::math::atan2)' — byte-identical to what bench_atan2_oldpath was. e2849ebca's atan2 had a 4-line C99 axis specialization in front of it: 'if y == 0.0 && x > 0.0 && runtime_policy::math_membrane_fastpath() { return y; }'. So a shipped perf lever was silently reverted, and the example was left asserting bit-identity between two bodies that no longer differed — a tautology that could never fail, sitting inside a target that could never compile.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED FOR TEN WEEKS: an unbuildable example is not reported as a red test, it is reported as a build error at the top of a run nobody completes, and the repo's workaround (build --tests --keep-going, execute binaries directly) routes around examples entirely. This is the [dark test targets] hazard with a new entry point: examples, not just unlinkable test targets.

FIX (this bead): restore both the fast path and the hook, verbatim from e2849ebca. Gate = the example itself, which asserts new-vs-old bit-identity on the axis cases AND against live glibc, plus the full abi suite finally running to completion.

FOLLOW-UP worth its own bead: audit every OTHER example in the workspace the same way, and add a CI step that builds examples, since nothing today does.

title: [RED][gate conflict] conformance_diff_sysconf and conformance_diff_sysconf_values make CONTRADICTORY demands on _SC_SYMLOOP_MAX (40 vs -1) — one of them is wrong
description:
Two live gates in this repo assert opposite things about the same call, so fl cannot make both green and exactly one of them encodes the wrong contract. Found while restoring the deleted sysconf keys (bd-d3cav6); NOT caused by that change, and deliberately NOT resolved by editing either gate, because picking one at random is gate self-weakening.

  crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/conformance_diff_sysconf.rs:83
      assert_eq!(unsafe { fu::sysconf(libc::_SC_SYMLOOP_MAX) }, 40);
    with the header comment calling it one of THREE 'intentional' divergences:
      _SC_SYMLOOP_MAX      fl=40 (Linux MAXSYMLINKS) vs glibc -1 (indeterminate)
      _SC_GETGR_R_SIZE_MAX fl=4096 vs glibc 1024
      _SC_GETPW_R_SIZE_MAX fl=4096 vs glibc 1024

  crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/conformance_diff_sysconf_values.rs:109
      asserts fl == glibc for _SC_SYMLOOP_MAX, and fails:
      'sysconf(_SC_SYMLOOP_MAX): fl=40 glibc=-1'   (observed on rch worker ovh-a)

Live host oracle agrees with the second gate about what glibc DOES:
    glibc sysconf(173 /*_SC_SYMLOOP_MAX*/) -> -1, errno 0
so the question is not what glibc returns, it is whether fl is allowed to be more informative.

WHY IT MATTERS, and why -1 is probably right: -1 with errno unchanged is glibc's 'indeterminate'
signal, and the standard idiom is 'n = sysconf(k); if (n < 0) use_a_default();'. fl returning 40
silently takes callers down the other branch. The same argument applies to the two _R_SIZE_MAX keys,
where fl's 4096 vs glibc's 1024 changes how much buffer a caller allocates — that one is arguably
safe (bigger), while SYMLOOP_MAX is not obviously either.

DONE = a decision recorded in ONE place and both gates made consistent with it: either fl returns
glibc's -1 and conformance_diff_sysconf drops its pin, or fl keeps 40 and
conformance_diff_sysconf_values excludes the key WITH the justification written next to it. Whoever
takes this must also say which of the other two intentional divergences survive the same test —
they are pinned by the same comment and have never been argued for separately.

NEGATIVE CASE: whichever way it goes, a gate must still fail if fl returns something that is neither
40 nor -1 (e.g. falls through to EINVAL). Deleting the assertion is not a resolution.
close_reason: Implemented and pushed in 9c2b2f2f6: sysconf(_SC_SYMLOOP_MAX) now returns glibc's indeterminate -1 without touching errno; the direct regression compares both value and preserved errno so an EINVAL fallback fails. Remote RCH executed crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/conformance_diff_sysconf.rs: test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed. conformance_diff_sysconf_values compiled and executed (2 passed, 1 failed), with the remaining failure at _SC_XOPEN_VERSION (fl=-1, glibc=700), before SYMLOOP_MAX; it is unrelated to this resolved conflict.

title: [bug][resolv] conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases RED at HEAD — servent_reentrant_matches_glibc fails; services _r family likely lost its aliases the same way protoent did
description:
Found while fixing bd-870h4v (be12f2191). Same defect class, different family, independently
pre-existing.

MEASURED AT CLEAN HEAD, with my own tree excluded so it cannot be mine:
  RCH_ENV_ALLOWLIST=CARGO_TARGET_DIR RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec \
    --base HEAD --clean-overlay --no-overlay -- \
    cargo test -j 2 -p frankenlibc-abi --test conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases
  -> test servent_reentrant_matches_glibc ... FAILED
     panicked at crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases.rs:250:5
     test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

The sibling gate conformance_diff_netdb_aliases (non-reentrant
getservby_and_getprotoby_match_glibc) PASSES 1/1, so this is specific to the reentrant `_r`
service path.

WHY THIS IS PROBABLY THE SAME REVERT
bd-870h4v turned out to be e634aff2a reverting bd-qds9jk's shipped protocols lever: the reentrant
entry points went back to a per-call file re-read AND lost the `aliases` argument to
fill_protoent_r, so p_aliases came back empty — which is exactly what
conformance_diff_protoent_r_aliases was failing on. bd-xmng5n shipped the equivalent lever for the
SERVICES family on the same day (2026-07-10), and this gate is its alias counterpart. Check
whether the services `_r` path lost its alias packing the same way.

Start here:
  - `getservbyname_r` / `getservbyport_r` live in crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/inet_abi.rs (~line 999
    and ~1134), NOT unistd_abi.rs. Their comments at HEAD still describe the borrowed,
    allocation-free index, so the lookup path may be intact and only the alias packing broken —
    verify rather than assume.
  - `fill_servent_storage` is in crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/resolv_abi.rs:3492. Compare its
    alias handling against `fill_protoent_r` as restored in be12f2191, and against
    `git show fc181036f:crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/inet_abi.rs`.
  - Read the gate's assertion at conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases.rs:250 first so you fix what it
    actually checks.

DONE = conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases green with a quoted non-zero passed count, the fix stating
which field diverged and against which live glibc values, and the gate shown RED at clean HEAD
beforehand (already recorded above) so the change is demonstrably load-bearing.
close_reason:
FIXED. Source commits 00ead159f (the two bugs) and 7267ea87e (test repairs found in the same run).

The bead's hypothesis — "services _r family likely lost its aliases the same way protoent did" —
was HALF right. Aliases were indeed dropped, but that was the SECOND bug; a byte-order bug was
sitting in front of it.

STEP 0, DIAGNOSTICS. The gate failed with only "getservent_r enumeration diverged: fl_len=322
glibc_len=322" — equal lengths, so the message said nothing about what actually differed. Made it
print the first differing entry. That is what turned a dead end into two concrete defects, and it
stays in the gate.

BUG 1 — s_port was byte-swapped as 32 bits instead of 16. First divergence, index 0, tcpmux/tcp:
    fl 16777216    glibc 256
16777216 = 0x01000000 = htonl(1); 256 = 0x0100 = htons(1). The code was
`(entry.port as c_int).to_be()`, which widens the u16 to c_int FIRST and then swaps 32 bits.
Correct is `entry.port.to_be() as c_int` — swap as u16, then widen — which is exactly what
inet_abi.rs already did at its own s_port sites. TWO sites had the wrong order:
  crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs  getservent_r
  crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/unistd_abi.rs  serv_iter_next   (backs the NON-reentrant getservent)
so every port from both the reentrant and non-reentrant iterators was wrong, not just aliases.

BUG 2 — aliases dropped. With ports fixed, the next divergence was index 3, discard/tcp:
    fl []    glibc [sink, null]
getservent_r wrote a bare NULL alias list rather than packing entry.aliases. Now packed through
crate::inet_abi::pack_caller_aliases, the same helper fill_protoent_r uses, which also subsumes the
hand-rolled alias offset/alignment arithmetic that preceded it.

GATES (compiled and executed, non-zero passed counts):
  conformance_diff_netdb_r_aliases     FAILED (0 passed; 1 failed)  ->  ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
  conformance_diff_netdb_aliases       ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
  conformance_diff_protoent_r_aliases  ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
The RED was confirmed at CLEAN HEAD before the fix (rch exec --base HEAD --clean-overlay
--no-overlay -> 0 passed; 1 failed), so it is pre-existing and the fix is demonstrably load-bearing.

TWO DEFECTS OF MY OWN, FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME RUN (7267ea87e). Running the WHOLE
resolv_abi_test target — rather than the name filter I had used when closing bd-79p18u — showed
clean HEAD at 185 passed / 3 failed, and one of those 3,
bd_dcfj5_etc_hosts_iteration_reads_ipv4_entries, was caused by MY OWN committed bd-79p18u fix.
  - That test's fixture leads with `::1 ipv6-localhost` and it expected the line to be SKIPPED, i.e.
    it encoded fl's pre-fix divergence. Rather than regenerate it to fit, I re-measured the oracle
    on that exact fixture (bwrap --bind <fixture> /etc/hosts + ctypes drain of glibc gethostent):
    ipv6-localhost/127.0.0.1, then legacy-name/203.0.113.8, then second-name/198.51.100.4, TOTAL=3.
    The expectations are now the oracle's output, quoted inline.
  - My own two gethtent tests did not hold RESOLVER_ENV_LOCK. They compare fl against host glibc
    over the REAL /etc/hosts, but fl honours the HOSTS_PATH_ENV override that with_resolver_backends
    installs process-wide and libtest runs tests concurrently — so fl could read a sibling's fixture
    while glibc read /etc/hosts. Both now take the lock. This is why they passed under a filter and
    failed in a whole-target run.
  Whole target now: 186 passed; 2 failed, against the clean-HEAD baseline of 185 passed; 3 failed.
  The 2 remaining (nss_files_gethostbyname_uses_hosts_backend,
  nss_files_gethostbyname4_uses_gaih_addrtuple_backend) are pre-existing at clean HEAD, untouched.

LESSON RECORDED: a name-filtered run is not a gate. Run the whole target.

title: obsolete signal wrappers reject invalid signals with errno
description: sighold, sigrelse, and sigignore should reject invalid signals with -1/EINVAL like glibc. The current wrappers ignore sigaddset/raw sigaction errors, so invalid sighold/sigrelse can succeed and sigignore can drop errno.
close_reason:
FIXED + GATED. Commit ec6a508c1. The 'superseded' claim was HALF right, and the missing half was a live defect.

TWO agents (ubuntu 2026-08-04, PurpleLake 2026-08-04) independently marked this superseded by e15ca8951 'with regression coverage'. Both the fix and the coverage are real — signal_abi_test.rs::obsolete_signal_wrappers_reject_invalid_signal_with_errno asserts rc==-1 and errno==EINVAL for all three wrappers. But it passes ONLY signal 0, which cannot distinguish a genuine range check from an implementation that special-cases zero. Strengthening it to the full invalid-signal space found a defect neither agent saw.

GROUND TRUTH (measured on live glibc 2.42 with a compiled C probe, not recalled) for sighold/sigrelse/sigignore:
  (0) (-1) (32) (33) (65) (9999) -> rc=-1 errno=22 EINVAL
  (64)                           -> rc= 0            <- 64 is the HIGHEST VALID signal

DEFECT FOUND: fl matched on every row except sigignore(32) and sigignore(33), where it returned (0, 0) against glibc's (-1, EINVAL).
  fl=(0, 0)  glibc=(-1, 22)
Cause: the KERNEL accepts signals 32/33 in rt_sigaction — they are ordinary real-time signals as far as it is concerned — and it is glibc that reserves them for SIGCANCEL/SIGSETXID. sighold and sigrelse inherit the rule for free by routing through sigaddset, which already refuses reserved signals; sigignore builds a sigaction directly and went straight to the syscall, bypassing the libc-level rule entirely. Same root cause as bd-wh14ly (closed earlier this session), one function over.

FIX (crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/signal_abi.rs::sigignore): reject !valid_signal(sig) || glibc_reserved_signal(sig) with EINVAL before touching sigaction, reusing the core predicates rather than open-coding the range.

GATE: crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/conformance_diff_sighold.rs, 2 new arms alongside the file's existing 2.
- obsolete_wrappers_reject_invalid_signals_like_glibc: all three wrappers x {0, -1, 32, 33, 65, 9999}, comparing (rc, errno) against LIVE glibc, reading each side's own errno slot. Each row additionally asserts what the ORACLE produced (-1, EINVAL) — if BOTH impls started accepting these, equality alone would still hold.
- obsolete_wrappers_accept_signal_64_the_top_of_the_range: the NEGATIVE half, and the reason the gap was detectable at all. Without it, 'reject everything above 31' — or rejecting every signal outright — would satisfy every rejection assertion. Saves and restores the process mask and signal-64 disposition, since these three calls have real side effects.
- glibc reached by dlsym with assert_ne against fl's own address for the new arms; the file's plain extern declarations would bind to fl itself in a release test build where no_mangle is active.

EVIDENCE (rch remote, source commit ec6a508c1):
  cargo test -j2 --no-fail-fast -p frankenlibc-abi --test conformance_diff_sighold --test signal_abi_test
    conformance_diff_sighold: 4 passed; 0 failed  (was 3 passed / 1 FAILED before the fix — the failure was sigignore(32), quoted above)
    signal_abi_test:         58 passed; 0 failed, including e15ca8951's original regression test left unchanged
  cargo clippy -j2 -p frankenlibc-abi --lib --test conformance_diff_sighold -- -D warnings -> zero findings on touched files
  ubs on both touched files: reported, no new criticals attributable to this change

SENSITIVITY: measured, not deduced — the new arm ran RED against the pre-fix tree in the same invocation that produced the diagnosis above, then GREEN after the one-line guard.

NOT INVESTIGATED, deliberately out of scope: whether sigset() and other obsolete wrappers share sigignore's bypass of the reserved-signal rule. The bead names sighold/sigrelse/sigignore only. bd-npv3br already covers sigset semantics and should be checked against this finding when it is taken.

Unrelated agent changes were not reverted.

title: read fortify wrappers overflow abort coverage
description: __read_chk, __pread_chk, and __pread64_chk all guard requested byte count against the real destination buffer length, but fortify_abi_test only covers safe read paths. Add fork-isolated overflow coverage so each wrapper aborts before attempting a read syscall when nbytes exceeds buflen.

ALREADY SATISFIED — closing on run tests matched to this bead's contract.

COVERING TESTS, the whole read-family rather than just read(): read_chk, pread_chk, pread64_chk,
readlink_chk and readlinkat_chk each have a _len_over_real_buffer_aborts_child_process arm plus a
_safe counterpart. This bead said 'read fortify wrappers' plural, and all five are pinned.

EVIDENCE. crates/frankenlibc-abi/tests/fortify_abi_test.rs, run just now:
  cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --test fortify_abi_test
  -> test result: ok. 152 passed; 0 failed; 0 IGNORED; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
Zero ignored matters here: a sibling bead last round nearly closed on a suite that reported 24
ignored, where the arm in question could have been one of them.

WHY THE ABORT ARMS CANNOT PASS VACUOUSLY — I checked the harness rather than trusting the test
names. assert_child_sigabrt forks, and if the child RETURNS NORMALLY it calls _exit(127); the parent
then asserts WIFSIGNALED(status) and WTERMSIG(status) == SIGABRT. So a fortify wrapper that failed to
abort would exit 127, WIFSIGNALED would be false, and the assertion would fail. The sentinel exit is
what makes these real tests rather than 'we called it and nothing happened'.

NOT CITED BY BEAD ID. None of the eight fortify beads is named anywhere in the test tree, so the
bead->gate mapping that settled earlier batches returned NONE for all of them. Coverage was
established by matching each bead's CONTRACT to a named executing test instead. Bead-ID citation is
a convenience, not the definition of coverage — and its absence is not evidence of absence.

No code change was needed or made for this bead.

title: detect_scanf_type misparses suppressed bracket matches
description: `detect_scanf_type` in `frankenlibc_conformance/src/lib.rs` uses `while chars.next().is_some_and(|c| !c.is_alphabetic() && c != '[') {}` to skip suppressed specifiers (`%*`). However, if the suppressed specifier is a bracket match like `%*[^%]`, the loop terminates early on the `[` character. The remaining characters (`^%]`) are then parsed by the outer loop, which incorrectly identifies the `%` inside the bracket expression as the start of a new format specifier. This can cause the test harness to allocate an incorrect number of output variables for `sscanf` cases.
close_reason: Fixed misparsing of suppressed bracket matches in detect_scanf_type.

title: ffs-types: superblock offsets/sizes + BTRFS_MAGIC lack kernel-conformance pin
description:
Finding (via /testing-conformance-harnesses skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-types/src/lib.rs declares core ext4 + btrfs filesystem layout constants used by every superblock parser:

  EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_OFFSET    = 1024     (fs/ext4/ext4.h: 1024 bytes from start)
  EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_SIZE      = 1024     (sizeof(struct ext4_super_block) = 1024)
  EXT4_SECTOR_SIZE          = 512      (logical sector size)
  EXT4_SB_CHECKSUM_OFFSET   = 0x3FC    (offset of s_checksum within superblock)
  BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_OFFSET   = 64*1024  (fs/btrfs/disk-io.h)
  BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_SIZE     = 4096     (sizeof(struct btrfs_super_block))
  BTRFS_MAGIC               = 0x4D5F_5366_5248_425F  ("_BHRfS_M" LE)

Each constant determines where on disk the parser looks for the superblock and what magic it must find. A drift in any value would silently fail every mount of every image — but the constants currently have NO conformance pin (bd-jbilz pinned EXT4_SUPER_MAGIC + ext4 state flags but not these layout constants).

Critical: BTRFS_MAGIC is a u64 representation of the byte sequence "_BHRfS_M". A regression that swapped the byte order or changed any byte would silently fail to recognize every btrfs filesystem.

Acceptance: ext4_btrfs_layout_constants_match_kernel_header test in crates/ffs-types/src/lib.rs that pins all 7 values to canonical kernel macros from fs/ext4/ext4.h, fs/ext4/ext4.h checksum offset, fs/btrfs/ctree.h, and fs/btrfs/disk-io.h. Plus the BTRFS_MAGIC byte-decomposition asserting the on-disk byte sequence is "_BHRfS_M".
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Shipped ext4_btrfs_layout_constants_match_kernel_header in crates/ffs-types/src/lib.rs. Pins 7 layout constants to canonical kernel values: EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_OFFSET=1024, EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_SIZE=1024, EXT4_SECTOR_SIZE=512, EXT4_SB_CHECKSUM_OFFSET=0x3FC (last 4 bytes), BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_OFFSET=64*1024, BTRFS_SUPER_INFO_SIZE=4096, BTRFS_MAGIC=0x4D5F53665248425F. Plus structural invariants: EXT4_SB_CHECKSUM_OFFSET == EXT4_SUPERBLOCK_SIZE - 4 (last 4 bytes of superblock), and BTRFS_MAGIC LE byte decomposition is exactly '_BHRfS_M' with from_le_bytes round-trip. rch exit code 0.

title: fnmatch: unterminated '[' bracket should be treated as literal (matches glibc)
description: fnmatch_impl in crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/string_abi.rs returns false when a '[' bracket expression hits NUL without a closing ']'. Glibc treats an unterminated bracket as a literal '[' character (POSIX leaves this undefined; glibc's choice is the de-facto contract). Surfaced by fuzz_pattern_match: pattern='**[' (collapses to '*['), string='[', flags=FNM_NOESCAPE|FNM_CASEFOLD: ours returns 1 (no match), glibc returns 0 (match). Fix: pre-scan the bracket for a closing ']' before NUL; if absent, fall through to literal-byte comparison.
close_reason: classify_bracket() now reproduces glibc's three-way handling of unterminated [ — Terminated/LiteralFallback/Invalid. fnmatch_impl also resets at_start to false whenever any string char is consumed, fixing a leading-period false-positive surfaced by the same fuzz run. Three regression tests added; 180s fuzz pass with 35K execs found no further divergences. Committed 40e2a69.

title: BLOCKER: workspace manifest fails to load — harness inherits frankenlibc-fixture-exec with an illegal default-features override
description:
cargo (1.97.0-nightly, the pinned nightly-2026-04-28 toolchain) refuses to load the workspace at all:

  error: failed to load manifest for workspace member .../crates/frankenlibc-harness
  Caused by: error inheriting frankenlibc-fixture-exec from workspace root manifest's workspace.dependencies.frankenlibc-fixture-exec
  Caused by: default-features = false cannot override workspace's default-features

Every cargo invocation in the repo fails, including cargo metadata --no-deps, cargo check -p <anything>, and every rch remote build. Reproduced both locally on thinkstation1 and remotely on rch worker vmi1227854.

Offending line, committed (not an in-flight working-tree edit) since d8738e82c 2026-06-17:
  crates/frankenlibc-harness/Cargo.toml:44
    frankenlibc-fixture-exec = { workspace = true, default-features = false }
The root manifest declares no default-features for that entry, so cargo now rejects the member-level override instead of silently ignoring it.

frankenlibc-harness is the ONLY consumer of the workspace dependency, and the override was inert under the older cargo behaviour (defaults stayed ON), so the behaviour-preserving repair is to drop the inert key rather than disable defaults workspace-wide:
    frankenlibc-fixture-exec = { workspace = true }
Disabling defaults instead would drop fixture-exec's asupersync-tooling feature, which harness's own asupersync-tooling feature does not forward.

Found while validating bd-nwrdyu.
close_reason: Workspace manifest loads again; fix in 4a1065016 (crates/frankenlibc-harness/Cargo.toml:44), verified by cargo metadata --no-deps exiting 0 on thinkstation1. Evidence and the feature-resolution argument are in the bead comment.

title: [perf][malloc][STRUCTURAL] Three locked RMW executions per pair: guard CAS on malloc and free, slot swap on free; contracts cannot share one atomic
description: MODEL-INTEGRITY CORRECTION (2026-07-27). The matched no-call-graph profile attributes 22.85 percent to segment_free, with 91.27 percent of that frame on its locked slot swap, and 8.72 percent to enter_allocator_reentry_guard, with 95.18 percent of that frame on its locked CAS. Those are TWO RMW sites but THREE executions per ordinary malloc/free pair: allocator-entry CAS on malloc, allocator-entry CAS on free, and requested-size slot swap on free. The old one-atomic-for-both-contracts question was unsound. The guard linearises allocator entry before a pointer is known and excludes signal reentrancy on both calls. The slot swap linearises one pointer liveness transition and detects double, interior, and never-allocated frees. They are separate contracts and cannot be folded into one atomic operation. Treat future work as two surfaces: a liveness bitmap may replace only the slot swap if it preserves free semantics and requested-size accounting; reducing guard CAS multiplicity requires a separate signal-reentrancy proof. The former bd-uj3sg7 and bd-ummyux crash blocker is fixed and closed. Retry only after a fixed-path 8-thread churn run completes 20/20 and a matched no-call-graph MT profile still attributes at least 15 percent to segment_free with at least 80 percent on the RMW, followed by a written equivalence proof and an adversarial concurrent-double-free test that fails against a deliberately non-atomic implementation. Lane B must not benchmark.

This bead treats the two locked RMWs as removable cost and gates the segment_free slot-swap lever on an MT profile showing >=80% of the frame on the RMW. The GUARD half of that premise is now measured and it does not hold: deleting the allocator-entry compare_exchange OUTRIGHT (single-threaded branch, full equivalence proof, gate green) recovers ~0.35 ns per guarded call, against GUARD_AB's 5.63-7.45 ns/call and this bead's own 95.18%-of-frame attribution. IMPLICATION FOR THIS BEAD: a high self-time percentage on a frame whose body is one lock-prefixed RMW does NOT imply a removable multi-ns cost -- the deployed path hides most of the lock prefix behind independent work, which an isolated enter/exit loop cannot. Before spending the 8-thread churn 20/20 prerequisite on the segment_free slot swap, note that the same over-attribution may apply to it; the liveness-bitmap replacement should be sized against a DEPLOYED base/candidate pair, not against the frame percentage. The guard-CAS-multiplicity half of this bead is now closed by bd-7wubke's retry predicate: do not re-run any variant that only changes the cost of the guard claim.

title: perf: gcvt loses 1.40x/1.16x vs glibc on SIMPLE irrationals (gcvt(pi,6)=101ns vs 72ns; gcvt(pi,17)=126 vs 109) — Rust flt2dec + sci-reformat fixed overhead vs glibc's tuned dragon
close_reason: HOLD/REJECT — structural floor + genuine trade-off, no clean lever (BlackThrush 2026-07-16, taskset -c60 pinned, gcvt_glibc_bench core-vs-glibc). Full ratios: dblmax_p17 0.197x, round_p6 0.269x, simple_p6 0.434x, mid_p17 0.632x, small_p17 0.929x (all WIN), pi_p17 1.156x, pi_p6 1.399x (LOSE). KEY REFRAME: fl gcvt is ~UNIFORM (~127ns@p17) while glibc's dragon VARIES (fast on pi 109ns, slow on mid 205ns/dblmax 640ns). fl loses ONLY the 2 simple-irrational cases where glibc's dragon is fast; wins the 5 where it's slow. Root of the pi gap: the +29ns@p6 vs +17ns@p17 (FIXED, not per-digit) = Rust core::fmt  flt2dec machinery + the correctness-required sci->fixed reformat (format_fixed_from_sci_into; exp must come from the actual rounded digits, so a direct Display-fixed write is buggy at 9.999->10 boundaries). Fast-path checks (try_gcvt_exact_small_fixed / integer_sci / dyadic) are CHEAP (dyadic_decimal_scale is bit-ops, fails pi fast via >19 guard) — NOT the bottleneck, and they are exactly what wins the large/dyadic cases. Removing them to help pi would regress the 5 winners. No stable faster correctly-rounded digit generator (flt2dec internal API). gcvt is legacy (printf %g has its own separate fast path). HOLD.

title: bd-66wz subtask: Arena quarantine drain invariants + regression tests
description:
Background
- The membrane arena uses a quarantine queue to detect UAF while bounding memory retention.
- If quarantine drain semantics are wrong, we either: (a) lose UAF detection prematurely, (b) leak/quasi-leak freed metadata, or (c) fail under adversarial free storms.

Scope
- Add targeted regression tests in `crates/frankenlibc-membrane/src/arena.rs` for quarantine drain behavior and metadata lifecycle invariants.
- Tests must be deterministic, fast, and failure messages must identify the violated invariant and the sequence that triggered it.

Key Invariants (must be asserted explicitly)
1) Quarantine max-bytes bound: when total quarantined bytes would exceed `QUARANTINE_MAX_BYTES`, the arena deterministically drains/evicts the oldest entries until within budget.
2) Generation safety: drained/evicted entries must not re-validate as live allocations.
3) Metadata hygiene: after drain, allocation headers/canary bookkeeping must not allow stale pointers to validate as Writable/Valid.
4) Idempotence: repeated drain triggers under the same sequence cannot oscillate internal counters.

Test Plan
- Construct a deterministic sequence of alloc/free operations that exceeds the quarantine byte budget (use a small number of large allocations to cross the threshold quickly).
- Assert: drain occurs; arena lookup for freed pointers yields a restrictive state (Freed/Invalid/Quarantined as appropriate) and never Valid/Writable.
- Assert: quarantine accounting counters are non-negative and monotone w.r.t. operations.

Acceptance
- New unit tests in `crates/frankenlibc-membrane/src/arena.rs` cover the above invariants and pass under `cargo test -p frankenlibc-membrane`.
- Tests complete quickly (<1s locally) and are deterministic (no time dependence, no RNG without fixed seed).
- Failure output includes: invariant_id, step index, alloc size, and pointer class (live/freed/foreign).

Notes
- This bead is a pure test+invariant closure; do not change arena behavior unless a test demonstrates a real bug.

title: bd-66wz subtask: TLS validation cache epoch invalidation regression tests
description:
Background
- The TLS validation cache is a hot-path speed feature; correctness depends on preventing stale CachedValid hits after global validity changes (free/quarantine/generation bumps).
- The design uses a global epoch (`GLOBAL_TLS_CACHE_EPOCH`) to invalidate cache entries across threads.

Scope
- Add unit tests in `crates/frankenlibc-membrane/src/tls_cache.rs` that explicitly exercise the epoch bump path and prove stale hits cannot survive an epoch change.

Key Invariants
1) Epoch mismatch forces miss: an entry inserted at epoch E must not hit when the current epoch is E+1 (or any !=E).
2) Epoch mismatch self-cleans: when addr matches but epoch mismatches, the entry is invalidated to avoid repeated epoch checks.
3) Hits/misses counters reflect behavior (hit does not increment on epoch mismatch).

Test Plan
- Insert a known entry; assert lookup hits.
- Call `bump_tls_cache_epoch()`; assert lookup for same addr misses and entry invalidates (follow-up lookup still misses without reinsert).
- Optionally: ensure bump affects caches across independent `TlsValidationCache` instances (epoch is global, not per-cache).

Acceptance
- New tests in `crates/frankenlibc-membrane/src/tls_cache.rs` cover the above invariants and pass deterministically.
- Tests include clear assertion messages that point to the invariant being validated.

Notes
- Do not add non-deterministic timing; this is purely functional correctness.
