Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests validate manifest schema, required lane detection, stale SHA/schema handling, redaction, artifact hash checks, broken links, duplicate scenario ids, and generated summary output.
2. E2E script builds a sample bundle, validates it, corrupts or removes one required artifact, and proves the validator fails with a useful diagnostic.
3. The bundle has pass/fail/skip/error totals and links raw logs for conformance, xfstests, FUSE, differential oracle, repair lab, crash/replay, performance, writeback-cache, and release gates.
4. Users can inspect the bundle offline without a live build tree.
5. README or harness docs describe bundle creation, validation, and interpretation.

title: Add a chaos and replay laboratory for crash consistency under adversarial schedules
description:
Create a deterministic chaos/replay lab that stresses crash consistency and recovery under adversarial operation schedules. Cover fsync-like boundaries where implemented, rename/write/truncate/unlink sequences, transaction commit and abort points, unmount/reopen, journal replay, MVCC visibility, and repair interactions.

This bead should expose whether FrankenFS preserves user-visible guarantees when operations are interrupted or reordered within allowed semantics. Failures must be replayable by schedule id and linked to narrow implementation beads.
design:
Implementation shape:
- Define a schedule/fault taxonomy: pre-commit crash, post-commit/pre-flush crash, replay interruption, repair interruption, concurrent writer conflict, metadata/data ordering boundary, and mount teardown race.
- Use deterministic seeds and recorded operation traces so every failure can be replayed.
- Prefer existing asupersync deterministic facilities for core/concurrency paths where possible; mounted-path lanes should use explicit scripts and artifact capture.
- Compare survivors against the executable model from bd-rchk0.5.1 when available and against fixture/differential expectations otherwise.
- Distinguish true filesystem failure from worker capability limitations or unsupported host mount semantics.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover schedule generation, crash-point enumeration, replay manifest parsing, expected survivor classification, and failure report rendering.
2. At least one core-path replay suite and one mounted-path smoke script exist, with mounted path allowed to capability-skip only with structured skip reason.
3. Artifacts capture schedule id, seed, operation trace, injected crash point, mount/core mode, before/after hashes, replay logs, expected survivors, observed survivors, and invariant/differential verdict.
4. Tests include positive recovery cases and negative cases where unsupported or unsafe recovery remains explicitly blocked.
5. Failures discovered during lab development become narrow follow-up beads before this closes.
notes: Root cause this bead targets: filesystem correctness is schedule-dependent. Without deterministic crash/replay evidence, a clean happy-path write test does not justify reducing experimental caveats in the README.

title: Refine crash replay lab with schedule minimization and dual-lane coverage
description:
Plan-space polish for bd-rchk0.5.5 after fresh review. Crash-consistency evidence needs both deterministic core schedule exploration and mounted-path smoke coverage, with minimization so failures are actionable.

Scope: split core LabRuntime/asupersync schedule tests from permissioned mounted scripts, define crash-point taxonomy, and require minimized reproduction artifacts for any failure.
design:
Implementation refinement:
- Core lane: use asupersync/LabRuntime or equivalent deterministic schedule control for MVCC, journal, repair, and writeback-cache paths.
- Mounted lane: use permissioned FUSE scripts for smoke coverage, with capability skips recorded through the shared artifact schema.
- Define crash points as data: pre-commit, post-commit/pre-flush, fsync boundary, replay interruption, repair interruption, unmount/reopen, and process termination where safe.
- Minimize failing operation traces where practical and preserve full raw logs.
- Compare survivors against invariant oracle output when available, otherwise against explicit scenario expectations.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover schedule generation, crash-point enumeration, replay manifest parsing, minimization behavior, survivor-set comparison, and failure report rendering.
2. E2E scripts cover at least one mounted write/reopen case and one repair-interruption or writeback-cache-relevant case when the lane supports it.
3. Artifacts include schedule id, seed, lane type, operation trace, crash point, expected survivors, observed survivors, cleanup status, raw logs, minimized reproduction command, and classification.
4. Host capability skips are structured and do not hide product failures.
5. Any unreduced flaky failure gets a follow-up bead with the raw schedule and logs.
notes: Why this matters for users: crash-consistency bugs are expensive because they are hard to reproduce. Minimized schedules and dual-lane coverage make failures actionable instead of anecdotal.
close_reason: Completed crash replay schedule minimization, survivor-set artifacts, structured host skips, and refinement E2E smoke

title: Set release-grade ambition gates and kill-switch criteria
description:
Define the objective criteria that control FrankenFS public claims and feature exposure. The project needs explicit gates for when README caveats can be softened, when mounted read-write can be recommended, when automatic repair is allowed to mutate data, when writeback-cache can be enabled, and when a feature must stay hidden or disabled.

This bead turns ambition into policy: every risky user-visible claim needs evidence, and every missing evidence lane needs a clear deferral or kill-switch rule.
design:
Implementation shape:
- Define gates as data, not scattered prose: required lanes, minimum pass criteria, acceptable skip classes, confidence thresholds, required artifact versions, and feature-state outcomes.
- Include kill-switch criteria for read-write mount, automatic repair mutation, writeback-cache, background scrub mutation, and any native-mode feature that can affect user data.
- Make the evaluator conservative: missing evidence fails readiness unless explicitly marked exploratory.
- Tie every README/FEATURE_PARITY status phrase to a gate result, a deferral, or a blocked bead.
- Keep policy close to the proof bundle so users can inspect why a feature is recommended, experimental, hidden, or disabled.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Gate policy document or data file exists with criteria for mount/write, automatic repair, writeback-cache, scrub/repair, conformance, xfstests, performance, fuzz, and crash/replay evidence.
2. Unit tests cover pass/fail/skip semantics, missing artifact handling, confidence thresholds, and kill-switch decisions.
3. E2E or integration smoke evaluates a sample proof bundle and fails when a required artifact is missing or below threshold.
4. README and FEATURE_PARITY claims are updated to reference gate-backed statuses, not informal optimism.
5. Every caveat remaining after this bead maps to an enabling bead, a concrete blocked dependency, or an explicit non-goal.
notes: Root cause this bead targets: without objective gates, ambitious evidence can still decay into subjective release claims. Gates keep public wording, feature exposure, and proof artifacts synchronized.
close_reason: Completed canonical release-gate policy and validation coverage

title: Refine release gates with fail-closed evaluator and feature states
description:
Plan-space polish for bd-rchk0.5.6 after fresh review. Release gates should be executable policy with fail-closed behavior, not a checklist that docs can bypass.

Scope: define feature states, kill-switch semantics, missing-evidence behavior, and a policy evaluator that consumes proof bundles and produces README/FEATURE_PARITY-safe statuses.
design:
Implementation refinement:
- Define stable feature states such as hidden, disabled, experimental, detection-only, dry-run-only, opt-in mutating, validated, and deprecated/blocked.
- Make missing required evidence fail closed for readiness claims. Exploratory mode may warn, but cannot upgrade public status.
- Consume proof-bundle fields directly and produce machine-readable status plus generated human wording.
- Include kill-switch criteria for read-write mount, mutating repair, writeback-cache, background scrub mutation, and native-mode features affecting user data.
- Require every status downgrade to include remediation beads or explicit non-goal rationale.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover every feature state transition, missing artifacts, stale artifacts, threshold failures, capability skips, explicit deferrals, and kill-switch decisions.
2. E2E/integration smoke runs the evaluator against a passing sample bundle, a missing-evidence bundle, a stale bundle, and a threshold-failing bundle.
3. Generated README/FEATURE_PARITY-safe wording is tested from policy data so docs cannot drift from gates.
4. Logs identify which artifact or threshold controlled each decision.
5. No public claim can be upgraded by hand-editing docs without corresponding gate evidence.
notes: Why this matters for users: gates are how the project stops saying less experimental before the evidence really supports it. The evaluator makes safety policy enforceable.
close_reason: Completed fail-closed release gate evaluator, CLI, catalog docs, and E2E coverage

title: Curate a real-world workload and failure corpus for ambitious proof runs
description:
Build a curated corpus of realistic filesystem workloads and failure scenarios that can feed the differential oracle, crash/replay lab, repair fault lab, performance gates, and operator proof bundle. The corpus should include small deterministic scenarios, boundary cases, and representative user workflows rather than only synthetic unit cases.

This bead exists so ambition proof remains grounded in how users actually use filesystems: editor save patterns, package extraction, build directory churn, database-like append/fsync patterns where supported, metadata-heavy trees, small-file storms, sparse files if in scope, xattrs if in scope, and mount/unmount recovery sequences.
design:
Implementation shape:
- Define corpus schema with scenario id, operation sequence, required capabilities, supported filesystems, expected invariants, expected differential behavior, workload class, seed data, and logging requirements.
- Keep corpus entries compact and deterministic; large generated artifacts should live under the existing conformance/golden or tests fixture patterns rather than bloating tracker data.
- Include both positive and negative scenarios: success paths, unsupported operations, permission-boundary cases, corruption cases, and capability-skip cases.
- Make scenarios reusable across unit/model tests, mounted E2E scripts, repair lab runs, and operator bundle generation.
- Every corpus item should state why it exists and what user risk it covers.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Corpus schema and initial entries cover at least editor-save, package-extract-like churn, metadata-heavy tree operations, append/truncate workflow, mount/unmount/reopen, one ext4-specific scenario, one btrfs-specific scenario, one repair corruption scenario, and one expected capability-skip case.
2. Unit tests validate schema parsing, capability classification, stable scenario ids, and expected-artifact declarations.
3. At least one E2E script consumes corpus entries and emits per-scenario logs with pass/fail/skip plus reproduction commands.
4. Corpus integrates with at least two ambition beads, such as differential oracle plus crash/replay or repair fault lab.
5. README or harness docs explain how to add a scenario without hiding unsupported behavior.
notes: Root cause this bead targets: ambitious proof systems can become brittle if every harness invents its own scenario format. A shared corpus turns user-risk examples into reusable evidence inputs.
close_reason: Completed: workload corpus parent now owns the schema-validated real-world corpus, CLI --select validates scenario IDs, e2e exercises selected reproduction scenarios, FEATURE_PARITY records the corpus coverage, and targeted ffs-harness workload_corpus tests passed.

title: Refine workload corpus with P1 user-risk coverage and schema validation
description:
Plan-space polish for bd-rchk0.5.7 after fresh review. The workload corpus should be treated as a P1 proof substrate because it feeds the invariant oracle, differential oracle, repair lab, crash/replay lab, proof bundle, and release gates.

Scope: define versioned corpus schema, user-risk traceability, positive and negative scenarios, capability requirements, and schema validation so scenario drift is caught early.
design:
Implementation refinement:
- Corpus entries must include scenario id, user risk, operation class, supported filesystems, required capabilities, expected artifacts, expected logs, positive/negative status, and linked proof consumers.
- Include scenarios for editor-save, package extraction, metadata-heavy tree churn, append/truncate, mount/unmount/reopen, ext4-specific behavior, btrfs-specific behavior, repair corruption, unsupported operation, permission boundary, and expected host-skip.
- Keep entries deterministic and compact; large generated images should be referenced through fixture/golden mechanisms.
- Treat schema validation as a hard gate before any proof runner consumes the corpus.
- Make every scenario reusable by at least two proof systems where practical.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests validate corpus schema, stable ids, capability tags, user-risk fields, required artifact declarations, duplicate detection, and unsupported/skip classification.
2. E2E smoke consumes at least three corpus scenarios across two proof consumers and emits per-scenario logs with reproduction commands.
3. Corpus docs explain how to add scenarios without weakening support scope or hiding unsupported behavior.
4. The initial corpus explicitly includes one host capability skip and one btrfs DefaultPermissions/image-ownership diagnostic case.
5. The proof bundle can summarize corpus coverage by user risk and filesystem flavor.
notes: Why this matters for users: the proof systems should be driven by realistic risk examples, not only by developer-selected happy paths.
close_reason: Completed P1 workload corpus validator, initial corpus, docs, and E2E smoke

title: Add operator recovery and rollback drills for automatic repair
description:
Fresh review gap: the ambition workstream proves repair internals and bundles evidence, but users also need an end-to-end recovery drill that answers what they should actually do when corruption is detected.

Scope: create a user-facing dry-run to mutation workflow for repair, including preflight checks, backup or snapshot guidance where applicable, repair plan display, mutating repair execution where supported, post-repair verification, rollback or refuse-to-continue behavior, and clear logs. This bead should turn automatic repair from a subsystem claim into an operator-safe workflow.
design:
Implementation shape:
- Define an operator recovery drill that runs from a corrupted fixture or image through detect, dry-run, plan review, optional mutate, verify, and rollback/refusal.
- Require clear CLI/TUI or documented command output that explains risk, confidence, evidence, and next action without requiring code knowledge.
- Integrate with repair confidence outcomes from bd-rchk0.5.3 and proof-bundle artifacts from bd-rchk0.5.4.
- Use temporary images and non-destructive defaults; mutating repair must be opt-in and artifact-backed.
- Preserve complete logs for preflight, corruption manifest, repair plan, user-facing warnings, mutation decision, verification, cleanup, and reproduction.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover recovery-plan validation, preflight failures, dry-run rendering, refuse-to-mutate decisions, verification summaries, rollback classification, and log/artifact schema validation.
2. E2E script runs at least one detection-only drill, one dry-run successful plan, one mutating repair where supported, and one refused unsafe repair.
3. Logs include exact commands, image hashes, corruption manifest, confidence threshold, repair plan, operator warnings, post-repair verification, rollback/refusal outcome, and cleanup status.
4. README or operator docs describe the drill and make clear which paths are experimental, detection-only, dry-run-only, or validated.
5. The proof bundle can include the drill result as a first-class readiness lane.
notes: Why this improves the system for users: proof is not enough if the operator workflow is unclear at the moment of corruption. This bead creates a rehearsed recovery path with safe defaults.
close_reason: Completed: added the operator recovery drill validator/spec/CLI, proof-bundle lane artifacts, runbook and E2E docs, plus unit/E2E/validator coverage for detection-only, dry-run, verified mutating, and refused unsafe recovery paths.

title: Add long-running soak and canary campaigns for mount and repair readiness
description:
Fresh review gap: single E2E scenarios and crash tests are necessary but not enough to know whether mounted writes, repair, and writeback-cache policy work for real over time.

Scope: define long-running but bounded soak/canary campaigns that repeatedly exercise realistic workloads, mount/unmount cycles, repair checks, writeback-cache states where enabled, and artifact aggregation. The campaigns should be suitable for CI nightly, RCH, or a controlled local host, with detailed logging and flake triage.
design:
Implementation shape:
- Define campaign profiles: smoke, nightly, stress, and canary. Each profile lists duration, workload mix, required capabilities, failure thresholds, and artifact retention.
- Reuse the workload corpus from bd-rchk0.5.7 and classify host capability skips separately from product failures.
- Include repeated mount/unmount/reopen, metadata-heavy churn, read/write/verify loops, repair scrub/dry-run checks, and writeback-cache scenarios only when gated.
- Emit heartbeat logs and periodic summaries so long runs are diagnosable before completion.
- Convert reproducible product failures and recurring flakes into narrow follow-up beads with seed/campaign ids.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Unit tests cover campaign manifest validation, duration/profile parsing, failure-threshold evaluation, heartbeat summary rendering, flake classification, and artifact aggregation.
2. E2E smoke campaign runs in a bounded time and emits valid pass/fail/skip/error artifacts with detailed logs.
3. Long profile is documented for RCH/CI/manual permissioned hosts and records kernel, FUSE capability, toolchain, git SHA, workload ids, seeds, duration, resource usage, and cleanup status.
4. Campaign output feeds the operator proof bundle and release gate evaluator.
5. Failures are never swallowed as flakes without preserving reproduction data and creating or linking a follow-up bead.
notes: Why this improves the system for users: a filesystem can pass isolated tests and still degrade under repeated realistic use. Soak and canary campaigns provide endurance evidence before reducing experimental warnings.
close_reason: Completed: added executable soak/canary campaign manifest, validator, CLI, E2E smoke, docs, resource caps, heartbeat summaries, flake follow-up rules, and proof-bundle/release-gate consumers

title: btrfs send/receive corpus must not count refusal rows as supported subset coverage
description: Fallback /testing-conformance-harnesses slice while xfstests real execution is ACK-gated and peer work owns xfstests/ext4 surfaces. validate_btrfs_send_receive_corpus currently records supported_subset coverage before checking outcome semantics, and refusal outcomes do not have to use supported_subset=unsupported. description: The operational-readiness recency gate computed age with reference_epoch_days.saturating_sub(created_epoch_days), so artifacts whose created_at is after the reference timestamp were treated as age 0 and classified fresh. Future-dated evidence could bypass --max-age-days and make fabricated readiness artifacts look current.

title: Large-host swarm responsiveness evidence lane
description:
Background: FrankenFS already has swarm tail-latency, cache-controller, backpressure, and proof-bundle pieces, but there is no single permissioned lane that turns 64+ CPU / 256GB+ host claims into reproducible evidence. The README and scripts/e2e/README.md require explicit host fingerprints, CPU/RAM/NUMA visibility, queue/backpressure counters, resource caps, raw logs, artifact paths, and release-claim state before large-host responsiveness wording can improve.

Goal: create a self-contained evidence lane for massive-agent-swarm workloads. It should prove whether mounted/runtime behavior remains responsive under high parallelism, separate small-host smoke from large-host claims, and feed proof-bundle/release-gate consumers so stale or underspecified artifacts cannot upgrade public claims.

Non-goals: do not claim production readiness from synthetic smoke alone; do not run mutating mounted or large-host campaigns without the same explicit permission/capability contracts used elsewhere; do not duplicate existing swarm_tail_latency or swarm_cache_controller logic when it can be reused.

Success: child beads define the manifest contract, validator, E2E dry-run/permissioned runner, p99 attribution ledger, proof-bundle integration, docs wording guard, and final evidence closeout. Every child includes unit tests and E2E/logging requirements.
notes: Idea-wizard phase notes: I generated a 30-idea set for making FrankenFS more robust, performant, and compelling for massive agent swarms, then winnowed it against the rubric. Top five were: (1) permissioned large-host swarm responsiveness evidence lane; (2) proof-bundle claim evaluator for stale or overbroad readiness wording; (3) adaptive mounted backpressure/per-core scheduling opt-in with evidence gates; (4) deterministic repair-writeback stress arbiter across client writes, repair writes, cancellation, and stale symbols; (5) isolated xfstests capability broker for safe mutating baseline runs. Next ten were: crash-replay farm, fuzz-crash promotion pipeline, operator explain view for proof failures, multi-host repair lease chaos lane, performance quarantine manager, hostile-image resource-cap fuzz lane, RO-to-RW promotion dry-run manifest, btrfs send/receive corpus expansion, evidence-ledger query index for long campaigns, and metamorphic workload seed catalog. Overlap checks found no open bead for swarm tail latency / claim evaluator / backpressure CLI / xfstests broker. I chose the large-host swarm package first because it directly serves the user goal of 64+ core / 256GB+ responsiveness and composes with existing ffs-harness swarm_tail_latency, swarm_cache_controller, proof-bundle, and release-gate infrastructure instead of duplicating them.
close_reason: Closed out-of-port-scope per maintainer directive: the large-host swarm-responsiveness evidence lane is operational/infra (host provisioning + campaign execution), not a libc code-change deliverable; its task child bd-rchk0.53.8 is closed for the same reason.

title: Define large-host swarm campaign manifest
description:
What: define the canonical manifest schema for a permissioned large-host swarm responsiveness campaign. The schema should cover host fingerprint, CPU count, RAM, NUMA topology, kernel/FUSE capability, RCH/local lane identity, worker isolation notes, resource caps, workload ids, seeds, queue depth, backpressure state, cleanup policy, expected artifacts, raw-log paths, and release-claim state.

Why: large-host claims are easy to overstate if smoke runs omit host capability or artifact context. This bead creates the contract future validators and E2E runners must enforce.

How: reuse field names and semantics already present in scripts/e2e/README.md plus ffs-harness swarm_tail_latency and swarm_cache_controller structures. Prefer a serde-friendly Rust model in ffs-harness or an adjacent existing module, not ad hoc shell parsing.

Risks: duplicating existing manifest concepts, allowing small-host smoke to masquerade as large-host evidence, or accepting incomplete cleanup/raw-log fields.

Success criteria: unit tests accept a complete large-host manifest, accept a small-host smoke manifest only as a downgraded claim, and reject missing host fingerprint, CPU/RAM/NUMA visibility, resource caps, backpressure state, raw logs, artifact paths, cleanup status, or release-claim state.
close_reason: Completed: manifest requires workload seeds and cleanup status; harness rejects missing seeds and unknown cleanup state.

title: Add contention evidence summary rollup
description:
The evidence CLI already exposes a ledger-backed contention preset for merge_proof_checked, merge_applied, merge_rejected, policy_switched, and contention_sample records, but --summary only produces replay/repair/pressure rollups. Long swarm and MVCC contention campaigns therefore require raw-record inspection to see merge acceptance/rejection counts, valid proof counts, policy switches, latest effective policy, and latest sampled rates.

Scope: extend the ledger summary schema with an optional contention_summary populated from the existing contention evidence records, print the rollup in text mode, and update focused unit/E2E schema guards.

Acceptance: ffs-cli evidence summary tests cover merge proof checked valid/invalid, merge applied/rejected, policy switches, sampled conflict/merge/abort rates, latest effective policy, and JSON omission when absent; the evidence presets E2E schema guard knows the new field; scoped ffs-cli validation passes.

Updated evidence summary unit coverage and ffs_evidence_presets E2E schema guard. title: Implement swarm campaign validator
description:
What: implement a fail-closed ffs-harness validator for the large-host swarm campaign manifest. It should parse the manifest with structured serde types, produce a machine-readable report, and classify each lane as pass, fail, skip, or error using the shared readiness vocabulary.

Why: a manifest schema is not enough; release gates need a validator that rejects stale, underspecified, or overclaimed campaign evidence before docs or proof bundles can rely on it.

How: add or extend an existing ffs-harness module near swarm_tail_latency and swarm_cache_controller. Prefer reusable validation helpers for required strings, artifact paths, numeric host thresholds, freshness windows, and release-claim downgrades. Expose a cargo-run subcommand only if that matches existing harness command patterns.

Risks: accepting proxy signals such as a completed benchmark without host capability, treating missing large-host prerequisites as pass, or creating a validator that cannot be consumed by E2E scripts.

Success criteria: targeted unit tests cover complete pass, small-host downgrade, stale artifact rejection, missing raw-log rejection, missing cleanup rejection, missing NUMA/CPU/RAM rejection, invalid backpressure state rejection, and a report that lists exact error paths.
close_reason: Completed: fail-closed swarm campaign validator report with structured pass/fail/skip/error verdicts, exact issue paths, freshness gates, and CLI reference timestamp/max-age controls.

title: Add large-host swarm E2E runner
description:
What: add a permission-aware E2E runner for the swarm responsiveness lane. The runner should emit a dry-run/small-host smoke manifest locally and only emit large-host pass claims when host capability and explicit real-run permission are present.

Why: future agents need one reproducible command that collects the exact evidence expected by the validator without ad hoc host probing or undocumented cleanup behavior.

How: follow existing scripts/e2e patterns. Route cargo-heavy validation through rch. Preserve stdout/stderr paths, raw mount or workload logs, generated manifest, validator report, cleanup status, command transcript, worker identity, and skip/blocker reasons. Reuse ffs-harness workload generators when possible.

Risks: accidentally running mounted or high-load work without permission, leaving artifacts ambiguous after partial failure, or using local host data to imply 64-core/256GB readiness.

Success criteria: bash syntax gate passes; a safe local plan/smoke mode emits skip or downgraded artifacts with no large-host claim; permissioned mode records host capability and exact commands; E2E assertions verify manifest/report paths, logs, cleanup status, and partial-run preservation.
close_reason: Completed: permission-aware swarm workload E2E runner emits downgraded local smoke artifacts, permissioned blocker/rerun contract, command transcript, worker identity, cleanup status, and validated manifest/report paths without a large-host pass claim.

title: Validate p99 attribution ledger for swarm runs
description:
What: validate the p99/tail-latency attribution ledger for swarm campaigns. Rows should attribute queueing, service time, I/O, retries, synchronization, allocator, repair backlog, cache pressure, WAL fsync, and FUSE wrapper costs, with host fingerprint, workload id, seed, queue depth, backpressure state, reference state, reproduction command, raw logs, and artifact paths.

Why: aggregate p99 latency alone is not actionable for large agent swarms. Operators need to know whether delay came from scheduling, FUSE wrapper overhead, cache pressure, repair backlog, WAL fsync, or another component before tuning anything.

How: reuse or extend ffs-harness swarm_tail_latency structures and snapshots. Validate component sums/tolerances, required dimensions, release-claim downgrade rules, and missing-reference handling.

Risks: allowing totals without component attribution, accepting rows that cannot be reproduced, or hiding missing references behind a generic experimental claim.

Success criteria: unit tests reject missing component attribution, invalid totals, missing workload seed, missing raw logs, missing reference state, missing reproduction command, and unsupported release-claim upgrades; accepted fixtures produce a compact report that a proof-bundle consumer can embed.
close_reason: Completed: swarm tail-latency ledger now requires workload seeds, validates component p99 sum tolerance, reports seed/sum/delta fields, and has unit coverage for missing attribution, invalid totals, missing seed/raw logs/reference/reproduction command, and unsupported authoritative upgrades.

title: Connect swarm campaign to proof-bundle gates
description:
What: connect the swarm campaign validator and p99 attribution report to proof-bundle and release-gate consumers. The proof bundle should preserve lane status, host class, manifest hash, validator report, p99 attribution artifact, raw logs, freshness, and downgrade/skip rationale.

Why: without proof-bundle integration, large-host swarm artifacts remain side evidence and can drift away from the release claims they are supposed to guard.

How: extend the existing proof-bundle/release-gate manifest policy in the same style as other readiness lanes. The consumer must fail closed on stale artifacts, missing lane records, host class mismatch, missing raw logs, or attempted production/large-host wording from small-host smoke.

Risks: creating a disconnected validator with no release impact, loosening existing gates, or treating absence of swarm evidence as a pass.

Success criteria: unit tests cover accepted large-host evidence, accepted small-host downgraded smoke, stale artifact rejection, missing p99 ledger rejection, host-class mismatch rejection, missing raw logs rejection, and proof-bundle summary wording that clearly separates pass, skip, fail, and error.
close_reason: Connected swarm workload and p99 attribution evidence to proof-bundle/release-gate gates

title: Guard swarm readiness wording and runbook
description:
What: update operator-facing docs and wording guards for the swarm responsiveness lane after the validator and proof-bundle consumer exist. The docs should explain small-host smoke, permissioned large-host evidence, artifact locations, validator commands, skip/blocker meaning, and which public claims each lane may strengthen.

Why: users and agents need a precise path from artifact to claim. Without wording guards, future README or readiness edits can accidentally imply large-host responsiveness from incomplete local evidence.

How: update README or scripts/e2e/README.md only where needed, and prefer a harness/doc validator if the repo already has one for release wording. Include E2E checks that fail if required command names, artifact names, and downgrade language disappear.

Risks: over-documenting future behavior before implementation, duplicating existing readiness text, or weakening experimental caveats around mounted/write paths.

Success criteria: docs mention the validator command, E2E runner, host-class distinction, artifact contract, release-claim state, and proof-bundle lane; tests or script checks reject missing downgrade wording and stale/unsupported large-host claim text.
close_reason: Documented swarm responsiveness claim boundaries and added E2E wording guard

title: Run and publish swarm responsiveness campaign
description:
What: execute the completed swarm responsiveness lane on an appropriate permissioned host or RCH/CI worker and publish the resulting evidence. This bead is the final campaign closeout, not the place to build the validator from scratch.

Why: the lane only improves readiness when it has a dated run with host capability, command transcript, manifest, validator report, p99 attribution ledger, raw logs, cleanup status, and proof-bundle integration.

How: run the E2E runner in small-host smoke locally if that is all the environment permits, but only close the large-host evidence objective after a worker with the required CPU/RAM/NUMA profile produces accepted artifacts. File narrow follow-up beads for product failures, harness failures, or host blockers.

Risks: closing from a dry run, losing partial artifacts after a worker failure, or mixing host blockers with product failures.

Success criteria: artifacts are dated and linked; validator report is pass for the intended host class or explicit skip/blocker for unavailable permission; p99 attribution ledger is accepted; proof-bundle consumer includes the lane; docs/readiness wording reflects the evidence tier; one follow-up bead exists for every actionable product failure.

title: Add a metamorphic workload seed catalog
description: Current workload and proof artifacts carry deterministic seeds in multiple places: workload corpus reproduction commands, soak/canary campaigns, swarm workload manifests, crash replay artifacts, repair/writeback schedules, and fault-injection corpora. There is no single dry-run catalog that links those seeds to metamorphic relations, invariants, proof consumers, and exact reproduction commands. Scope: add a checked-in catalog plus ffs-harness validation that references existing artifacts and fails closed when seed rows lack a relation, invariant, source artifact, proof consumer, or dry-run/permission classification. Non-scope: do not execute permissioned xfstests, mounted mutation, or large-host swarm workloads.
design: Implement as a narrow catalog+validator slice in ffs-harness. Prefer structured JSON parsing over shell/string checks for catalog semantics. The catalog is evidence metadata only: reproduction commands are recorded and classified, not executed. This keeps the slice non-permissioned while making future metamorphic workload campaigns reproducible.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: ffs-harness exposes validate-metamorphic-workload-seeds with JSON and Markdown output; the checked-in catalog references at least five existing seed sources spanning workload corpus, soak/canary, swarm workload/tail latency, crash or chaos replay, repair/writeback or fault injection; every row declares a stable seed_id, numeric or symbolic seed, source artifact, relation type, invariant, proof consumers, reproduction command, and execution_mode. The validator rejects duplicate seed IDs, missing source artifacts, unknown relation/execution modes, missing invariants, permissioned rows without an explicit ack requirement, and rows that do not reference any existing proof consumer. A dry-run E2E script validates the checked-in catalog, verifies report coverage and invalid variants, and does not execute mutating or permissioned workloads.
notes: Created from the post-bd-rchk3.14 idea-wizard/beads pass because live ready work is permission-gated (real xfstests and large-host swarm). Duplicate searches for metamorphic workload seed, seed catalog, and metamorphic returned no existing bead.

title: Run and document a fresh xfstests baseline
description: Reality-check gap: docs/xfstests-known-failures.md contains historical passability notes and future work, but current parity claims need a fresh executable baseline. design: Decompose into prerequisites, subset policy, real execution, and product-failure bead creation. Do not widen scope to all xfstests before the curated V1 subset is reproducible. The baseline is a gate for operational confidence, not a new parity denominator unless docs are intentionally revised.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: a future agent can run or reproduce a current xfstests baseline without relying on old notes. The work must record prerequisite packages and helper build state, the selected supported subset and skip rationale, exact commands, environment metadata, logs/artifact paths, pass/fail/not-run counts, and one follow-up bead per product failure. Environment blockers such as missing xfs/xfs.h, libaio, fsstress, FUSE permissions, or dpkg locks must be captured as reproducible host blockers rather than silently treated as product failures. The baseline runner must emit the shared QA artifact format, and its helper/unit tests must cover result parsing, skip classification, and failure-to-bead extraction.
notes: Historical blocker from 2026-05-01: previous selection logic passed against not-run results, while real execution stopped before tests because xfstests helpers were unbuilt and required development packages were unavailable behind a dpkg lock. Current blocker as of 2026-05-06: the 2026-05-05 explicit-path preflight in docs/xfstests-known-failures.md shows xfs/libaio/helpers/FUSE/scratch prerequisites pass, and safe dry-run planning artifacts exist, but no product pass/fail signal exists until a permissioned real xfstests run is authorized with XFSTESTS_REAL_RUN_ACK=xfstests-may-mutate-test-and-scratch-devices and artifact-scoped TEST_DIR/SCRATCH_MNT/RESULT_BASE.

It requires a permissioned environment with explicit operator authorization to mutate test/scratch block devices (XFSTESTS_REAL_RUN_ACK) — an autonomous coding agent cannot grant that. Re-file scoped product-bug beads directly if a permissioned operator later runs the baseline and finds real failures. All child tasks closed for the same reason.

title: Define the supported V1 xfstests subset and skip policy
description: Select the minimal xfstests subset that matches FrankenFS V1 scope. The suite must be small enough to run routinely but broad enough to cover mount, directory, file data, metadata, xattr, fsync, and supported write behavior. Anything outside V1 scope should be skipped with an explicit reason tied to README/FEATURE_PARITY scope rather than hidden in harness logic.
design: The subset definition should become the stable contract that makes future baseline diffs meaningful.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. Checked-in docs or harness metadata list every selected xfstests case, expected filesystem flavor, required capabilities, skip reason for excluded tests, and classification as expected failure, environment-blocked, unsupported-by-V1, harness-blocked, or product-actionable.
2. Unit or metadata-validation tests reject duplicate test IDs, missing skip reasons, unknown classifications, unsupported tests without explicit rationale, and stale references to README/FEATURE_PARITY scope.
3. E2E/dry-run script renders the selected subset through the shared QA runner, emits the exact command plan, and records per-test IDs, skip decisions, capability checks, artifact paths, and reproduction command even before the full suite executes.
4. The policy distinguishes ext4, btrfs, read-only, experimental rw, and unsupported writeback-cache behavior, with classification values aligned to bd-rchk0.4.1.
5. CI cannot treat missing mounted coverage or not-run rows as a passing baseline unless the skip is explicitly classified and linked to a host blocker or follow-up bead.
notes: Future self: resist expanding to the whole suite until the core subset is repeatable and artifacted. The subset policy should make expected skips explicit enough that CI cannot accidentally treat missing mounted coverage as a pass.
close_reason: Completed xfstests subset policy btrfs coverage and validation artifacts

title: Refine bd-rchk3.2 with non-deceptive xfstests subset evidence policy

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/schema tests validate every selected and skipped test row has test id, filesystem flavor, V1 scope mapping, required capability, expected operation class, user-risk category, expected outcome, skip or failure rationale, owning bead for unresolved product behavior, and artifact requirements.
2. The subset includes at least one representative case for read-only mount, experimental read-write create/write/readback, directory mutation, rename/link semantics, xattrs, fsync/fsyncdir boundary, unsupported writeback-cache behavior, and expected host capability skip.
3. E2E/dry-run script renders the subset policy into both JSON and human-readable reports, runs no destructive host operations by default, and verifies every selected test has a runnable command plan plus every excluded test has a concrete V1 scope rationale.
4. Logs include source xfstests id, policy row id, flavor, risk category, selected/skipped decision, capability requirement, linked artifact or bead, docs scope citation, and reproduction command.
5. CI and README wording cannot summarize xfstests as passing unless product failures, environment blockers, harness blockers, expected unsupported cases, and not-run rows are counted separately.

title: Execute the fresh xfstests baseline and publish artifacts
description: Run the selected xfstests subset on the prepared environment and turn the result into durable evidence. This is the bead that converts planning into a dated baseline. The E2E runner script emits shared QA artifacts with exact commands, worker identity, stdout/stderr paths, raw xfstests log dirs, cleanup status, and partial-run preservation.

title: Add CI-compatible mounted FUSE runner coverage for critical paths
description: Reality-check gap: important mounted-path tests can silently skip when local FUSE permissions or kernel support are absent. Scope: audit ffs-fuse and harness mount tests, decide the CI/worker execution model, add or update scripts and docs so critical FUSE E2E coverage runs in a permissioned environment, and make permission skips visibly reported instead of silently substituting for coverage. Acceptance: CI or documented RCH workflow exercises representative mounted ext4 and btrfs paths; local permission skips emit actionable diagnostics; README or test docs explain how to reproduce the gate.
design: Decompose into capability discovery, permissioned lane provisioning, critical mounted scenario execution, and fail-closed behavior for expected lanes. This workstream is the prerequisite for any claim that FUSE behavior works for real rather than only through direct ffs-core tests.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: mounted ext4 and btrfs critical paths run in a known permissioned CI/RCH lane, or fail with structured, actionable capability diagnostics. Local lack of /dev/fuse, fusermount3, user namespace support, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, or kernel module availability must produce a visible skip artifact. The gate must exercise representative mount, lookup/read, write where supported, sync/unmount/reopen, xattr, and mounted repair-policy cases without quietly substituting unit tests for mounted coverage. Unit tests must cover capability classification and artifact validation; E2E scripts must use the shared QA runner/logging schema and preserve logs for every pass/fail/skip.
notes: Memory-derived pitfall: this repo has historical FUSE permission soft-skips and btrfs write EACCES caused by root-owned image roots under DefaultPermissions. Future work must classify those as host/harness setup issues before blaming filesystem logic.
close_reason: Completed: parent mounted FUSE coverage closeout. Children bd-rchk4.1, bd-rchk4.2, bd-rchk4.3, bd-rchk4.4, and refinement bd-9vzzk are closed. The shipped surface includes structured FUSE capability skip/error artifacts, documented permissioned FUSE lane invocation, production lane worker/kernel/fusermount/mount-option/log/cleanup metadata, mounted ext4 and btrfs scenario matrix rows, and fail-closed authoritative lane identity/freshness checks for unavailable, stale, mismatched, or incomplete mounted coverage. FEATURE_PARITY.md now records bd-rchk4 as complete. Validation for this closeout reused the child evidence and parent status update; no mounted code changed in this commit.

title: Add FUSE capability probe and explicit skip artifact
description: Mounted tests currently risk soft-skipping when the host lacks FUSE permissions. Add or revise the probe layer so every mounted test run reports whether /dev/fuse exists, fusermount3 is present, the kernel module is loaded or loadable, user namespaces/capabilities allow mounting, and the current user can mount/unmount safely.
design: This should be reusable by xfstests and mounted conformance work. Keep it separate from product behavior tests.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: local runs emit a structured capability artifact or clear machine-readable diagnostics; skip reasons include the missing capability and remediation hint; tests never collapse a missing FUSE environment into a silent success; docs explain how to read the artifact. Unit tests cover /dev/fuse missing, fusermount3 missing, kernel module unavailable, user namespace/capability failure, mount success, unmount failure, and DefaultPermissions/EACCES classification using synthetic probe outputs.
notes: Future self: prefer a small deterministic probe over ad hoc checks spread across tests. The probe should preserve enough logs to tell host limitation from product behavior.
close_reason: Implemented structured FUSE capability probe report, harness CLI, shell hook, docs, and synthetic classification tests

title: Provision or document a permissioned CI/RCH FUSE lane
description: Define where mounted FUSE tests are expected to run for real. The lane may be GitHub Actions with appropriate privileges, a documented RCH worker, or another controlled Linux host. The important point is that there is a repeatable permissioned path that agents can invoke and trust.
design: This is infrastructure, not filesystem semantics. It should unlock mounted-path tests and performance measurement without making every agent rediscover FUSE host setup.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: a checked-in script, CI job, or documented RCH command runs the FUSE capability probe successfully, mounts and unmounts a minimal FrankenFS ext4 and btrfs image where practical, captures logs, and fails loudly if the lane loses required permissions. Include worker identity, kernel, fusermount version, mount options, stdout/stderr paths, cleanup status, and shared QA artifacts. Unit/script tests validate command construction, missing-lane classification, and artifact emission without requiring privileged local execution.
notes: Future self: do not close on a one-off manual mount unless the reproduction path is durable. The lane should help users reproduce failures, not just prove that one agent had a privileged shell once.
close_reason: Implemented permissioned FUSE lane in scripts/e2e/ffs_fuse_production.sh with pre-skip fuse_capability.json, post-mount required probe, fuse_permissioned_lane.json worker/kernel/fusermount/mount-option/log/cleanup artifact summary, btrfs strict probe controls, documented local/RCH invocation, and static runner coverage. Validated with bash -n, git diff --check, ffs-harness verification_runner tests, fuse-capability-probe CLI, and UBS.

acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: scenario results are captured with filesystem flavor, mount options, operation sequence, expected outcome, actual outcome, logs, and artifact paths. title: Make expected mounted coverage fail closed when the lane is unavailable
description: Once a permissioned mounted-test lane exists, the project should stop treating missing mounted coverage as harmless. Local developer runs may still skip with diagnostics, but CI/RCH gates that promise mounted coverage must fail closed if the lane cannot mount.
design: This is a reliability guard around the lane. Implement after the matrix has a stable execution target.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: the configured mounted gate fails when the capability probe says the permissioned lane is unavailable, while local non-permissioned runs still produce explicit skip artifacts; README or test docs describe the distinction; false green CI caused by skipped FUSE coverage is prevented. Unit tests cover local skip versus authoritative fail-closed decisions, stale capability artifacts, missing logs, and remediation hints. An E2E or CI dry-run proves the gate exits nonzero for an unavailable authoritative lane and preserves diagnostic artifacts.
notes: Future self: preserve developer ergonomics locally while making authoritative gates strict. This bead protects users from false confidence, so skipped required coverage must be visible and actionable.

title: Establish fresh performance baselines against spec targets
description: Reality-check gap: README and specs make throughput, latency, and scaling claims that need current measurement against the implemented code. Scope: run criterion, fio, or hyperfine baselines for the documented representative workloads, compare against any kernel ext4/btrfs or previous FrankenFS baselines available, and record deltas and environment metadata. Acceptance: a dated performance baseline artifact or doc section records commands, hardware/runtime context, current results, target comparison, and follow-up beads for regressions or unmeasured claims.
design: Decompose into benchmark manifest, core benchmark execution, mounted FUSE benchmark execution, and delta/regression triage. Use one optimization lever per later performance commit and preserve behavior proofs before optimizing.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance: performance claims have dated measurement artifacts. Record workload definitions, image sizes, datasets, command lines, worker/host hardware, kernel, FUSE mode, Cargo profile, target dir, warmup/run counts, medians/p95 where applicable, and comparison against previous FrankenFS baselines or kernel ext4/btrfs references where available. Any missing measurement or regression must become a linked bead instead of prose. Benchmark scripts must use the shared QA artifact schema for environment metadata and failure classification, with unit tests for result parsing and E2E smoke runs proving logs/artifacts are retained.
notes: The README currently contains quantitative subsystem claims and a general performance readiness caveat. This bead is about evidence capture first; tuning work should only start after the baseline is trustworthy.

title: Define the performance baseline manifest and datasets
description: Create the manifest for what FrankenFS performance evidence means. It should cover representative block I/O, ARC cache, MVCC conflict/merge paths, repair/scrub/refresh paths, CLI inspect/parity paths, and mounted FUSE workloads where permissions exist. Include image sizes, data shapes, warmups, runs, profiles, and environment fields.
design: Baseline first; do not optimize in this bead.
acceptance_criteria:
Required proof before close:
1. A checked-in or documented manifest lists each workload, command template, required features/capabilities, expected output artifact, comparison target, regression threshold or missing-data note, and required structured log fields.
2. Unit/schema tests reject missing workload IDs, missing thresholds, unknown capability names, invalid units, missing environment fields, and artifact fields that cannot be aggregated.
3. E2E or dry-run script validates the manifest end to end, expands command templates without running heavyweight benchmarks by default, emits a sample shared QA artifact, and preserves detailed logs for manifest errors.
4. The manifest maps performance artifacts to the shared QA schema from bd-rchk0.4.1 so another agent can run and compare baselines without reconstructing intent from README prose.
5. The bead must not tune performance; any missing dataset, noisy target, or suspected regression becomes a linked implementation or measurement bead.
notes: Future self: make the manifest small enough to run, but explicit enough that results are comparable over time. Include how benchmark scripts validate and retain logs before any tuning bead begins.
close_reason: Completed: added checked-in performance baseline manifest, validator, CLI dry-run, E2E smoke, docs, and gates

title: Refine bd-rchk5.1 with performance noise and stale-baseline quarantine policy
description:
Supplemental plan-space refinement for bd-rchk5.1. Performance evidence should not let noisy, stale, or environment-incomparable runs upgrade public claims. This child bead adds a quarantine policy to the performance manifest before measurement and tuning start.

Required proof before close:
1. Unit/schema tests validate workload id, command template, cargo profile, target dir, worker/host metadata, kernel/FUSE mode, input fixture hash, warmup/run counts, statistical summary fields, comparison target, regression threshold, stale-baseline expiry, noise classification, and required raw-log references.
2. The manifest distinguishes core non-mounted benchmarks, permissioned mounted benchmarks, repair/scrub/refresh benchmarks, CLI inspect/parity benchmarks, and long-campaign performance observations, with explicit capability requirements and skip semantics for each.
3. E2E/dry-run script validates the manifest, expands command templates without running heavy workloads by default, ingests fixture benchmark outputs for pass/warn/fail/noisy/stale/missing states, and emits shared QA artifacts plus detailed logs.
4. Logs include workload id, baseline id, current artifact id/hash, environment fingerprint, metric unit, observed value, threshold, noise decision, stale decision, comparison verdict, raw stdout/stderr paths, and reproduction command.
5. Public performance claims remain experimental or unknown for any quarantined workload, and every missing/noisy/stale/regressed important workload creates or links a follow-up bead.

title: Investigate mount_cold latency regression against 20260218 reference
description: Measured bd-rchk5.3 sudo FUSE cold mount p99 is 171096 us versus the 20260218 reference 36029 us (+374.884%) and throughput is 5.981086 ops/s versus 27.018364 ops/s (-77.863%). Scope: profile the cold mount path, identify whether the delta is code, build profile, probe script, environment, or FUSE setup overhead, then implement one measured optimization or quarantine the claim with a stronger environment explanation. Required proof: behavior-preserving isomorphism note, before/after hyperfine artifact, probe report with cleanup_status=unmounted, and targeted ffs-harness validation.
close_reason: Completed: cold mount probe now disables background scrub for plain mount latency and records fast readiness polling policy; checked-in current p99 improved from 171096us to 84602us, while the 20260218 comparison remains quarantined because end-to-end sudo/bash/FUSE orchestration is still slower than the old reference.

title: Investigate mount_warm remount latency regression against 20260218 reference
description: Measured bd-rchk5.3 sudo FUSE warm remount p99 is 300114 us versus the 20260218 reference 58275 us (+414.996%) and throughput is 3.407422 ops/s versus 17.138407 ops/s (-80.118%). Scope: profile the warm remount path after a prepared image, separate CLI startup/daemon/mount negotiation costs from actual filesystem readiness, then implement one measured optimization or downgrade the public claim. Required proof: before/after artifact, probe labels warm_prepare and warm_measure, cleanup_status=unmounted, and behavior-preserving isomorphism note.
close_reason: Completed: updated warm probe evidence after the bd-rchk5.5 scrub-disabled probe fix; median improved from 291845us to 137268us and throughput improved to 6.335347 ops/s, but p99 remains effectively unchanged at 302981us versus 300114us, so the warm tail-latency claim stays quarantined.

title: Investigate mount_recovery latency regression against 20260218 reference
description: Measured bd-rchk5.3 sudo FUSE recovery mount p99 is 74217 us versus the 20260218 reference 35020 us (+111.927%) and throughput is 14.143184 ops/s versus 28.458766 ops/s (-50.303%). Scope: profile the recovery probe path and separate recovery policy overhead from generic mount overhead, then either optimize one measured lever or keep recovery performance downgraded with explicit caveats. Required proof: before/after recovery probe artifact, cleanup_status=unmounted, repair/recovery behavior unchanged, and targeted ffs-harness validation.
close_reason: Completed: measured the scrub-disabled recovery probe and kept the recovery latency claim quarantined; final p99 is 82198us versus checked-in 74217us and 20260218 reference 35020us, with cleanup_status=unmounted and ffs-cli mount_complete around 18.5ms showing wrapper overhead dominates.

title: PORT: mq_clocksend + mq_clockreceive (clockid_t variants of POSIX mq_timed*)
description: POSIX mq_clocksend(mqdes, msg, len, prio, clockid, abstime) and mq_clockreceive(mqdes, msg, len, *prio, clockid, abstime) — clockid_t variants of mq_timedsend/receive added in glibc 2.34. Dispatch on clockid: CLOCK_REALTIME forwards directly to mq_timedsend/mq_timedreceive (which already use the realtime kernel ABI). CLOCK_MONOTONIC converts the supplied monotonic abstime into a realtime abstime via "realtime_abs = realtime_now + (mono_abs - mono_now)" then forwards. Other clockids return -1 with errno=EINVAL. NULL abstime forwards as-is (means "block forever" per POSIX).
close_reason: shipped: mq_clocksend + mq_clockreceive with CLOCK_REALTIME passthrough + CLOCK_MONOTONIC abstime rebasing + EINVAL guard for unknown clockids; 4 abi tests including round-trip on both clocks and ETIMEDOUT path

title: PORT: __cxa_vec_new/new2/new3 + __cxa_vec_delete/delete2/delete3 + __cxa_vec_cctor
description: Add the Itanium C++ ABI vector new/delete/copy-ctor family (7 entries) on top of our existing __cxa_vec_ctor/dtor primitives. (1) __cxa_vec_new(count, size, padding, ctor, dtor) -> *mut c_void: malloc(count*size + padding), if padding > 0 stash count at the start of the padding so __cxa_vec_delete can recover it, run ctor on each element, return array (= raw + padding). (2)/(3) __cxa_vec_new2/3 with custom alloc/dealloc functions. (4) __cxa_vec_delete(array, size, padding, dtor): if array NULL no-op; recover raw + count from padding, run dtor reverse, free raw. (5)/(6) __cxa_vec_delete2/3 with custom dealloc (delete2 takes ptr-only, delete3 takes ptr+size). (7) __cxa_vec_cctor(dest, src, count, size, ctor, dtor): copy-constructor variant. NULL ctor/dtor must be tolerated. count*size+padding uses checked arithmetic; overflow returns NULL. Implementations route through our crate::malloc_abi::malloc/free except where the user supplied custom allocators.

title: EPIC: Replace critical stubs with real implementations or host delegation
description:
The comprehensive audit identified several categories of stub/placeholder implementations:

1. SAFE NO-OP STUBS (~50 functions): Return 0/-1/NULL without doing real work. These are intentional for features we don't support (profiling, NSS, netgroups). LOW priority — they don't crash, just silently no-op.

2. HOST CALL-THROUGH DEBT (~70 symbols): Functions that delegate to host glibc via RTLD_NEXT. These work correctly but represent symbols we haven't implemented natively yet. LOW priority — they work fine via delegation.

3. CORE TERMIOS STUBS: tcgetattr/tcsetattr/tcflush/tcflow in frankenlibc-core return -1. NOT a real issue because the ABI layer (termios_abi.rs) uses raw ioctl syscalls directly and never calls these core stubs.

4. RPC SUBSYSTEM (~68 stubs): Return safe defaults. MEDIUM priority — RPC is legacy but some programs still use it.

5. ELF LOADER INCOMPLETE: Only Phase-1 relocations; IFUNC deferred. MEDIUM priority — affects shared library loading.

RATIONALE: Focus on items that break real programs first. The setjmp/longjmp stubs were already fixed (now delegate to host). The on_exit handler gap was already fixed.
close_reason: Both children closed: bd-reax.1 (RPC host delegation) and bd-reax.2 (IFUNC relocation). Remaining categories: safe no-op stubs (intentional for unsupported features like profiling/NSS/netgroups), host call-through (working via delegation), and core termios stubs (ABI layer uses raw ioctl, never calls core stubs). No critical stubs remain.

title: Add host delegation for critical RPC functions (xdr_*, clnt_*)
description:
FILES: crates/frankenlibc-abi/src/rpc_abi.rs
CURRENT: ~68 RPC symbols use rpc_native! macro returning safe defaults (0/NULL).
PROBLEM: Programs using Sun RPC (portmap, NFS tools, ypbind) get silent failures.
FIX: For the most commonly used RPC functions (clntudp_create, clnttcp_create, xdr_int, xdr_string, etc.), resolve the host glibc symbol via our ELF resolver and delegate. Keep the safe-default fallback for symbols not found in host.
CONSIDERATION: RPC is deprecated and being replaced by gRPC. Many modern systems don't even have RPC tools installed. This is low priority unless a specific program needs it.

title: Add IFUNC relocation support to ELF loader
description:
FILES: crates/frankenlibc-core/src/elf/loader.rs:222
CURRENT: Only Phase-1 relocations supported. IFUNC (STT_GNU_IFUNC) relocations are deferred.
PROBLEM: glibc itself uses IFUNC for CPU-specific optimized versions of memcpy, memset, etc. When we try to resolve these from the host ELF, we may get the IFUNC resolver instead of the final address.
FIX: Detect IFUNC symbols and call the resolver function to get the actual implementation address.
IMPACT: Affects host_resolve.rs which parses the glibc ELF to find symbols like malloc, dlvsym, etc. If any of these are IFUNCs, we'd get the wrong address.
CONSIDERATION: On modern x86_64 glibc, malloc and dlvsym are NOT IFUNCs (they're direct symbols), but memcpy/memset ARE IFUNCs. Since we only resolve non-IFUNC symbols from host_resolve.rs, this may not be an immediate problem.

title: [fuzz-harness] fuzz_pidfd_timer: TimerDelete leaves id so kernel could reuse it (same class as bd-2t616 / bd-tw26d)

title: [RED] math errno: y0/y1/yn pole is ERANGE not EDOM; fdim + nextafter/nexttoward miss ERANGE
description:
The non-fmod remainder of conformance_math_errno's divergences, separated out from bd-xkpa5i as that
bead instructed. After bd-xkpa5i's fmod-family fix the gate went 35 -> 17 divergences; these 17 are
three unrelated groups:

GROUP 1 — Bessel pole misclassified (6 cases). y0/y1/yn and y0f/y1f/ynf report EDOM at x == 0 where
glibc reports ERANGE. x == 0 is a POLE (result -inf), which is a RANGE error; only x < 0 is a domain
error. The current guard collapses both into 'x <= 0.0 && x.is_finite() -> EDOM'.
  y0(0) y1(0) yn(2,0) y0f(0) y1f(0) ynf(2,0): fl=EDOM want=ERANGE
  (y0(-1)/y1(-1)/yn(2,-1) already correctly EDOM and must stay EDOM.)

GROUP 2 — fdim overflow (1 case). fdim(1e308,-1e308) overflows to +inf from finite operands and
owes ERANGE; fl sets nothing.

GROUP 3 — nextafter/nexttoward family (10 cases). No errno at all is set. glibc's contract, read off
the gate:
  overflow  -> ERANGE:  nextafter(dmax,inf), nextafter(-dmax,-inf), nextafterf(fmax,inf),
                        nexttoward(dmax,inf), nexttowardf(fmax,inf)
  underflow -> ERANGE:  nextafter(5e-324,0) [-> 0], nextafter(min_norm,0) [-> largest subnormal],
                        nexttoward(5e-324,0)
  NOT a range error:    nextafter(0,1) -> smallest subnormal, and nextafter(1,2).
The x == 0 exemption is not incidental: glibc early-returns for x == 0 before any errno handling, so
GROWING out of zero into a subnormal is not an underflow. A naive 'result is subnormal -> ERANGE'
rule breaks nextafter(0,1). Also exempt x == y (glibc returns y early).

DONE = conformance_math_errno green with a quoted non-zero passed count. Verify the three
already-correct negative cases stay correct: y0(-1) EDOM, nextafter(0,1) 0, nextafter(1,2) 0.
close_reason:
FIXED. Commit 4c932c4f1 (same commit as bd-xkpa5i; both cited). Gate conformance_math_errno: 17 remaining divergences -> 0. Final: 'test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out'.

Progression was 35 -> 17 -> 2 -> 0, so each group is independently attributable rather than jointly
asserted at the end.

GROUP 1, Bessel poles (6): y0/y1/yn + y0f/y1f/ynf reported EDOM at x == 0. Zero is a POLE (result
-inf) and therefore ERANGE; only x < 0 is EDOM. The old guard collapsed both into
'x <= 0.0 && x.is_finite() -> EDOM'. All six call sites now share one classifier; the f32 ones widen
with .into(), which is exact and preserves the sign/zero/finiteness the classification reads. The
negative cases this bead told me to protect still hold — y0(-1)/y1(-1)/yn(2,-1) remain EDOM.

GROUP 2, fdim (1): x - y overflows from two FINITE operands and glibc reports ERANGE; fl set
nothing. Guarded on both operands being finite, because an infinite OPERAND is not an overflow.

GROUP 3, nextafter/nexttoward +f32 (8): no errno at all. Now ERANGE on overflow to inf and on
underflow below the RESULT type's smallest normal — f32 results are judged against f32's threshold,
not f64's, which matters for nextafterf/nexttowardf. The two exemptions this bead flagged as
load-bearing are implemented and verified: x == 0 stays errno 0 (glibc early-returns, so growing out
of zero into the smallest subnormal is NOT underflow — nextafter(0,1) passes), and x == y likewise.
The naive 'result is subnormal -> ERANGE' rule would have broken nextafter(0,1); it was avoided.

GROUP 4, NOT IN THIS BEAD'S DESCRIPTION — logb/logbf (2). They were setting ERANGE at zero; glibc
reports that pole through FE_DIVBYZERO alone and leaves errno untouched (C99 logb has no SVID errno
wrapper), and the gate says so explicitly at its line 211. They were invisible when I wrote this
bead because fl's panic printer TRUNCATES the divergence list at ~12 entries, so I enumerated from
the visible head and the arithmetic hid the rest. The counts reconcile exactly: 6 + 1 + 8 + 2 = 17.
Only the errno was removed; the FE_DIVBYZERO flag is raised in core and is untouched.
Worth remembering: when a gate reports a COUNT plus a truncated list, reconcile the count before
believing the list is complete.

NO REGRESSION: conformance_diff_fmod_rem_flags 1 passed; conformance_diff_significand_flags 1
passed; conformance_diff_fp_exceptions 1 passed; conformance_diff_math_exact 2 passed; math_abi_test
118 passed. cargo fmt --check clean.

title: ffs-fuzz: fuzz_btrfs_devitem only checks no-panic, missing structural MR coverage
description:

target that just calls `parse_dev_item(data)` on arbitrary bytes:

This catches panics but provides ZERO structural assertions. The
proptest layer (bd-t2nrx, just landed) has 32 cases per MR; libfuzzer
runs millions of inputs per session. Lifting structural assertions
(tail-invariance + field-offset round-trip) into the fuzz target
gives us continuous discovery for any future drift in:

    generation@44, start_offset@52, dev_group@60, seek_speed@64,
    bandwidth@65, uuid@66..82, fsid@82..98)
  * the bytes_used <= total_bytes accounting check

Acceptance: a new fuzz target
fuzz/fuzz_targets/fuzz_btrfs_devitem_roundtrip.rs that uses a
ByteCursor pattern (same as bd-38xrn fuzz_ext4_group_desc_roundtrip)
to synthesise a structured 98-byte payload, parses it, asserts every

description:
Third of the three failures found by the core --lib sweep (bd-aykfv1, widened). NOT an oracle problem like the log2f pair — this is fl disagreeing with itself.

  math::float32::tests::powf_profile_exp_1_337_grid_matches_polynomial_bits_and_sha256
  crates/frankenlibc-core/src/math/float32.rs:2058
  assertion failed: public powf grid k=0 base=0.5
    left:  1053469677   (powf(0.5, exp))
    right: 1053469675   (powf_profile_exp_1_337_poly(0.5))
where exp = f32::from_bits(POWF_PROFILE_EXP_1_337_BITS).

The arm asserts three things must agree: powf_profile_exp_1_337_grid(base), powf_profile_exp_1_337_poly(base), and the public powf(base, exp). The first two still agree with each other (the 'grid k=0' assertion above it passes); it is the PUBLIC powf that has drifted 2 ULP away from the profile polynomial it is supposed to reproduce.

That points at the public powf path no longer routing base=0.5 through the profile fast path — e.g. a gate condition that stopped matching, or a kernel change upstream of it. NOT diagnosed here.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH FIRST, and do not skip it: which of the three values is correct against the HOST. The log2f pair in this same file was red because the ORACLE was wrong, not fl — so do not assume the polynomial is the truth just because it is the older code. Probe glibc powf(0.5, exp) and a long-double reference before changing anything.

Related context: the powf fused-kernel work and the 'math overfit' vein. A profile polynomial fitted to a narrow grid is exactly the shape that silently stops matching when the general path improves.

DONE = the arm green with the correct value established against the host, or the profile fast path deliberately retired with the arm updated to say so.
close_reason:
DONE at 780eae8d7. The last red in core --lib.

EVIDENCE:
  cargo test -p frankenlibc-core --lib powf
  test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 3220 filtered out
  cargo test -p frankenlibc-core --lib
  test result: ok. 3222 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
  cargo test -p frankenlibc-abi --test math_abi_test
  test result: ok. 118 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
core --lib was 3219 passed / 3 failed when this vein started; it is now fully green.

I FOLLOWED THIS BEAD'S OWN INSTRUCTION not to assume the polynomial was the truth, and it mattered — the polynomial was the wrong one. Probed the host first:
  base=0.5, exp=0x3fab22d1 (1.337)
    glibc powf                bits = 1053469677
    powl() long double -> f32 bits = 1053469677   (correctly rounded)
    fl public powf            bits = 1053469677
    fl profile polynomial     bits = 1053469675   <-- 2 ULP out

CAUSE: the arm asserted powf(base, exp) == powf_profile_exp_1_337_poly(base). That is false BY DESIGN. powf routes normal bases through the fused ARM/glibc __ieee754_powf kernel, and that kernel's own comment in the source states it supersedes 'the exponent-1.337 grid below (same domain, but bit-exact to glibc and faster)', leaving the profile path only for the residual subnormal-base / overflow cases the fused guard rejects. The supersession was deliberate and documented; the test was never updated to match, so it sat red asserting fl must reproduce a path it had outgrown.

FIX: the public-powf check now compares against the HOST. That is both the real parity contract and strictly STRONGER than what it replaced — fl is bit-exact to glibc across all 64 grid points, which the old assertion never established. 'grid == poly' is retained (internal consistency of the profile tables still matters for the residual domain), and the sha256 corpus is UNCHANGED because grid and poly were not touched. No golden was regenerated here.

PATTERN, now three for three in this file family: log2f_dyadic_profile_grid (bd-m63gy7), golden_log2f_dyadic_profile_corpus (bd-m63gy7) and this one were all red because the GATE named a worse reference than fl's own output — libm in two cases, an outgrown internal polynomial in the third. When a math gate goes red, probe the host before touching the implementation; in this file the implementation has been right every time.

FROM bd-aykfv1: core --lib is now clean. Remaining sweeps: frankenlibc-membrane --lib, the abi non-conformance_diff targets, and 25 abi conformance_diff rows.

title: Test sharpened generality mechanism on live glibc rpmatch
description: Pre-registered mechanism test. Sharp predicate: a FrankenLibC specialization advantage is predicted only when (a) the claimed semantic slice is closed and full-domain equivalence is proved, (b) live glibc still dispatches a data-driven interpreter on every call after all legitimate caching and hoisting, and (c) the deployed FrankenLibC path is already a bounded, allocation-free decision procedure rather than a second general interpreter. rpmatch predicts a win: live glibc 2.42 caches compiled C-locale YESEXPR and NOEXPR regex objects, but still performs nl_langinfo plus one cached regexec for yes and two cached regexec calls for no or invalid on every invocation; FrankenLibC classifies the first byte. Pre-registered shape: every conformant rpmatch case is faster than glibc, and glibc no and invalid absolute time exceeds yes because it traverses the second cached regex. Refute if any valid corrected-gate row has an effect CI at or above 1, or if that absolute-time shape fails. Contract: directly linked live glibc called in the same invocation, distinct object paths and SHA-256, A/A per arm, corrected median-bias plus 2x-null gate, exhaustive C-locale leading-byte conformance for rpmatch, CV telemetry only.
notes: Pre-measurement correction: live glibc rpmatch caches compiled YESEXPR and NOEXPR regexes; the irreducible per-call mechanism is one cached regexec for yes and two for no or invalid, not repeated compilation. Frozen harness SHA-256 9928af498322578fac44de2e056baba729ab7b5b4171fbbb9c6bc295964a7a3e, Build ID 9050c04203372ae9a46580d820905dae05b84791; strict FrankenLibC ABI SO SHA-256 84a5b1f84bc3fce22d6ccd1ac2135defe47dc1d7129a08218fb4d24d3fd5dc25; live glibc SHA-256 6791cc9bdc08295aafcfae01a7d66d788ee5577cbe94db00ace5f1ee04ef2b09. Harness passed deterministic remote check on hz1, 519/519 same-process live-glibc comparisons, and existing differential 200033/200033. Booked claim 6991 emitted no timing because preflight timed out after 298 samples with cpu38=100%; claim 7003 was released before invocation because an unrelated git fsck used 100% CPU97. Valid unchanged claim 7008 passed first-five-sample pre and post host guards on threadripperje. FL/glibc medians and CI95: yes 0.063574 [0.063547,0.063689], no 0.039717 [0.039576,0.039733], invalid 0.037402 [0.037279,0.037453], empty 0.030956 [0.030794,0.030989]. Every FL/FL and glibc/glibc null median was within 2%, every effect cleared twice the widest null distance, all four rows were FL_FASTER, and glibc no=66.639 ns plus invalid=59.050 ns both exceeded yes=38.151 ns. Prediction verdict CONFIRMED. Valid log SHA-256 d03e6a31c1b48f4e3b982ed721371cc26ade9da79bfc92c538c49781c579992a. No production optimization was attempted.
close_reason: Closed with a valid booked same-invocation result: the sharpened three-condition mechanism predicted rpmatch and was confirmed across four corrected-gate rows, with 519/519 live conformance, per-arm A/A, complete identity and host provenance, and no production optimization.

title: ffs-harness benches: ext4_casefold_key has no Criterion benchmark across UTF-8/ASCII/invalid input classes
description:
Finding (via /profiling-software-performance skill, NEW target): crates/ffs-harness/benches/ondisk_parse.rs has 22+ Criterion benchmarks covering ext4 inode/group_desc/dir_block/extent_tree/xattr/dx_root/dx_hash parsing and btrfs sys_chunk/leaf_items/internal_items/superblock/header/dev_item parsing, but NONE measure ext4_casefold_key throughput.

ext4_casefold_key is on the hot path for every directory lookup on a casefold-enabled ext4 filesystem (lookup_in_dir_block_casefold calls it once per target plus once per scanned entry). Its performance has 3 distinct code paths:
  1. Valid UTF-8 ASCII — fast path, only ASCII lowercase
  2. Valid UTF-8 with multi-codepoint expansion — sharp-s ß/ẞ -> 'ss', plus char.to_lowercase() chain
  3. Invalid UTF-8 — byte-by-byte ASCII fallback

A regression in any branch (e.g., introducing per-char allocation, switching from chars() to grapheme iteration) would silently slow every casefold dir lookup. Without a bench, such a regression has no signal until end users notice slowness on casefold filesystems.

The newly-added bd-6rsow proptest + bd-c7nid fuzz target establish correctness; this bench establishes the perf baseline. Pairs with bd-7pfh0 (dx_hash benches across 6 hash versions).

Acceptance: 4 Criterion benches in crates/ffs-harness/benches/ondisk_parse.rs:
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_ascii — pure ASCII input (typical filename)
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_mixed_utf8 — ASCII + sharp-s expansion
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_long_utf8 — long all-UTF-8 (no ASCII)
  * bench_ext4_casefold_key_invalid_utf8 — ASCII-fallback branch

Each uses black_box on the input; compares Criterion measurement noise floor against the 3 code paths.

title: PORT: funopen (BSD callback-based stdio over fopencookie)
description: BSD funopen(cookie, readfn, writefn, seekfn, closefn): callback-based custom stdio stream, the BSD analog of glibc fopencookie. Different conventions: read/write fns return int (truncated ssize_t), take int byte count; seek fn takes/returns fpos_t (off_t = i64) directly instead of via *offset pointer; mode is inferred from which callbacks are NULL (readfn+writefn=r+, readfn only=r, writefn only=w; both NULL=EINVAL). Implement by allocating a heap trampoline holding the BSD callbacks + original cookie, building a CookieIoFuncs that adapts each call (clamp size to INT_MAX, route seek through *offset), passing the trampoline pointer as the fopencookie cookie, and freeing the trampoline in the close trampoline regardless of whether user closefn succeeded.
